Schoolgirl told teacher 'Sir, I've been stabbed'

BBC News Thu, 08 Oct 2026 15:52:54 GMT

A schoolgirl who was stabbed by a masked fellow pupil at school described how she told a teacher "Sir, I've been stabbed" after the attack.

Police were called to Thorpe St Andrew School, near Norwich, on 11 March, following reports that a 15-year-old girl had been stabbed in the back.

The defendant, who is now 16 and cannot be named for legal reasons, has denied a charge of attempted murder, but has admitted possessing a kitchen knife without lawful authority and wounding with intent.

In a police interview played to the jury at King's Lynn Crown Court, the girl said she had been in "panic mode" and felt numb and weak.

Describing the attack, which took place in a corridor, she said she had seen a masked person dressed "head to toe in black, no school uniform whatsoever".

The boy did not say anything to her and she did not recognise him, she added.

She said she turned away and it "felt like he touched me on the shoulder, then it felt like he punched me".

She said she "didn't know I was stabbed at this point" but after turning into a classroom, "I went 'Sir, I've been stabbed.'"

The girl said the school lockdown bell sounded and staff gave first aid.

Of the incident itself, she said that once she had opened the door, "I felt sharp pain shooting through my back, I went like that and it was blood all over my hands".

She said in the interview, carried out days after the incident: "I don't think it's hit me properly yet.

"It's just a bit of a shock."

Stephen Rose KC, for the defence, asked the girl, who gave evidence in court, whether she had had any issues with the boy. She said she had not.

She wiped tears from her eyes and asked for a break during her evidence.

Another female pupil at the school, who witnessed the attack, said in a video-recorded police interview that the boy "came up behind [the girl] and just stabbed her in the back near her shoulder".

She said she "didn't think he realised I was there until after he did it" and that she ran off and told a teacher.

Asked at what point she had first seen the knife, she said: "As he raised it."

The court has already been told that the defendant had written notes saying he hated women.

One note, which prosecutors said was found by police pinned to the wall of his bedroom, said: "My barren world... Hello. To all readers out there in the UK and perhaps even the world. If you're reading this, I am either dead or in custody.

"I imagine the police will be the first to read this and seize it as evidence, so I will make something very clear. I made this decision to do so on my own."

Another note read: "Am I evil for that? Probably. Am I an incel? A misogynist? No. I just have good judgement."

Christopher Paxton KC, in opening the prosecution case, said: "We, the prosecution, say his intention is made plain not just by those moments of the stabbing, but made plain by his notes and his obsession with killing and being fuelled by hatred."

The trial continues.

Birmingham Airport announces £2bn expansion

BBC News Thu, 08 Oct 2026 15:01:15 GMT

Birmingham Airport has announced a £2bn expansion plan which bosses say could more than double passenger numbers and create thousands of jobs.

The draft plan, a spokesperson said, sets out the use of existing runway capacity alongside "significantly enhanced" passenger facilities over the next 15 years.

Unveiling an eight-week public consultation, chief executive Nick Barton said the scheme aims to ensure the airport was "ready for the future" but needed a "fair and stable taxation environment".

Transport secretary Heidi Alexander said the government was "backing our aviation sector to continue growing, right across the country".

In 2025, the airport said it had seen a record year with more than 13 million passengers travelling through it. Bosses want to see this rise by more than double, up to 30 million a year.

Airport chiefs said the proposals set out a "clear commitment" to continue serving the region and create more than 50,000 jobs, including 3,800 at the airport site.

They added that they wanted to make sure the growth was "delivered responsibly and sustainably" for the people living closes to the site.

The first stage of development could start in 2027, with significant investments in areas such as baggage and terminal facilities, additional aircraft stands and improvements in surface access.

Hundreds of passengers were affected by issues with the airport's baggage system in August, with many left without their luggage.

People can give feedback on the plans online, by post or attend any of the 20 events, which start in Hampton on Arden on 16 October.

"The £2bn proposed investment is unprecedented at Birmingham Airport and will take our airport close to 30 million passengers," said Barton.

"This level of ambition sends a strong signal of support and confidence in our airport and wider region.

However, Barton added that the plan came at a time the airport was faced with increased running costs from wage bills, energy prices and taxation.

"Unless tax and regulatory environments are made more favourable and stable for major infrastructure investment, they [the plans] may not materialise," he said.

Alexander said the city's plan was a "massive boost" to the West Midlands, unlocking investment and "creating 50,000 well-paid local jobs to get people into employment".

Richard Parker, the Labour mayor of the West Midlands, also welcomed the "ambitious masterplan" which he said would improve international links and unlock vital backing for local businesses and supply chains.

"This consultation gives local people and business owners a chance to have their say and help shape the airport's expansion so that it brings lasting benefits for our communities," he said.

Cummins not worried about potential Khawaja revelations

BBC News Thu, 08 Oct 2026 14:38:18 GMT

Usman Khawaja (left) and Pat Cummins played 56 Tests together for Australia

Pat Cummins has spoken to Usman Khawaja about his former team-mate's upcoming autobiography, but the Australia captain said he has no concerns about potential sandpapergate revelations.

On Friday, Australia will begin their first Test series in South Africa since the ball-tampering scandal erupted in Cape Town in 2018.

At the time, captain Steve Smith, vice-captain David Warner and batter Cameron Bancroft were banned for their part in the plot.

Since then, the four Australia bowlers who played in that match, including Cummins, have denied they had any prior knowledge of the plan to cheat.

The quartet, who released a joint statement about the episode in 2021, are once again set to be united in the first Test against South Africa in Durban.

Khawaja played in all four Tests in 2018 and retired from international cricket in January. His autobiography will be released in November.

"Uz gave me a buzz a few weeks back that he is releasing a book," said Cummins. "He didn't go into too much detail, just basically gave me the heads-up that he is doing a book and, as always, no worries.

"Tell your story. It's fine. It's obviously a long time ago and all the investigations, everything was done back then and we answered every question a million times.

"It was dealt with then and all I can say is that as a group, we have moved on and we are very happy with the last eight to nine years how we have been as a group and evolved and obviously my focus is on captaining the cricket team."

At the time of the ball-tampering controversy, Smith explained it was devised by the "leadership group" of the Australian team on the third day of the third Test in Cape Town. Bancroft was caught rubbing sandpaper on the ball the same day.

While Smith, Warner and Bancroft – all batters – were punished, there was never an explanation of how bowlers Cummins, Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon did not notice a change in the state of the ball.

In a 2021 interview with the Guardian, Bancroft was asked if the bowlers knew and replied: "It's pretty probably self-explanatory."

How an 'absolute fluke' exposed sandpapergate scandal

Test cricket's biggest scandals - your results revealed

Days after Bancroft's interview was published, Cummins, Starc, Hazlewood and Lyon released their statement which said: "We feel compelled to put the key facts on the record again.

"We did not know a foreign substance was taken onto the field to alter the condition of the ball until we saw the images on the big screen at Newlands.

"And to those who, despite the absence of evidence, insist that 'we must have known' about the use of a foreign substance simply because we are bowlers, we say this: The umpires during that Test match, Nigel Llong and Richard Illingworth, both very respected and experienced umpires, inspected the ball after the images surfaced on the TV coverage and did not change it because there was no sign of damage.

"We respectfully request an end to the rumour-mongering and innuendo. It has gone on too long and it is time to move on."

Earlier this week, left-arm seamer Starc referenced the scandal when he said: "What's left to come out after eight years?"

And, speaking on Thursday, Cummins said the episode was "a long time ago".

"It's nothing new," the 33-year-old told ABC. "We've spoken about it a little bit. If the crowd gets rowdy or whatever, if someone needs an extra helping hand, we're around.

"To be honest, it's so long ago and we, as a group, move on from things pretty quickly. It hasn't taken up too much of our time."

The trip to South Africa is the first in a year of high-profile away series for Australia. After what appears to be a stern challenge against New Zealand in their home summer, Cummins' men then travel to India and defend the Ashes in England next year.

With all-rounder Cameron Green ruled out because of injury, the tourists are likely to choose between Cooper Connolly and Nic Maddinson for a place in the middle order.

On a Durban pitch expected to turn, South Africa have included two spinners – Keshav Maharaj and Simon Harmer - in their XI.

Russell to take further grid penalty this season

BBC News Thu, 08 Oct 2026 13:48:17 GMT

George Russell is 84 points behind Mercedes team-mate Kimi Antonelli in the drivers' championship

George Russell says he will be taking a further grid penalty this season in addition to the one he has been hit with for this weekend's Singapore Grand Prix.

The Briton will start Sunday's race from the back of the grid because he needs to fit a new engine which takes him beyond his permitted number for the season.

But he says that he will have to take another new engine, as soon as a planned upgrade is ready, to get him to the end of the season.

Russell said: "You get (a limit of) four engines a season, so six races on each, and we have seven races to the end. So I will be taking another penalty, so yeah it's pretty relentless at the moment."

Russell's engine failure in Malaysia scuppered Mercedes' previous plan for him to last out with his older engine until the upgrade was ready, most likely for the next race, the United States Grand Prix in Austin.

F1 heat hazard declared for fourth time this season

Russell to start from back of Singapore grid after penalty

"I knew I was going to have a penalty," Russell said. "The plan was always to go in Austin, and obviously Singapore is the second hardest track to overtake on on the calendars. So you would never choose to do it (here).

"But we have no engines because of all of the various failures, so there was no engine I could have reverted to from earlier in the season. With the failure I had to take it.

"We don't have the (upgrade) this weekend, and because there are seven races remaining, you can either choose to roll the dice and hope it lasts for seven races, but also suffer a performance offset (as the engine degrades), or just accept I'll be taking another penalty."

Antonelli will also likely have another back-of-the-grid penalty when the upgraded engine is introduced, following his previous one at the Italian Grand Prix, which he won from 19th on the grid.

Russell will also be reverting to an older specification car in Singapore this weekend.

Mercedes introduced an aerodynamic upgrade in Malaysia last weekend, but it did not give the car the performance uplift expected.

So in an attempt to prove whether that was because of idiosyncrasies to do with the Sepang track or a problem with the upgrade itself, Mercedes is splitting the specification of their cars.

Russell will drive the specification with which he won in Azerbaijan, the week before Malaysia, while Antonelli will run the new spec.

Russell said: "I actually asked a question already on Friday in Sepang. At the end of the day it's the car I'm reverting to is a car that was on pole by 0.8secs and Kimi won the race before, so it's important to remember the context. It's not like reverting back to a launch car.

"Given the circumstances of the grid penalty as well, it just seemed like a no-brainer. For me, unfortunately we're not going to be fighting for a podium this weekend, it's exceptionally unlikely, so it's more important for us to try and understand, was Malaysia a one-off or was it the upgrade?"

Singapore Grand Prix

9-11 October

Live commentary on BBC Radio 5 Sports Extra; live text updates on BBC Sport website and app

Russell's retirement in Malaysia, along with Antonelli finishing second to Red Bull's Max Verstappen, meant the Italian's lead in the drivers' championship has extended to 84 points.

Both Mercedes drivers have suffered reliability problems this year but Russell believes his season has been disproportionately affected by factors outside his control.

"I've probably had more failures this year than I've had in the three seasons put together, and of course it's tough to take," he said.

"If I'm being 100% fair with myself, as I've said before, the performance this season hasn't been strong enough, and it probably would have affected me more if I'd have still been in the fight.

"But obviously the pressure and the momentum, every setback has an impact on that momentum.

"Since the start of the year (an engine failure) in Canada was the big one, and then, you know, the drive-through penalty in Monaco. The loss at the weekend has basically compromised two weekends for me.

"Two races, Silverstone and Spa, with the PU issues we had (involving a loss of performance from the engine), it's been pretty incredible how things have panned out this year, but I think just focus on what you can control."

Three sisters who drowned in sea off Brighton took own lives, inquest finds

BBC News Thu, 08 Oct 2026 13:11:01 GMT

Three sisters who drowned in the sea off Brighton took their own lives, a coroner has ruled.

Jane Adetoro, 36, Christina Walters, 32, and Rebecca Walters, 31, had been living "very secluded lives" following the death of their mother, who drowned in 2010, senior coroner Penelope Schofield said.

On 11 May, the women - who had all been living together in Greenford, London - visited an area of Birmingham close to where their mother died before travelling the next day to Brighton beach, where they drowned in adverse sea conditions in the early hours of 13 May. The coroner said they could not swim.

Their father Joseph Jacobsen said it was heartbreaking to lose "all three of my precious daughters".

He was among family members who followed proceedings via video link.

In an emotional statement read out on his behalf, he said he watched his daughters grow from little girls to beautiful, intelligent women "with a special place in my heart".

He said: "There are no words that can adequately express the pain of losing a child.

"To lose all three of my precious daughters is a heartbreak beyond anything I could ever have imagined."

He could not understand why his daughters' lives ended so suddenly, and hoped they were reunited with their mother "in God's eternal care", he added.

The coroner told the court: "These three sisters lived very secluded lives, they were incredibly private, we don't know why they took this course of action or indeed why they chose to do it in Brighton.

"It is not for the court to speculate and sadly these reasons may never be known."

The hearing was told the sisters left their home in London and arrived in Brighton together by taxi at 22:21 BST on 12 May.

The Uber driver had noted the lack of conversation during their journey.

The three appeared to pace the seafront in the darkness, with CCTV sightings of them at different points along Brighton's east beach. They were last seen alive at 02:42 on 13 May.

Police searched Christina's laptop and found 227 references to water and 179 references to suicide.

The coroner said Christina had been experiencing anxiety and depression since the death of her mother.

Rebecca's medical records showed "nothing of note" and Jane was not registered with a doctor, Det Ch Insp Mark Cullimore told the court.

A previous inquest into their mother's death had found her cause of death was drowning.

Postmortem tests revealed toxicology results for all three sisters were negative for drugs and alcohol. There was no evidence to suggest they had been subject to violence.

Ms Adetoro was brought to shore by an RNLI crew and declared dead at the scene on the morning of 13 May, the inquest heard.

Christina Walters, who worked in accountancy, was recovered from the sea by an RNLI lifeboat, and Rebecca Walters, who worked in HR, was washed on to the shore of Brighton beach. They were also pronounced dead that morning by paramedics.

Royal Navy sailor in court accused of preparing to spy for Russia

BBC News Thu, 08 Oct 2026 12:44:03 GMT

A junior Royal Navy sailor accused of preparing to spy for Russia has appeared in court.

Able Seaman Teddy Young, who specialised in warfare intelligence, allegedly retained UK defence and intelligence material that he had access to and made preparations to disclose sensitive information, a court was told.

The 24-year-old appeared at Westminster Magistrates' Court on Thursday after being charged under the National Security Act.

The BBC understands that the allegations against Young include translating a message into Russian and looking for a web portal that invited people to submit information to Russia.

Wearing a police-issue grey sweatshirt, Young spoke in court to confirm his name, date of birth and his address in Clapham, near Bedford.

He is formally charged with engaging in conduct in preparation for disclosing protected information, and obtaining, copying, recording or retaining protected information, intending the conduct to benefit a foreign power.

The charges cover a period between 26 November 2024 and 21 May 2025.

"The allegation is that while serving as a Royal Navy warfare intelligence rating with high level security clearance and intelligence-system access, Teddy Stanley Greenidge Young accessed and retained sensitive UK defence and intelligence material and engaged in activity consistent with preparing to pass protected information to a foreign power," the Crown Prosecution Service told the court in a written summary of the allegations.

Police said the alleged offences were not related to the recent RAF Fairford incident that resulted in a number of arrests after suspicious activity was reported near the base.

In total, seven men have been arrested and later released on bail in connection with the incident, which is being investigated by counter-terror police.

Young was arrested at his home address in Bedfordshire on Tuesday.

He is the first member of the armed forces to be charged under the new National Security Act 2023.

Cdr Helen Flanagan, head of Counter Terrorism Policing London, said: "These are very serious charges against a serving member of the armed forces.

"We have worked extremely closely with relevant operational colleagues within the Ministry of Defence as our investigation has progressed to ensure appropriate measures could be taken to mitigate any potential risks linked to this matter."

A Royal Navy spokesperson confirmed a service member had been charged and added: "As legal proceedings are ongoing, it would be inappropriate to comment further at this stage."

Judge Annabel Pilling remanded Young in custody. He will next appear at the Old Bailey on 16 October.

'Ominous signs' of winter pressures as NHS waiting list grows

BBC News Thu, 08 Oct 2026 12:42:56 GMT

There are "ominous signs" that winter pressures are already affecting the NHS in England, according to senior health leaders.

The warning comes as new data reveals the waiting list for routine hospital treatment in England rose for the second month in a row.

An estimated 7.37 million treatments were waiting to be carried out at the end of August, relating to 6.24 million patients.

The numbers are the highest since October 2025 and have raised questions over whether the NHS will meet a government target of treating 92% of patients within 18 weeks by 2029.

The rise in waiting lists comes despite the NHS in England delivering what were described as record levels of planned, elective care over the summer, while demand for services also reached its highest level ever.

A record 4.7 million planned treatments, procedures and appointments occurred across June, July and August – more than in any previous summer.

But both A&Es and ambulance services also saw a record number of patients for the month of September.

NHS England's national medical director, Professor Frankie Swords, warned that despite the progress delivered by frontline teams, winter pressure was already building.

"Staff are already seeing the ominous early signs of pressure, with more patients coming to A&E with flu and other respiratory viruses than usual for this time of year, and unfortunately many people are still waiting longer than we would like them to," she said.

The NHS Alliance, which represents hospitals, says the government in England is not going to achieve its manifesto promise of hitting the 18-week hospital waiting time target by the end of the parliament in 2029.

That 18-week target hasn't been hit for a decade.

A separate analysis by the Health Foundation think-tank said progress on cutting waiting times had stalled over the past year, with referrals on to the waiting list rising at a much quicker rate than the number of patients being treated.

Sir Ciarán Devane, the chief executive of the NHS Alliance which represents NHS trusts, said: "The NHS continues to respond to record demand for care, but the relentless growth in demand for services is putting NHS staff under real pressure."

Francesca Cavallaro, of the Health Foundation, said: "Thanks to the hard work of staff, the NHS has made progress in bringing down waiting times, but a rise in referrals mean that the service is having to run faster just to stand still and the prospects of meeting the government's pledge are receding.

"Andy Burnham's government have yet to set out whether they will give the 18-week target the same priority as it had under Keir Starmer, but our analysis shows the pledge is becoming increasingly hard to deliver."

There will be concern too that the pressures of a long, hot summer have merged almost seamlessly into the pressures associated with the winter months.

More patients, including children, have been arriving at A&E departments with flu and other respiratory viruses.

The number of patients seen within four hours in A&Es last month fell to 74.4%, down from 75.0% in August.

The number of people waiting more than 12 hours in A&E departments from a decision to admit to actually being admitted – what is known as "corridor care" – stood at 50,582 in September, up from 44,951 in August.

That has alarmed Dr Vicky Price, president of the Society for Acute Medicine.

"A 13% year-on-year rise in 12-hour emergency department waits as winter approaches should set alarm bells ringing.

"More than 50,000 patients waited over 12 hours from the decision to admit to admission in September - 1,686 people every day.

"These are not just numbers.

"They represent vulnerable people who are waiting far too long for a bed and staff trying to deliver safe care in overcrowded emergency departments."

The government says the 18-week mark could still be achieved, saying it was investing in NHS buildings and equipment to make services more productive.

It also pointed to disruption to care that was caused by the strikes by resident doctors, a dispute which has now been settled.

But the strain that services are feeling in September, before winter has even really got going, will be a cause for concern among NHS leaders and their political bosses alike.

Gaten Matarazzo on life after Stranger Things as he makes West End debut

BBC News Thu, 08 Oct 2026 11:09:34 GMT

Keeping your balance on a revolving stage probably sounds easy when you compare it with battling demogorgons, but Gaten Matarazzo points out one big difference.

You don't get the luxury of "thirty takes" to get it right in front of a live audience.

The former Stranger Things star's currently playing Mark in a modern revival of rock musical Rent on London's West End.

He tells BBC Newsbeat that having a proper schedule and remembering to stay hydrated makes a "refreshing change" from filming the Netflix smash-hit that made him famous.

Matarazzo shot to fame in 2016 as endearing super-geek Dustin Henderson - a role he calls "the greatest honour of his life".

The saga finally concluded last December after five seasons, and there's been interest in what the show's cast will do next.

"It's something you do inevitably step away from," says Matarazzo

"We finished filming in 2024 - there's no more show to film."

"I still love what I do very much, I want to keep on doing it."

Casting big names from TV and film in theatre shows is a growing trend, and one that sometimes provokes accusations of cashing in.

But Matarazzo has plenty of stage experience, having performed on Broadway when he was a child.

He says the time commitment involved meant it was impossible to "blend both worlds".

"My favourite part of theatre specifically is the schedule," he says.

"Going to bed at the same time and waking up at the same time.

"I've always thrived under a schedule and when I don't have one I feel insane."

In Rent, Matarazzo plays struggling film-maker Mark, who chronicles and narrates the lives of his friends.

It has been 30 years since the show first opened off-Broadway in New York, but the actor says there are "certain songs that weirdly resonate now".

"What You Own, which feels like a reflection on information overload, is incredibly relevant," he says.

"That's really fun to sing in context of today."

When it was first performed, Rent shone a light on young friends and artists living in late 1980s and early 1990s New York during the HIV/Aids crisis.

It was considered groundbreaking at the time for tackling social taboos and centering stories of LGBT people.

Writer Jonathan Larson died suddenly the night before its premiere.

Matarazzo's co-star, Travis Ross, who plays Roger, says the show's themes still "ring true" today.

The 25-year-old says having Rent tends to attract people who "care so deeply" about the show's message, resulting in a connection between actors and the audience.

He calls it a "really beautiful community-driven piece of art".

Both Ross and Matarazzo are keen to acknowledge their fellow cast members and point out Rent is "an ensemble" piece.

"In the same way we get our moments to tell the story there's also ten other people who get their moments to tell the story as well," says Ross.

Many of those in the audience will be there to watch Matarazzo, and he says he's determined to get the role right.

"I'm on stage for the majority of the show and singing the whole time," he says.

"It's not anything that's particularly high or out of my range, it's actually a part that I think fits nicely in my pocket.

"But it's just so much singing, and making sure I'm doing it correctly is essential," he says.

Matarazzo also plans to embrace his return to the stage.

"Once we're in the run it will be great," he says.

"I just always love the opportunity to start and finish a character arc and story in real time.

"You don't get an opportunity to do that when you're filming."

Speaking of which - if he ever got the call to go back to Hawkins and step into Dustin's shoes, would he take the chance?

"If that happens, that's great, and if not, that's completely fine.

"I've loved doing the show so much, it's literally the greatest honour of my life."

Rent is at The Tom Stoppard Theatre, London. Gaten Matarazzo is booked to perform until 10 January.

Actor Simon Pegg reveals ADHD diagnosis: 'It's just who I am'

BBC News Thu, 08 Oct 2026 09:35:30 GMT

Shaun of the Dead and Mission: Impossible films star Simon Pegg has revealed he has been diagnosed with ADHD, which he said "confirmed a lot of stuff that I'd been wrestling with".

Pegg, 56, who also co-created and starred in films Hot Fuzz, The World's End, and TV series Spaced, said "there was a lot of build-up and suspicion, and it just took a while actually to get there."

Speaking on the podcast I'm ADHD! No You're Not on Thursday, he said he pursued a diagnosis as he "just wanted to know".

ADHD symptoms focus on three main areas - inattention, hyperactivity and impulsivity plus lack of concentration.

Although many people may feel like they have some similar symptoms, genetics play an important role in ADHD and a full diagnosis is given to those who are negatively affected on a daily basis.

Pegg said he had previously been putting his symptoms down to "just character fault".

The actor and writer also spoke about his mental health, including having clinical depression and struggling to control his drinking, which he said he initially thought had "caused" his diagnosis.

"I felt like it was something that had come on in later life because I wasn't a naughty child.

"I've had bouts of depression in my adult life since 18 and I thought maybe it had come on with that.

"Maybe over the years with therapy and medication - whatever - I've been treating the symptoms and not the cause of why I feel that way."

Pegg said: "I did feel different in a way I might not be able to put my finger on. Maybe everybody feels that way.

"I just assumed ADHD kids were kind of chaotic and difficult and didn't pay attention in school," he added.

"But there were other things that I did do as a kid – fidget or whatever – that made me think, 'Oh no, maybe I've had this longer than I thought'."

Pegg said his wife has been supportive and is "dealing with it as if I'd been diagnosed ages ago", adding: "It's just who I am, and it's just things that I do.

"She makes allowances for forgetfulness and and lack of concentration."

Pegg had previously said he felt his poor driving was down to undiagnosed ADHD.

The star, who has had several speeding convictions, told LBC last year that he felt an ADHD diagnosis would help explain his poor concentration when it comes to driving.

He reversed into a post while on holiday in Greece, which prompted him to look up the symptoms of ADHD.

"I looked up on the phone 'Do people with ADHD get into more car accidents than people who don't have it' and the answer was yes.

"And it's because of a lack of focus and ability to kind of totally focus.

"And that was the final straw that broke my ADHD camel's back. I need to speak to a psychiatrist and find out for sure if I have this thing."

Other celebrities who have been diagnosed with ADHD in adulthood include comedian and actor Johnny Vegas, comic and presenter Sue Perkins, presenters Ant McPartlin and Richard Bacon, comedian Rory Bremner and model Erin O'Connor.

ADHD is described by the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (Nice) as "a behavioural syndrome characterised by hyperactivity, impulsivity, and inattention".

The NHS estimates that about 2.5 million people in England have ADHD, including those without a formal diagnosis.

Diagnosis rates of ADHD and autism have soared, and waiting lists for assessments on the NHS in England are at record levels, with lists even closing in some areas due to the huge demand.

Research from University College London suggests nearly a 20-fold increase in the number of UK adults diagnosed with ADHD between 2000 and 2018.

Despite these rises in diagnosis and referrals, some studies suggest ADHD is actually underdiagnosed.

In June, the Lancet Regional Health Europe journal published research suggesting that while around 1.2% of adults in England had an ADHD diagnosis, international prevalence data estimates it affects 3-5% of people. The authors of the study said this indicates it could still be under-diagnosed, particularly in older age groups.

Clubs fear political interference in Man City appeal

BBC News Thu, 08 Oct 2026 09:16:56 GMT

Andy Burnham was mayor of Greater Manchester from 2017 until he became prime minister this summer

Some Premier League clubs were so "astonished" by comments made by Andy Burnham - appearing to downplay the verdict against Manchester City - that they are now "concerned" about political interference in the appeal process, sources have told BBC Sport.

Senior club figures say they were shocked when they heard the prime minister tell the BBC he would be "really concerned" if Manchester City's owners decide to sell up after the club were found guilty of Premier League financial rule breaches.

They have questioned what his comments to the BBC were designed to achieve, and said it had put the Independent Football Regulator in a difficult position.

Burnham is under increasing pressure surrounding his relationship with the club's Abu Dhabi ownership during his time as mayor of Greater Manchester.

Such is the level of scrutiny that Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has demanded that No 10 release all details of meetings between the prime minister and senior figures at the club.

Asked to respond to the BBC's story on Thursday, Burnham said: "No I haven't downplayed the seriousness of the findings. They are findings that need to be considered with great care and seriousness and then the process that considers them needs to be fully independent.

"I said that last week and I will repeat it again. I think it's incumbent on everybody now to let the process run its course.

"I was asked a question about wider investment. I think it's important to separate the football issues from wider investment. The football issues have to be looked at fully and that is without question."

Despite clarification from Downing Street that Burnham's view is that no-one is "above the rules", his comments sparked unease among some senior Labour figures who fear his initial comments have had major cut-through with voters.

This video can not be played

PM: 'Football issues must be separated from wider investment' in City case

Your Manchester City Questions Answered By The Experts

Senior club sources have said they found the comments "absolutely bizarre", and that it was "at best naive and at worst quite manipulative, and that is not a good look".

A different source said it was "clumsy", while another said they were surprised that the prime minister had "misspoken".

The entire process involving the charges against Manchester City is independent of the Premier League.

An independent commission held a 42-day hearing in 2024 which led to the verdict announced last month, with a sanctions hearing still to come.

A separate independent appeal board will hear City's appeal. The club continues to deny any wrongdoing.

However, when asked about potential interference in the process off the back of Burnham's comments, one senior club source said: "Everyone would have a degree of concern. How much would depend on how much you read into that comment.

"I think everyone is concerned. Because no-one is stupid around the table. We understand the geopolitics as well. We understand the investment they have made in our country. I don't think anyone could doubt that or criticise that. But this is different, this is sport, this is our national game."

Another club source, however, said the degree of scrutiny on Burnham now means they think any interference would be impossible.

This video can not be played

The politics of Manchester City's guilty verdict

This is a sensitive area for the prime minister. Manchester City's dominance of English football has overlapped in large part both with a period of economic growth for the city of Manchester, and with Burnham's nine years as mayor from 2017 until earlier this year.

As mayor, Burnham championed investment from the Gulf as a way of growing Manchester's economy, a strategy which was initially pursued by the city's leaders before Burnham became the inaugural elected mayor of the Greater Manchester Combined Authority.

Regardless of Burnham's past career, there are additional sensitivities which would be true under other prime ministers too.

The UK as a whole is eager to trade with the UAE, and the country is an important diplomatic ally in the region at a time of turmoil and war.

When the guilty verdicts were announced, Richard Masters, the Premier League's chief executive, said the club had "systematically broke Premier League rules for nearly a decade".

PM: I’d be ‘really concerned’ if Man City owners sell club

Burnham's comments came in an interview with the BBC's political editor Chris Mason the next day.

When asked about 'Brand Manchester' taking a hit, the Prime Minister drew a parallel with a previous Premier League case with Everton, saying he still held the view "firmly" that they "weren't fairly treated".

Everton were deducted 10 points, later reduced to six on appeal, by an independent commission for breaching Premier League financial rules.

Asked if he was concerned that Manchester City's owners would now sell the club, Burnham said: "I would be really concerned to lose them.

"They've been such a huge partner in the building of modern Manchester and obviously the building of Manchester City into the global force that it is.

"I do actually thank the City Football Group and the wider ownership for the money that they didn't just put into the Etihad [Stadium] and the campus around it but also into the city," he added.

Burnham's comments provoked strong criticism.

The following day, a No 10 spokesperson sought to clarify the comments, saying: "As the prime minister made clear, the initial judgement is serious and there can't be any suggestion that anyone is above the rules. He also stressed that it is an ongoing independent process. It is essential that it is allowed to run its course and the outcome respected.

"If wrongdoing is established, those responsible should face the appropriate consequences."

However, this statement was amended following further criticism over the use of the word "if" - which was changed to "wherever".

The Premier League is viewed by governments of different political stripes as one of the country's major cultural exports, so ministers are eager for the row not to cause lasting damage to its brand.

Additionally, being a football fan is a core part of Burnham's political persona.

He is an Everton season ticket holder and, prior to becoming prime minister, he spoke of hoping to continue sitting in his usual seat at Hill Dickinson Stadium - but this has not been possible because of security concerns, as was the case for Sir Keir Starmer, his Arsenal-supporting predecessor.

Last month Burnham floated the prospect of lifting the ban on football fans drinking in the stands, though it was quickly clarified that this is not in fact government policy.

Could Christa Pike face execution again and by what method?

BBC News Thu, 08 Oct 2026 09:14:51 GMT

The botched execution of Tennessee death row inmate Christa Pike has thrust Tennessee's criminal justice system into uncharted territory.

A week after receiving two lethal doses of the drug pentobarbital, she is said to be walking and talking again in limited ways.

Tennessee Governor Bill Lee has ordered an independent investigation and suspended all executions for the rest of the year.

The fate of Pike, who has been on death row for 30 years for murdering Colleen Slemmer, now lies in a mysterious grey area.

At a hearing on Wednesday, an attorney for Tennessee said the decision on scheduling a new execution date was up to the state's supreme court.

But Pike's lawyers are seeking to have her death sentence commuted to life in prison without parole. Lee, who has commutation powers, has not indicated what the state will do.

Slemmer was murdered by both Pike and Pike's then-boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, who was not an adult at the time so was spared the death penalty and remains in prison.

The BBC spoke to multiple experts to explore what could happen next.

The Tennessee Department of Correction could attempt to execute Pike again by lethal injection, but the state would very likely run into legal challenges based on constitutional protections against cruel and unusual punishment.

"For the state to attempt to execute her again using the same methodology, they would have severe legal hurdles," Tennessee-based defence attorney Stephen Ross Johnson said.

Johnson said Tennessee had botched two executions in one year - it also failed to kill Tony Carruthers in May - which could give lawyers the grounds to argue broadly against the constitutionality of the state’s lethal injection protocol.

Pike's lawyers could also argue a lethal injection is what Johnson called "unconstitutional as applied", meaning it is cruel and unusual specifically for Pike, due to her medical condition.

Pike's lawyers had warned before the execution attempt that she has small veins and thrombocytosis, a blood-clotting condition that would complicate the procedure.

Her medical condition combined with the state's botched execution would make it difficult for Tennessee to present a convincing legal argument for attempting lethal injection again, Johnson said.

Johnson, president-elect of the National Association of Criminal Defense Lawyers, could see the state attempting an execution by a different method.

This would require "additional legal hoops", including approval from the governor's office and potentially the state legislature.

Since Pike's survival, political leaders in Tennessee have called for moving her death sentence forward through other means.

Senator Marsha Blackburn, the Republican candidate for governor in next month's election, said: "Bring back the electric chair."

Congressman Tim Burchett, posted on social media that he's already filed a bill to "bring back hanging".

Tennessee could be allowed to use the electric chair because Pike committed the murder in 1995 before the state changed its execution laws.

She would need to waive her right to lethal injection in writing, which means it would have to be her decision, Vanderbilt University law professor Chris Slobogin said.

Given that Pike's exact medical state is unknown, Slobogin said there was a scenario in which the state could be blocked from attempting to execute her again, regardless of method.

It was also considered cruel and unusual punishment to execute someone who is mentally incapable of understanding why it is happening, he explained.

Historically this has applied to prisoners with dementia or psychosis, but experts have said there is a chance that Pike has suffered brain damage.

There is a precedent of states finding a different method to execute a death-row inmate.

In 2024, Alabama executed a convicted murderer using a different method to the one that was originally planned. Kenneth Eugene Smith was put to death using nitrogen gas - having failed with its initial plan of lethal injection.

Tennessee is taking a long pause on carrying out capital punishment.

Only one person was due to be executed this year after Pike, which the governor has now postponed. Earlier, in May, the Carruthers execution was suspended by a year after state officials could not find a vein to administer the lethal injection - meaning that he has a year-long reprieve.

It will therefore probably take a while for any movement in Pike's case.

"At a minimum there's going to be some significant delay while this issue is studied by the state", defence attorney Johnson said, adding Pike's health would also need to be studied.

Slobogin suspects the governor will commute her sentence, especially if missteps by state officials are uncovered in the investigation he has ordered.

"If the investigation, in any way, shape, or form, suggests that the protocol was not followed, or is hard to carry out, that might be the easy way for him to go, given the complications with the execution and all the bad press," he said.

There is legal precedent for a death sentence to be commuted due to a botched execution combined with an inmate's poor medical state.

The execution of Alabama death-row prisoner Doyle Hamm was called off after more than two hours of attempts to establish an IV line failed.

The state gave up on executing him following a legal settlement that related, in part, to his health. He later died of natural causes.

'I was blamed for my baby's death, now NHS needs to change'

BBC News Thu, 08 Oct 2026 05:42:43 GMT

When Poppy Russell died shortly after birth, her parents were left bereft.

What followed made matters harder to bear - her mother was blamed for the death.

An inquest would later conclude that Poppy's death was preventable.

But instead of walking away from the trust that had failed them, Neil and Katie Russell are now working with it to bring compassionate care back into the NHS.

"We could have very easily been consumed by hate and anger and rage at what happened – and those feelings are still there," said Katie.

"But if no change comes from what happened to Poppy, then what's the point?"

Poppy Russell died in April 2021 at the Princess Royal Hospital in Telford.

She was just 12 hours old.

During her pregnancy her mother told midwives that she had tokophobia, a fear of natural birth and wanted a caesarean section.

Katie said she was repeatedly told however that she "couldn't just ask for a c-section."

When she went into labour, Katie was induced and then "we were left in a room for long periods of time where I had no care," she explained.

"Finally, when we got into the labour suite, I wasn't monitored appropriately and they missed signs that Poppy was in distress."

In a bitter irony, Poppy had to be delivered by emergency caesarean.

By then however, she had developed a hypoxic brain injury and died later the same day.

An inquest into her death found that had Poppy been born an hour earlier, she would have survived.

The Shrewsbury and Telford NHS Trust (SaTH), which ran the hospital, subsequently blamed Katie for her daughter's death.

They said she had refused foetal monitoring; the inquest concluded that was untrue.

"The trust left us in an appalling position," said Neil Russell.

"Not only were they found to have neglected our care, but in the months and years following, we uncovered that members of staff had tried to cover it up.

“Losing your daughter is one thing, but then to find that there was a cavalcade of lies was almost as bad."

Following the inquest in 2023 the trust said: "We recognise there were failings in the care we provided and we are truly sorry."

It said the death of any baby was a "tragedy" and promised improvements to maternity services.

In March 2024, the couple had a meeting with the trust to discuss all that had happened.

From the discussions, Neil and Katie decided they needed to honour Poppy.

"The first conversations about Poppy's Promise were about being human," said Neil, 45.

"It spun from our treatment, and not being treated like human beings."

Poppy's Promise is based on four care principles:

"It's seeing the person, not the diagnosis. It's someone coming into a room holding your hand, someone acknowledging the fact that this is difficult for you," said Katie.

Even in the midst of her poor care at the time of her daughter's death, Katie, 41, vividly remembers one midwife who showed some compassion.

"She came in and said, 'how are you doing? I just want to hug you.'

"She sat with me and she cried with me and she said, 'this should never have happened,' and that will always stay with me because it's exactly what I needed at that point."

At the time of Poppy's death, SaTH was in the middle of a large maternity inquiry.

The review found that 201 babies and nine mothers might have survived with better care.

As part of its improvement programme, the trust is now rolling out Poppy's Promise to all 8,000 staff.

As well as reminding its existing employees of the principles of compassionate care, the trust has embedded a question about it into its recruitment processes.

The most important part of the training is "to remind me that we are here on a woman's journey, they are not on our journey," says Tasha Simmons, a midwifery ward manager at the trust.

"They don't need to know that I've answered three emergency bells this morning, that's not important to them.

"What's important is I'm fully present with them to support them in their experience, with kindness and compassion."

No-one starts a shift intending to provide care that is lacking in compassion.

The problem, say staff, is the pressure they are under - from the sheer number of people in Accident and Emergency to the complexity of many of the patients in hospital.

Remembering to treat each person with kindness in those circumstances can be a challenge, said Dr Adrian Marsh, an emergency medicine consultant at the Princess Royal Hospital.

There is a "high risk of emotional and compassion fatigue. Day in, day out we have a significant amount of competing demands," he said.

"But there's been some research done that actually demonstrates if people are treated with compassion and empathy, they have less complications, [their] outcomes are better."

Poppy's parents say that other NHS organisations and some universities have been in touch to explore whether they can incorporate Poppy's Promise into their teaching programme.

Their goal is to embed compassionate care throughout the health service.

Faster than F1: The extreme motorsport where women keep winning

BBC News Thu, 08 Oct 2026 05:41:20 GMT

Faster than F1: The extreme motorsport where women keep winning

Like "being shot out of a cannon" is the closest comparison that driver Susanne Callin can come up with for the extreme motorsport she competes in.

She is a two-time European champion in Top Fuel drag racing - often described as the fastest sport on the planet.

Races begin with a bone-shaking roar, as the world's fastest-accelerating cars leave the starting line, flames bursting out of their exhaust pipes.

The cars surge to more than 300mph (483km/h) in races that last just four seconds, with drivers experiencing more g-force than an astronaut launching into space.

It is the only elite class of motorsport where women frequently beat men to major titles.

Women have won seven out of the past nine European Championships, while, until recently, female US driver Brittany Force held the world speed record in the sport. In comparison, it is 50 years since a woman even competed in a Formula 1 Grand Prix race.

Women account for about 10% of participants across motorsport, and just 4% of elite drivers, according to campaign group More Than Equal. However, they made up 20% of the drivers competing in this year's US and European Top Fuel seasons.

So why is this high-velocity motorsport bucking the trend?

Top Fuel drivers experience more g-force than an astronaut launching into space

More Than Equal has described drag racing as "the most gender-equal motorsport in the world". Top Fuel is its most extreme form, named in reference to the powerful nitromethane fuel the cars run on.

Races take place on a straight track, just 1,000 feet (305 metres) long. Usually, two cars race each other. The intense g-force hits in the first second of the race, as the cars go from stationary to 100mph, with a second gut punch following as the clutch fully engages about half-way through.

It can look terrifying. The adrenalin rush is "extremely addictive", Swedish driver Callin, aged 43, tells BBC Global Women. Concern over the risks "is always there" she says, but "the safety really does work". Drivers are highly protected and safety precautions have been boosted further after fatal crashes in nitromethane-fuelled cars in 2004 and 2008, with races reduced in length.

Callin says she has never felt underestimated or treated badly for being a woman in drag racing

Even just watching from the stands is a visceral experience, with vibrations shaking your body and the ground. Spectators are advised to wear ear defenders - the noise is comparable in decibels to standing next to a fighter jet taking off.

The highest official speed ever reached in a Top Fuel drag race is over 346mph, compared to 231mph in a Formula 1 Grand Prix. Brakes alone cannot slow the cars fast enough, so parachutes are deployed from the car's rear at the finish. The abrupt halt is "like someone kicking you in the chest", says Callin. "You lose your breath."

Top Fuel drivers need lightning-fast reactions and the physical endurance to withstand the intense forces. Precision driving skills are crucial as constant tiny adjustments are needed to keep the car on track.

"It has to be instant reactions with everything," says Callin. "By the time you've thought about it, it's too late… You really have to be one with the car."

And drivers need sheer guts. As Callin's rival and friend, 32-year-old Swiss driver Jndia Erbacher, jokingly tells the BBC - it takes "balls".

Top Fuel cars surge from zero to 100mph in less than a second

Callin clinched her second successive European Top Fuel title in September at the Santa Pod drag strip near Northampton. It is the fourth year in a row that a female driver has won the title. Meanwhile in the US, the record-setting Brittany Force won the US championship - run by the National Hot Rod Association (NHRA) - in both 2017 and 2022.

Drag racing is "highly unusual" among motorsports, says Fran Longstaff, chief innovation officer at More Than Equal, which supports and campaigns for women in motorsports.

Seeing women competing and winning in the sport has become "normalised rather than treated as exceptional", she says, including with "sustained success" in Top Fuel.

Research she co-led into why drag racing leads the way for equality in motorsport did not identify physical or biological factors, she says.

Instead, she points to a "continuous stream of visible female role models", as well as the sport's "accessible grassroots structure, junior programmes, open pits and family-oriented, collaborative culture".

Shirley Muldowney was the first woman to win the NHRA Top Fuel Championship

In drag racing, points out Callin, women started winning major races "decades and decades ago".

The best known is Shirley Muldowney, dubbed the "first lady" of drag racing. The first woman to gain a Top Fuel licence, Muldowney won the NHRA championship in 1977 and went on to become the first driver to win three titles, with further wins in 1980 and 1982.

She had to battle to be allowed to compete at high levels, and faced hostility at times from other competitors and fans, but is now lauded for her perseverance.

When the BBC spent time with Callin in the pits between races at Santa Pod, surrounded by roaring engines and the smell of burning rubber, she signed autographs for fans - young and old, male and female - as her team prepared her car.

"I never feel I've been underestimated or treated badly for being a woman - never," Callin says.

This is in stark contrast to the experiences of women seeking to enter Formula 1. Young female drivers have spoken about being deliberately pushed off karting tracks by male competitors, and facing sexist comments in person or online.

More Than Equal's research also highlights a close-knit, family-oriented, collaborative culture in drag racing.

Like many top drag racers, Callin is from a racing family. She has been involved since childhood, following in the footsteps of her father and uncle, who both raced competitively.

Similarly, Erbacher's father Urs was a three-time European Top Fuel champion. And Brittany Force is the daughter of John Force, who holds 16 NHRA drag racing titles.

The 300mph motorsport where women keep winning

Watch the full documentary following Susanne Callin as she bids to retain her European Top Fuel title

Female drivers have also shown that success is possible in Top Fuel in the years after having children.

Callin took a break for more than a decade to raise her daughter and stepdaughters. It was when she returned, aged 35, that her career really began to flourish. Similarly, Finnish driver Anita Mäkelä has won the European championship four times – three of them after a six-year break focusing on her children and running her family's chicken farm.

For Callin, racing is ingrained in family life.

Her dad is still part of her team. Her husband, Keith Bartlett - sometimes referred to as the "godfather" of UK drag racing - runs Santa Pod Raceway. Two of their daughters were driving junior dragsters at 80mph before they were old enough to sit a standard driving test. The youngest, Jacqueline, is now 19 and racing in adult classes.

The culture is collaborative, despite fierce competition - evident at last year's championship, when Erbacher offered Callin spare parts after her car was damaged.

"We hate each other at the starting line, but we love each other at the finish line," Erbacher says.

Erbacher jokes that it takes "balls" to compete in Top Fuel

Asked about safety, both Callin and Erbacher talk about having "respect" for the car and the risks.

Over the years, strict procedures and regulations in Top Fuel have evolved to improve safety.

Drivers wear fire-resistant suits and sit in highly protected cockpits. Even after dramatic accidents, drivers in many cases escape relatively unscathed. This includes Callin, who has had two major crashes, suffering a concussion and a bruised collar bone, but no lasting injuries.

She says serious accidents are a "very small percentage". Even so, she is still not sure she would be comfortable if her daughter wanted to race in Top Fuel, with its extreme speeds.

Erbacher says her father initially refused to let her race, but relented when she declared she would do it with or without his help. He now manages her team.

More Than Equal also points out that the financial barriers to participating in drag racing are lower than for some other motorsports.

It takes millions of pounds to reach Formula 1, requiring high levels of sponsorship. Elite drag racing is also expensive, but not on the same scale. At the lowest levels, accessible racing events called "track days" take place, where participants can turn up and drive their own ordinary cars.

In the biggest Top Fuel championships, drivers race for themselves and earn points based on how they perform against their competitors. The European championship consists of four events - two in the UK, and one each in Germany and Sweden - in which each driver takes part in six races. Prize funds are limited, mostly serving as a contribution towards costs.

The US championship is on a larger scale, with 20 events across the country. The NHRA has not published a breakdown of prize money, but according to drag racing website Competition Plus, there is $500,000 (£378,000) for the 2026 winner, and significant pots for winners of individual events throughout the season.

Indian driver Uvashri Kannadasan Balajeyanthi first raced in a modified Skoda Octavia

The US, Europe and Australia have all seen female drag racing champions, but in other parts of the world, the sport is less well established, Top Fuel is rare and the picture is more varied. Individual women are breaking barriers across a range of different motorsports, and in some countries female drivers are carving out space in drag racing.

Women have begun to make an impact in Brazil's popular drag racing scene, including Fabiola Dal Bo who has held a category record in recent years. A team in South Africa hosts all-female drag races, while the popular reality TV show The Fastest in Arabic has raised the profile of women racers in the Middle East.

In India, 35-year-old Uvashri Kannadasan Balajeyanthi has clinched victories over male rivals in India's major drag racing series, Valley Run, with wins across three different categories in events from 2022 to 2024.

Known as Octy Girl in reference to the modified Skoda Octavia she first raced in, she tells the BBC she has "mixed feelings" when her achievements are met with surprise: "Why do they have to get shocked? Anyone can drive, right?" But she adds "sometimes I feel proud… I'm breaking the barrier of being in a male-dominated sport".

Back in Europe, however, Callin says being a woman on the drag strip is "super-normal".

She describes winning the European championship two years running as a "massive achievement". And she is already looking towards her next goal: becoming the first person, male or female, to win the title three years in a row.

This is part of the Global Women series from the BBC World Service, sharing untold and important stories from around the globe

The world’s oldest known land animal – Jonathan the giant tortoise – has had his genome probed for the first time. This has revealed that parts of his genome to do with mitochondrial function are as efficient as those of a 5-year-old member of his species. Efficient mitochondria may give his DNA repair systems more energy to fight off the effects of ageing, enabling him to live to an estimated age of 194.

What’s more, some of his genetic changes seem similar to those of supercentenarians. “This study adds to the body of evidence that the mechanisms of ageing may be conserved across species,” says Stephen Clark at the Kallel Foundation, a non-profit organisation focused on interventions to extend human healthspan, in Nashville, Tennessee.

There are only a few anti-ageing supplements that actually work

Jonathan, an Aldabra giant tortoise (Aldabrachelys gigantea), and Napoleon Bonaparte are the two most famous residents of St Helena island in the South Atlantic. Napoleon arrived at the remote British territory after he was exiled in 1815, while Jonathan is thought to have been shipped there, possibly from Aldabra Atoll, in 1882. Jonathan arrived as a fully grown adult that was thought to already have half a century under his belt, putting him at around 194 years old today.

Advertisement

The researchers calculated that Aldabra tortoises have an average lifespan of around 80 years, but they can live much longer. To understand the mechanisms behind Jonathan’s extraordinary longevity, Clark and his colleagues have studied his genome.

“I firmly believe we can learn about the global mechanisms of ageing by looking at the exceptions,” says Manel Esteller at the Josep Carreras Leukaemia Research Institute in Barcelona, Spain, who led a study into a 117-year-old woman, once officially the world’s oldest person.

Free newsletter

Esteller and his team found that the woman had exceptionally efficient mitochondrial function, which led Clark and his colleagues to suspect Jonathan similarly had “very efficient and very young” mitochondria, says Clark.

They had to study his genome via saliva samples and cheek swabs. This was because St Helena authorities refused their requests to draw Jonathan’s blood, given his fame and the risk of infection.

This was a major limitation, because it meant the researchers were unable to isolate large pieces of DNA, which are more stable in blood. Instead, they had to assemble fragments from Jonathan’s saliva, where DNA is more prone to bacterial contamination, and fill in the gaps using DNA from another Aldabra tortoise.

Once they had made the best possible composite of his genome, they compared it to the DNA of four other Aldabra tortoises. “We found 287 genes that had changes in them that were unique to him,” says Clark.

A clinical trial to reverse age-related vision conditions using stem cell treatment could finally deliver on the promise of a major discovery in ageing and regeneration made 20 years ago, says columnist Graham Lawton

Of these genes, 41 are though to be functionally significant, meaning they actively contribute to an organism’s biology, survival and regulation. A dozen of them were also found in ageing databases of the genes of other long-lived animal species.

Parts of Jonathan’s genome to do with mitochondrial function were as young as a 5-year-old Aldabra, says Clark. “This, in turn, has helped him manage the effects of ageing by giving the DNA repair systems more energy from the mitochondria to fight off the effects of ageing.”

Kousuke Hashimoto at the University of Osaka, Japan, says the work is “fascinating”, but notes that Jonathan’s genome was compared against that of only a few other tortoises, which may have unique genetic changes themselves.

Neanderthal Europe was as much a wooden age as a stone age

New Scientist October 07, 2026

Wooden tools, weapons, building materials and domestic items discovered in a Spanish cave challenge the assumption that Neanderthals’ technological life was based primarily on stone.

The finds have given an unprecedented glimpse into everyday Neanderthal life and are a rare opportunity to recover part of their missing world, says Josep Vallverdú at the Catalan Institute of Human Paleoecology and Social Evolution in Spain.

“Neanderthal technology was not only made of stone; it was also made of wood,” he says.

Advertisement

Before the Stone Age: Were the first tools made from plants not rocks?

“The archaeological record gives us a very biased picture of prehistoric technology. We see the stone because it survives, while a huge part of their material culture has simply disappeared.”

Vallverdú and his colleagues have now completed the first systematic review of nearly 600 wooden objects, all between 40,000 and 62,000 years old.

The finds have been collected by generations of archaeologists since the 1980s, excavated at a rock shelter site called Abric Romaní near Barcelona. They include timber imprints in travertine – a rock rich in calcium carbonate that precipitates out of water in certain environments. The rock preserves the patterns of the wood grain even though the timber long ago rotted away. Charred artefacts and actual preserved timber have also been found at the site.

See Alice Roberts at New Scientist Live 2026

The researchers’ first job was to determine exactly which pieces were used or made by Neanderthals. Only 13 qualified. Most of the remainder consist of trunks, branches, twigs, roots and firewood accumulations.

Maria Gema Chacón, also at the Catalan Institute, says the researchers have been surprised at how “complex Neanderthal woodworking could be, and how well they understood the properties of wood”, with the two spears being especially striking to her.

“Producing long, straight shafts and shaping them deliberately into pointed weapons required planning, skill and careful selection of the raw material,” says Chacón.

The technological behaviours preserved at Abric Romaní are comparable to those documented for Homo sapiens, she says.

Stick shaped by ancient humans is the oldest known wooden tool

Other finds included a mysterious wooden tripod, as well as timber trays reminiscent, in terms of likely utility, of the coolamons traditionally used by Indigenous Australians to carry food and water. Some of the wooden objects appear to be structural poles.

But perhaps the item that has most surprised the team is a “club-like” object that has no precedent from any other palaeolithic site.

Palmira Saladié, also at the Catalan Institute, says the club-like object is “not simply a stick with a thicker end”.

“There is a distinct narrow handle and an enlarged, asymmetrical head, giving the object a much more complex and deliberate form,” she says. “This particular configuration is what we have not been able to find a convincing parallel for in the prehistoric record.”

Vallverdú says the site shows that wood was a normal and important part of Neanderthals’ everyday life.

Why early humans radically changed their toolkits 200,000 years ago

“We have evidence of woodworking across many archaeological levels and over thousands of years, and the objects are associated with very different activities: hunting, domestic tasks, containers and the organisation of living spaces,” he says.

Chris Stringer at the Natural History Museum in London says the archaeological record of wooden artefacts has been “severely constrained” by the generally poor preservation of organic materials.

The finds reveal a much wider technological repertoire of woodworking skills, he says.

An analysis of ancient human artefacts finds that the container, a simple but critical tool, may have originated 500,000 years ago. Columnist Michael Marshall explores how slings, ostrich eggs and wooden trays helped our ancestors survive

“This is of course evidence from only one site, in one area, and one time span,” says Stringer, “so it’s just the tip of the iceberg in terms of a whole and mostly hidden technology that ran in parallel with the much better-known stone tools of the Palaeolithic.”

“Wood, plant fibres, hides, bone and other organic materials must have been central to daily life, but they normally disappear,” says Mariana Nabais, also at the Catalan Institute. “So when a site like Abric Romaní preserves wooden imprints and charred wooden objects, it is almost like suddenly seeing the missing half of the toolkit.”

Naoki Morimoto at Kyoto University in Japan describes the wooden objects as “remarkable”.

“Preserved organic materials are truly rare, and they reveal a ‘hidden’ aspect of Neanderthals that we have been missing,” says Morimoto.

The big unanswered question about Russia’s ‘plague’ death

New Scientist October 08, 2026

The recent death of a lab worker at a plague research institute sparked fears of another pandemic. But on 7 October, Russia’s health watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor, said it was ending precautionary measures and that most of the nearly 200 people put under quarantine have been released, after tests found no dangerous pathogens.

Was this all much ado about nothing? After all, we still don’t know what caused the pneumonia that killed the lab worker, nor, if it was plague, how she became infected. And the most pressing question of all: why did Russia respond so dramatically to her death? The measures taken went beyond what would be expected for a case of plague. There are two broad possibilities: conspiracy or colossal screw-up.

Nearly 200 people isolated after lab worker in Russia dies of plague

What we know is that Daria Shipilova, a 28-year-old lab worker at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia, died of pneumonia on 2 October, three days after being admitted to a local hospital. A “DN Shipilova” is an author on an abstract from a conference earlier this year about testing plague strains for antibiotic resistance, suggesting Shipilova worked directly with the plague bacterium Yersinia pestis.

Advertisement

After her death, nearly 200 people who might have had contact with her were placed in quarantine. Around 60 employees at the institute were reportedly locked in for days, and Federal Security Service officers escorted ambulances carrying those quarantined. The head of Rospotrebnadzor, Anna Popova, is said to have travelled to Irkutsk – a 6-hour flight from Moscow – on 2 October for an emergency meeting about “a particularly dangerous infection”, and some local companies imposed mask mandates.

The thing is, there are many plague cases around the world each year and they don’t trigger this kind of response. This is because basic hygiene measures can prevent the spread of the bacterium, while prompt treatment with antibiotics can stop people who might have been infected from developing any symptoms.

DNA evidence shows that plague bacteria devastated a community in Siberia more than 5000 years ago, challenging the idea that there were no major disease outbreaks before the advent of farming and large settlements

For instance, in 2025, a young man in Arizona died of pneumonic plague – where Y. pestis infects the lungs – acquired from sick cats. The 46 people he had potentially been in contact with were given a seven-day course of antibiotics, in line with guidelines from the World Health Organization. End of story.

So why did Russia quarantine all contacts? One explanation is that health officials knew Shipilova was exposed to something more dangerous than a natural strain of Y. pestis.

“Physical lockdown indicates it cannot be controlled with prophylactic antibiotics, implying engineered pan-resistance or that it isn’t plague at all,” biologist Kevin Esvelt at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology posted on social media. The response “clearly indicates that Russia believes an epidemic is possible – and that the responsible agent is likely a pandemic weapon or otherwise embarrassing for the government”.

Free newsletter

Esvelt created the first artificial gene drive capable of wiping out an entire species, and has since pivoted to preventing bioterrorism. He may well be right. There are certainly good reasons to suspect a cover-up.

We know that the Soviet Union had a massive bioweapons programme that included trying to make Y. pestis resistant to antibiotics (the “engineered pan-resistance” Esvelt mentioned), and it had a long history of denying related accidents. For instance, in 1979, at least 68 people died after the accidental release of anthrax from a bioweapons facility in the city of Sverdlovsk. The Soviet Union claimed the deaths were caused by food poisoning.

What’s more, a 2006 paper by Raymond Zilinskas at the Center for Nonproliferation Studies in California says the Irkutsk institute was involved in bioweapon research, though this was only “a small portion” of its activities. Bioweapons research has continued in Russia and probably expanded recently, though there is no evidence the Irkutsk institute is still involved.

Plague, leprosy, smallpox and other diseases didn’t jump from animals to humans when we thought. Ancient DNA is revealing where they come from and how they changed history

The other explanation is a secondary screw-up: that the officials who imposed the quarantine measures didn’t know what killed Shipilova and leapt to the conclusion it was something nasty. It can take three days to test for Y. pestis, after all, so the results might not have been available on 2 October. Even if the results were known, officials might not have believed them, given Russia’s history of lying about such things.

Alternatively, maybe Shipilova had a strain of plague that could have been treated with antibiotics if they had been given early enough (all the strains that were tested in the abstract linked to her were susceptible to these drugs), but officials overreacted because they weren’t aware of the appropriate procedures.

What really happened may never be clear. After all, Russia doesn’t have a reputation for being trustworthy – so even if it tells the truth, we won’t know it.
