50 men’s autumn fashion updates for under £100 (mostly) – some are even free

The Guardian Thu, 08 Oct 2026 17:00:25 GMT

Guardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more.

Oversized coats, relaxed-fit trousers and secondhand jumpers that will last for years to come … here’s how to build an effortlessly cool autumn wardrobe on a budget

The best men’s shirts for every occasion

It’s time to pack away your weekly rotation of T-shirts and shorts and start thinking about layers.

As always, there’s no shortage of inspiration for your autumn look. The menswear shows displayed their usual styling tricks: at Prada, the exaggerated shirt cuff became this season’s unlikely focal point. Then, there are the It boys, old and new, who are always good for a sartorial steer: comedian and actor Jack Innanen is the latest addition to the roster, though Brad Pitt’s 90s looks are just as current. And that’s all before you get to the colour palette: this year, bright colours can be thrown in among the traditional rich, earthy shades.

These 50 easy updates span style, grooming and the wider cultural stuff worth knowing as the leaves start to turn – and, besides a few investment pieces, they’re all less than £100.

Bright colours are in for autumn, but it’s still best to keep the look restrained. All you need to update your look is a couple of colourful T-shirts – say blue, red or green – to layer beneath shirts, coats and knitwear. For a steer in the right direction, check out Japanese designer Ssstein’s show.

Arket 170 GSM regular T-shirt

Though I’m always a fan of black, autumn is when you can switch it for brown because it has a softer, lived-in feel. It could be knitwear, trousers, outerwear or shirts; just stick to the richer, darker tones that look luxurious as opposed to toffee or caramel.

Abercrombie & Fitch baggy jeans

Autumn’s a good time to invest in outerwear because you can make the most of it throughout the colder months ahead – simply switch up what’s underneath as the weather gets cooler. As this is a long-term purchase, go for something you can see yourself wearing for years to come, like a big, oversized woollen overcoat. Take a look at Gant’s recent campaign with Theo James for style pointers.

Weekday double-breasted wool-blend coat

It’s time for trousers that feel cosy. It could be corduroy, flannel or wool; the key is to go for a relaxed fit that looks comfy rather than anything slim or constrained – something that would look at home next to an open fire with a book in hand.

Asos Design baggy corduroy trousers

Cos wool-blend wide-leg trousers

Need proof slogan tees are back? Look no further than Jack Innanen. The up-and-coming Adults star has been cycling through them, with phrases such as “are my lips moving?” and “horny”. The best place to get them is Idea – the rare books shop that moonlights in slogan merch, where you can find T-shirts that say everything from “Yoga Helps” to “Intern”.

Idea That Band You Like T-shirt

Plaids and flannels are trending this year, with checks seen everywhere from Ralph Lauren to Zegna and, of course, Burberry. Try not to go full-on lumberjack and instead keep the cut sharp: tucked into tailored trousers or layered under a blazer rather than paired with denim and boots.

Carhartt WIP Todrick checked flannel shirt

Thanks to Callum Turner – who has worn one everywhere from the red carpet to casual dinners out – the zip-up cardigan is the latest knitwear silhouette to add to your rotation. Turner has worn versions by Axel Arigato and John Smedley, but if you’d prefer something a little more accessibly priced, try the Danish high-street brand Selected.

Selected 100% cotton zip cardigan

Anyone who’s seen When Harry Met Sally will appreciate the appeal of a chunky Aran knit come autumn. Hand-knitted versions tend to be expensive, so Vinted is your best bet for a good, secondhand option.

A plain navy T-shirt is autumn’s answer to summer’s white tee. If the fabric’s premium and it fits properly, it’s a top that can elevate everything from jeans to tailored trousers. If you’re shopping luxury, Sunspel’s the spot, but Cos and Uniqlo are my top high-street options.

Uniqlo 100% Supima cotton T-shirt

While promoting The Dog Stars in London, Jacob Elordi wore the perfect transitional outfit: a lightweight windbreaker with a pair of wide-leg indigo jeans. For structure, look for untreated denim – a good-quality pair can develop its own patina; you’ll be wearing them for years.

Percival straight leg heritage denim jeans

Though hoodies are mostly relegated to the comfy drawer, some styles are appropriate to wear out and about. What you’re after is substantial fabric – natural, not synthetic – and smart shapes rather than anything too baggy. If you want to make it work for the office (at least, one with a more casual dress code), throw an oversized blazer on top. End is a great place to start, especially the retailer’s newly released own line.

End Worn Established hoodie

Running kit is increasingly crossing over into everyday fashion. The vibe is sportswear designed for day-to-day settings. Think 9-to-5k. Whether you actually make it to the run remains, as ever, optional.

Acid Running men’s long sleeve T-shirt

Ever since Burberry showed a leather bomber on Romeo Beckham this season, it’s a jacket I can’t stop thinking about. His was a rich plum shade with a fur-trimmed collar, but a more classic style will make a versatile investment piece for autumn. A loose fit is the key: you want some room through the shoulders and torso so it reads as expensive – although real leather costs more than synthetic, it can age well and last for years with proper care.

Zara regular-fit leather jacket

For more, read our guide on how to make your leather last a lifetime

Everyone from Dries van Noten to Tom Ford and Our Legacy sent fuzzy jumpers down the runway this season. If you’re buying mohair, look for pieces with ethical credentials – the Responsible Mohair Standard, for example. Or, for a more budget-friendly alternative, find something similar that’s made with synthetics, like this Topman jumper. Keep Kurt Cobain’s knitwear in mind while you’re shopping, and you can’t go far wrong.

Topman fluffy jumper

Bound Heaton gradient sweater

A long-sleeved T-shirt is one of the best layers you can own as the colder months close in: a base that works under anything, from casual shirts to jumpers, adding a pop of interest and extra warmth. A stripe or hit of colour peeking out at the cuff or collar works best.

H&M relaxed fit boxy long-sleeved T-shirt

If you buy one thing, make it cosy socks, whether in soft cashmere or grey marl merino. It’s a touch that makes your outfit feel completely autumnal – and it couldn’t be easier.

Pairs the merino set

Every time I’m out in London, I spot another guy wearing a sling bag – and it’s usually the best-dressed guy on the street. The style is similar to a crossbody, but with a more streamlined fit that sits diagonally across the body rather than hanging in one fixed spot. It looks easy and effortless – and, more importantly, big enough for all the essentials such as sunglasses, keys and a mini aftershave.

Cos module crossbody bag

Penny loafers are a year-round staple, but this is the best time for dark merlot red because, just like the wine, it gets along so easily with everything that’s in rotation at the moment, including rich navy and earthy green. Marks & Spencer, as always, has the classic nailed down.

M&S leather penny loafers

Dark sunglasses and autumn aren’t a good match – unless you’re Anna Wintour. Instead, go for a lighter tint that’s better suited to lower light levels. It could be brown, blue, yellow or orange. Theo James wears ones by Moscot – specifically the Miltzen frames with a yellow tint – but for a more affordable alternative, try Le Specs.

Le Specs Heart Throb

Ties have been rising in popularity for a while now and are showing no signs of slowing down. The trick is wearing them in a less formal way – with a casual-leaning shirt, without a blazer, under a hoodie. Go for something silk, striped and preppy-adjacent: vintage and charity shops are great places to look.

Vintage Christian Dior tie

Whatever boots you choose should last you for years to come, so it’s best to go with something classic and versatile. My preference? Chelsea boots. You can dress them up or down and they’ll never date.

Schuh Dice leather chelsea boots

Adidas has been head honcho in the trainer world for a few years, but it feels like the tide’s turning towards Nike thanks to the Moon Shoe. It’s a style from the brand’s archives brought back in collaboration with Jacquemus and has since made it into the mainline. The brown colourway is my top pick.

Nike Moon shoe OG

The It boys are wearing mini hoops – Drew Starkey, Colman Domingo, Paul Mescal. Michael Jordan and Brad Pitt wore this look in the 90s, so this wave could run. You’re looking for the kind of hoop that looks like you never take it out: minimal, low-key and a size that sits close to your lobe.

Serge Denimes silver huggie hoop

The men’s offering at jewellery brands can be full of dark gunmetal and chunky pieces that only really work if you’ve got measurements like Dwayne “the Rock” Johnson. But this season, it’s better if your pieces lean delicate: think thin chains, vintage bracelets and small signet rings. Don’t be afraid to shop in the women’s section – and always look for precious metals like sterling silver.

Mejuri oval link chain

after newsletter promotion

A baseball cap is always helpful: it protects from the sun, shields from the rain and helps retain warmth when it’s cold. This time of year calls for a weather-resistant finish, such as waxed cotton, or something warm like corduroy. Barbour’s Ashby hat has both.

Barbour Ashby cap

Autumn’s the perfect time to try clear glasses – the kind you’d expect a seasoned Oxford professor to wear with a neat blazer and corduroy trousers. Think something classic, rounded and tortoiseshell à la Matt Damon’s Mr Ripley. See it as an excuse to get your eyes tested; if you’re 20/20 it’s a bonus because you won’t have to pay for prescription lenses.

Jimmy Fairly the Cloud glasses

Though we’d all love a Rolex, dropping the equivalent of a house deposit on a watch isn’t feasible. If you like the Rolex Day-Date, Casio has a great alternative with a 40mm case, a classic stainless steel bracelet, and a similar day-and-date display. All for less than £60.

Casio MTP-1370D-1A1VEF

StockX’s August Big Facts report suggested the marketplace is betting on an incoming “skate boom” in clothing and footwear with brands such as Vans, whose sales on the platform rose 238% in the first half of 2026. So, consider it time to dust off your Old Skools – don’t worry, you can leave the board at home.

Vans Old Skool platform trainers

With cuffs in the fashion spotlight, what better time to upgrade your cufflinks? My favourites are all vintage and tend to cost way less than anything bought new – especially when you buy a job lot on eBay.

Vintage cufflinks

Call it the Labubu effect if you like, but the appetite for stacking your carabiner with charms has spread beyond the viral toy; at Charles Jeffrey Loverboy, for example, they were accessorised with keyrings. Whether you go for designer charms or antique keyrings picked up from eBay, clip a couple on to your carabiner and call it a day.

Cadillac black leather keyring

This is the time for warm notes such as sandalwood, leather, amber or vetiver – or, if you like something aromatic, look for spices like cardamom or clove. &Horace offers the perfect balance.

&Horace eau de parfum, 50ml

As we head towards winter, it’s worth reaching for more nourishing products, as cold air and central heating can strip moisture from your skin. A facial oil is one way to help combat the effects. My favourite is Aesop’s Damascan rose formula with camellia and rosehip oils. Blend a few drops with your moisturiser at night.

Aesop Damascan rose facial treatment, 25ml

Retinol can make your skin more sensitive to the sun, so you may have eased off during summer. If you did and you want to build it back into your routine, start gradually with a low-strength formula. Byoma’s retinol oil is ideal, and make sure you still don’t skip the SPF.

Byoma Sensitive retinol oil, 30ml

Winter skin can take a beating, so it’s important to replenish it with nourishing ingredients. As a bonus, fragrance tends to last longer on hydrated skin.

Hotel, Mike hand and body lotion, 350ml

While entry-level lip balms, such as Vaseline, will do the job, I find I have to reapply them much more regularly than formulas with active ingredients, such as Exist’s SpaceLip Origin, which contains a bioactive ingredient cultivated aboard the International Space Station. It’s the longest-lasting lip balm I’ve ever tried and comes in a suitably slick metal applicator.

Exist SpaceLip Origin, 3.2g

For more, read our guide to the best lip balms to hydrate and protect your lips

There’s never a bad time for eye patches, but some are better than others. My recent favourites are by Grown Alchemist. The brand says caffeine and ectoin can help brighten and hydrate the undereye area and reduce puffiness – and you get eight pairs for £20.

Grown Alchemist Hydra-Restore eye patches

Cold weather can be drying on hair, too, especially if you’ve got any substantial length, as the ends can be particularly vulnerable. Start with something light, as using a heavy formula on fresh hair is how you end up looking like you haven’t showered in a week.

Hair By Sam McKnight Light Nourish conditioner, 200ml

Hair By Sam McKnight Light Cleanse hair and scalp shampoo, 250ml

Using a gua sha or sculpting tool every morning can help your face look more defined by reducing puffiness and boosting circulation. FaceGym’s Multi-Sculpt has six edges for 10 different moves, all explained on the product page, but if you’re new to sculpting, you could start with a facial massage using just your hands. Apply an oil after cleansing to give your skin some slip so the tool (or your fingers) can glide rather than drag.

FaceGym Multi-Sculpt

Medicube’s PDRN pink collagen gel mask is a recent addition to my rotation that’s made a big difference. Niacinamide can help brighten your skin, while the cooling gel feels soothing. It also contains salmon-derived PDRN, an ingredient being studied for its potential in skin repair. The immediate glow afterwards is unrivalled.

Medicube PDRN pink collagen gel mask

Small cosmetic touches like curling your eyelashes, using a touch of concealer or a liquid blush can make a huge difference. An eyebrow gel is a good entry-level product that takes less than 30 seconds to apply, helps frame your face, and tidies away strays.

Refy Brow Sculpt, 8.5ml

Jacob Elordi might be the reigning menswear muse, but Adults star Innanen is the newcomer to watch. His style skews more playful than Elordi, but he’s just as fluent in the classics – think a green polo under a beige harrington or a striped breton with cream jeans.

If you’re familiar with my seasonal updates, you’ll know there’s always film homework; this autumn, it’s Good Will Hunting. From Matt Damon’s denim, T-shirts and jackets to Robin Williams’s tweedy academia-core, it’s full of inspiration for the months ahead.

Look past the crime-scene horror and this film is basically a masterclass in outerwear for the transitional months, from Morgan Freeman’s trench to Brad Pitt’s leather coat.

It might sound obvious, but the best way to get into the autumnal spirit is to go for a walk in the park. The changing leaves and moody grey skies should give you all the palette inspiration you need.

Where collars have been the main character on recent runways – worn skew-whiff, poking out of blazers and knitwear – autumn/winter 2026 is about cuffs. Look at Prada to see how it’s done: big, oversized shirting with the cuffs folded back over coats or jumpers to create a contrast pop of colour or stripe.

Try Brad Pitt’s Fight Club warrior cut on your next trip to the barber. It’s a choppy look that’s still got some length on the side: ask for two to three inches on top and a low taper cut with scissors – and a barber may use a razor blade to create extra texture. Style with a matte clay while it’s wet and follow with a salt spray before scrunching with your hands.

Add Tobias Wolff’s Old School to your book pile. Set at a New England boarding school in 1960-61, it has the tweed and atmosphere of Brideshead Revisited without the indulgence.

Old School by Tobias Wolff

Get into the new season zone by listening to Mk. gee, which mixes Bon Iver’s hazy melancholy with Frank Ocean’s slow-burn soul for a sound that’s moody but not miserable. A nice one to listen to on vinyl.

Mk. gee Two Star & the Dream Police vinyl

If you never got around to watching The Bear before it finished, now is the perfect time to binge. And not just for the high-intensity kitchen drama, but for the style: workwear jackets, gold chains and white T-shirts, including the now-famous 215 by German heritage label Merz b Schwanen, which the show helped turn into a cult favourite overnight.

Distressed T-shirts are on the up – Gallery Dept sells them with built-in holes and stains for hundreds of pounds (not a typo), but you can get the same look for free by digging out your old tees and roughing them up a little. For style cues, see Austin Butler, whose pieces seem to be genuine vintage rather than anything bought new.

Not since 9/11 has the UK faced such a security crisis – and threat to our liberal principles

The Guardian Thu, 08 Oct 2026 16:55:39 GMT

The combination of Iranian, Russian and Chinese aggression is deeply worrying: just how much more concerned about security should the country be?

The first time the window-rattling roar of a B-1 bomber woke me up this summer, I thought for one crazed second we were under attack. By the second time, I’d learned to recognise the sound of US planes taking off from their base at RAF Fairford for what it was: a reminder that although Britain wants no part in this war with Iran, we cannot quite escape the consequences.

We’ll feel them at the petrol pump, or in the supermarket this autumn, or in this winter’s heating bills. But living under the flight path adds an extra edge to it. The skies finally fell silent last week, but only because the bombers have been hastily summoned home after an alleged terrorist plot to attack Fairford, in which (according to the prime minister) there are “strong indications that Iran played a part”. If Fairford is now a target of war, did that threat disappear when the Americans did? Nobody knows.

Rural Oxfordshire is peppered with military bases, and after 15 years here I don’t bat an eyelid at helicopters practising low-flying drills, uniforms on the school run, or the stash of Day-Glo marshmallow cereal our local supermarket used to keep for homesick Americans. But the Fairford incident follows a serious security breach at RAF Brize Norton last year – and though this involved pro-Palestinian protesters rather than the Russians, it didn’t inspire confidence – and news this summer that the Manchester synagogue attacker had scoped out the security arrangements for the nearby Shrivenham defence academy. Bases nationwide are on high alert, with two Latvians arrested on Thursday on suspicion of trespass inside RAF Molesworth in Cambridgeshire, home to a Nato intelligence hub. At Fairford, it was a farmer who sounded the alarm, raising some difficult questions about how vigilant to be in small rural communities where strangers tend to stand out. I don’t want to become paranoid about every passing dog walker, or leap to ridiculous conclusions on hearing a Russian accent. But not since living in London in the aftermath of 9/11 have I felt more alert to anything seemingly out of the ordinary.

And that, of course, is how terrorism works. It’s not just the attacks themselves, but the fear and distrust they engender. For a while after the 7/7 bombings, people would change train carriages rather than stand next to some poor kid with a rucksack. At the height of the Troubles in Northern Ireland, Irish émigrés in Britain faced hostility. Sadly, it’s usually minorities who are singled out for suspicion or – in areas prone to far-right protests or antisemitic attacks – forced to wonder which of their neighbours might have joined the marches, or daubed graffiti on Jewish-owned shops. This time, there’s a particularly grim risk of a backlash against asylum seekers, with Reform pouncing on unproven reports that Tehran may be using small boat crossings to smuggle covert operatives into Britain. (For the record, those arrested and released on bail in connection with the alleged Fairford plot have British nationality. However, a Kuwaiti citizen recently convicted of a terror plot against the Israeli embassy and two Iranian nationals recently charged with allegedly plotting to target Jews in Manchester reportedly got here in dinghies.) Whatever the truth, Tehran must be delighted to see such destabilising ideas spread.

For the second time since 9/11, Britain faces a dilemma over how much of a securocracy – a country dominated by security concerns, whose citizens live at a pitch of constantly heightened anxiety – it should become in response to increasing threats. As Andy Burnham will remember, the “war on terror” forced the last Labour government, of which he was part, into a painful rolling back of civil liberties at home. Since the threat this time is less from an ideology than from three hostile nation states with domestic reach – namely Russia, Iran and China – the coming dilemmas may be more over the movement of technology, assets and people.

Historically, Britain’s economy has been a relatively open one, even after Brexit. We let Gulf states buy our football clubs, Russian oligarchs prop up the prime London real estate market, and Chinese money bail out our cash-strapped universities and build our power stations, despite concerns about espionage, censorship and interference in domestic politics. (Tom Tugendhat, the shadow foreign affairs minister and longstanding China hawk, revealed last week that he still gets letters from Beijing to the family home “that say, basically, ‘we know where you live’”.)

London’s tech startups, expanding faster than they could hire domestically, snapped up skilled young Russian coders understandably anxious to escape a country at war. We didn’t slap tariffs on cheap Chinese EVs when the EU did, despite concerns they could kill off domestic car manufacturing – or even that some of their software might still be controllable from China, because trade wars are generally bad for business. (Though the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, suggested recently that that debate is not entirely closed.)

We chose not to become a fortress because for a long time, the benefits of being open to the world felt worth the risks, but perhaps also as a statement of our values. But there is an increasingly live debate in Whitehall about whether, in retrospect, autocracies saw that openness as a weakness to exploit. If nothing else, they’re certainly weaponising it now: both Iran and Russia are throttling shipping routes in the strait of Hormuz and Black Sea respectively, with consequences for oil and food prices that are now ringing serious alarm bells within governments.

Though it’s not entirely clear yet what Burnham makes of all of this, there are early signs of attitudes hardening. The Cabinet Office recently summoned CEOs of critical infrastructure companies to brief them on the threat of Russian sabotage, while last week MI5 issued a rare public warning to academics against working with a Chinese organisation regarded as a front for espionage. The concrete barriers hurriedly going up around Fairford last week may be a harbinger of what is to come: a signal that as the world moves closer to a war footing, our relaxed way of life may have to change.

But there’s a difference between being vigilant and being paranoid, let alone xenophobic, and we are going to need to hold that line in months to come. No foreign national in the UK should ever be persecuted for the sins of their country of origin: there’s no going back to the dark days of 1939, when Jewish refugees fleeing Nazi Germany and Austria were shockingly interned in Britain as “enemy aliens”. New powers of surveillance should always come with new safeguards.

And this government should remember that if the “war on terror” taught us anything, it’s that security crises test liberal principles to breaking point. I just hope Burnham is ready for that.

Gaby Hinsliff is a Guardian columnist

Wiegman praises Toone’s attitude after late Lionesses recall for Greece playoff

The Guardian Thu, 08 Oct 2026 16:33:25 GMT

Manchester United midfielder left out of initial squad

First leg of World Cup playoff is on Friday in Crete

Sarina Wiegman heaped praise on Ella Toone for her positive reaction to being left out of England’s initial squad for their Women’s World Cup playoff against Greece, after recalling the Manchester United midfielder for Friday’s first leg in Heraklion, Crete.

An injury sustained by Lucy Bronze, described by Wiegman as “really small”, prompted the England right-back to return to Chelsea and Wiegman called up Toone, who travelled to Greece from Spain, where she had organised a training routine during the international window.

Toone has 69 caps and has scored 24 goals, including in the Euro 2022 final and 2023 World Cup semi-final, but Wiegman said when naming her squad that she had left out Toone and Chloe Kelly because “the levels weren’t what I expect from them on the pitch”. On Saturday, after starting Manchester United’s victory over Liverpool, Toone took ownership of things, telling the BBC: “It’s about me now. I’ve got to keep working hard and use it as fuel to come back even better.”

Wiegman, asked whether she had been impressed with Toone’s response, said: “Yes, very much. I think when I gave her the call, of course that was a hard call. But she took that straight away. Of course [she was] very disappointed, but the first thing she did [was say]: ‘OK, I’m going to get back, I’m going to do that.’ She has the support around her too.”

The head coach referenced Toone’s post-match comments when she said: “That answer in the game, also the way she spoke about it, I thought that was really good. And then getting everything ready to go to Spain instead, but go for training there, I think that really impressed me. Well done, I would say.”

That will be music to the ears of Toone, whose experience is also understood to have been a factor in Wiegman picking her rather than a replacement right-back. She could feature on Friday, when the European champions will hope to build a strong first-leg lead before Tuesday’s reverse fixture in Leicester.

To qualify for next summer’s finals in Brazil, England must overcome Greece and win another two-leg playoff, against Slovakia or Ukraine, in December.

(4-2-3-1) Hampton; Le Tissier, Morgan, Williamson, Greenwood; Stanway, Walsh; Mead, James, Hemp; Russo

Greece v England, Pankritio Stadium, Friday, 5.30pm BST

The draw for the World Cup will follow on 11 December and it would feel inconceivable for the 2023 runners-up to miss out. They are in the playoffs despite winning five of their six qualifiers in a group with Spain, the defending champions, who pipped England to top spot by virtue of their stronger head-to-head goal difference.

A better way to inspect and evaluate schools

The Guardian Thu, 08 Oct 2026 16:30:48 GMT

Gareth Jones and Richard Hooper draw on their experience as educators to offer alternatives to the Ofsted system that is not fit for purpose

The news that Ofsted inspections are to be overhauled again indicates that a fundamental rethink is required, rather than tinkering again with the grading system (England school inspections to be overhauled again after barrage of complaints, 2 October). As an educator with 30 years’ experience in international schools (21 years as head of two schools), I would suggest that when further changes are made, the first step should be to stop calling them “inspections”. The word implies an unfeeling, top-down procedure. While British curriculum international schools tend to use an Ofsted-style procedure, American international and international baccalaureate schools tend to use “evaluation” or “accreditation” procedures.

In these, the school evaluates its own performance against a set of standards. The people who work in the school, including students, plus parents and board members, spend a year discussing the school’s achievements and identifying areas for improvement. They submit their report to the agency, which then puts together a team who will visit the school. The team is made up of practising educators from other international schools. So the school is evaluated by fellow professionals, which is much less threatening than a team of inspectors. Their job is to decide whether the school has accurately evaluated its own performance.

My experience is that schools generally do an excellent job of self-evaluation, which means that the visitors can say: “Well done, you know your strengths and weaknesses, we can now offer our expertise in building on this report and helping you to move up to the next level.” The team visit is a positive, collegial experience whose aim is to validate the work that the school’s own staff has done. This contrasts with the seagull approach of an Ofsted visit – they fly in, make a lot of noise, disrupt everything and then take off, leaving a load of guano behind.

The sympathetic, supportive model of evaluation is already out there waiting to be adopted. Gareth JonesLondon

I have experienced four Ofsted inspections: as the chair of governors at a primary school, an early years group, head of a large adult learning service, and vice‑chair of governors at a further education college. Three received favourable judgments under the previous Ofsted framework; the fourth was rated “requires improvement”, severely affecting staff morale and mental wellbeing.

However courteous the inspectors, the methodology in all cases created considerable pressure and anxiety. The process sometimes resembled a police search: practices and records were scrutinised, staff questioned under suspicion and the final judgment delayed.

Educational institutions require rigorous inspection and poor practice must be addressed. But the current model appears to favour enforcement over constructive professional support. A more effective model would combine inspection with consultation. Inspectors would identify strengths and areas for improvement, followed by targeted support for a defined period. A shorter follow-up would assess progress. One has only to refer back to the more collaborative model adopted by the former Adult Learning Inspectorate to appreciate the difference.

This would retain rigour while reducing the punitive tone, and foster a more collegiate relationship between Ofsted and institutions. It would also require inspectors to offer remedies as well as judgments. Richard HooperPenistone, South Yorkshire

Legal rights must be retained for children with special educational needs

The Guardian Thu, 08 Oct 2026 16:30:39 GMT

Campaigners and Send parents including Chris Packham, Carrie Grant and Sally Phillips urge ministers to work with families and organisations to preserve individual provision and improve accountability in the system

The legal rights of children and young people with special educational needs and disabilities (Send) are still under threat. The government’s proposed Send and education otherwise than at school (Eotas) reforms would significantly reduce existing legal rights to enforceable education, health and care plans (EHCPs), parental choice of educational settings and independent routes of appeal.

We support the government’s ambitions for a more inclusive education system. Better teacher training, earlier identification of need, greater specialist expertise and a properly staffed workforce are all necessary. But none of these initiatives require children and families to surrender the legal protections they currently have.

The proposals impact everything from how children and young people qualify for statutory support, what can be written into EHCPs, who decides the provision delivered, where children and young people are educated, how families can challenge poor decisions, and whether children and young people who cannot attend school can secure suitable education elsewhere. The Children and Families Act 2014 places children and families at the centre of decision-making, and the current proposals reverse this.

This is not simply a technical change to Send law. When provision is unsuitable or unavailable, legal rights are often the mechanism through which families can secure a suitable education for their child. A promise that the system will work better cannot substitute for an enforceable right when it does not.

Lucy Powell was a member of the education select committee during its 2019 Send inquiry. The committee concluded that the 2014 reforms were the right ones if problems of implementation and funding were addressed, and specifically warned the government against responding to those problems by “weakening or watering down duties”. We therefore urge ministers to work with Send families and organisations to retain existing Send legal rights, preserve individual provision, improve accountability in the system, and retain meaningful independent routes of appeal.

A genuinely inclusive education system should reduce the number of families who need to enforce their rights. It should not reduce their rights when the system fails.

Campaigners led by Chris Packham urge prime minister to rethink Send overhaul

The Guardian Thu, 08 Oct 2026 16:30:23 GMT

Exclusive: Letter to government says changes will unfairly remove legal protections for children in England

Letter: Legal rights must be retained for children with Send

Campaigners are calling on Andy Burnham to abandon the core elements of the government’s overhaul of special educational needs provision in England, arguing they unfairly remove children’s legal protections.

A group of children, parents and experts, led by the broadcaster Chris Packham, have written a letter calling for the prime minister to gut the plans laid out under his predecessor Keir Starmer.

Starmer and Bridget Phillipson, the former education secretary, announced the sweeping changes this year, aiming to curb the increase in legally mandated education, health and care plans (EHCPs) and save money in the long term.

Now campaigners are hoping the change of prime minister and education secretary may bring a change of heart from the government – even though officials say it is unlikely.

In the letter, published in the Guardian, the campaigners say: “The legal rights of children and young people with special educational needs and disabilities (Send) are still under threat.

“The government’s proposed … reforms would significantly reduce existing legal rights to enforceable EHCPs, parental choice of educational settings and independent routes of appeal.”

They add: “We … urge ministers to work with Send families and organisations to retain existing Send legal rights, preserve individual provision, improve accountability in the system, and retain meaningful independent routes of appeal.”

The letter is signed by 36 people, including Packham, the actor Sally Phillips, the clinical psychologist Simon Baron-Cohen and the Guardian columnist John Harris.

The changes were announced in February after lengthy consultation by ministers with experts and Labour MPs.

Under the plans, instead of legally enforceable EHCPs, millions of pupils will be given individual support plans, which will be agreed between parents and schools but will not be subject to independent legal appeal.

These support plans will be administered by schools rather than local authorities, and parents who are unhappy with them will be asked to appeal to the school rather than being given recourse to an independent tribunal.

Schools will be given more resources to help support Send children, but the overall package is designed to curb the rapid escalation in costs under the current system, which has left councils in England facing a projected £6bn financial black hole in two years’ time.

However, the Guardian revealed on Thursday that the projected savings risk being undermined by a flood of new applications for EHCPs, as parents look to secure legal protections before the new system takes force.

The campaigners say they want significant changes to the proposals, including keeping the current threshold for EHCPs, allowing parents to appeal against decisions at a tribunal and scrapping the assessment system proposed for individual support plans.

Ministers are consulting on the measures and are expected to recommend some changes to Phillipson’s proposals.

However, those close to the process say Burnham and Lucy Powell, the new education secretary, are likely to adopt more minor modifications to reinforce legal protections rather than the wholesale changes called for by the campaign group.

A spokesperson for the Department for Education said: “We inherited a Send system under immense strain. Our once-in-a-generation reforms will change that.

“Legal duties on schools to identify and support children’s needs are getting stronger, not weaker. And we will never leave parents without a route to challenge decisions about their child’s support.

“We have consulted on our proposals to make sure we get these reforms right, and in the meantime we’re investing in schools to improve inclusion.”

To reduce reoffending, prisoners need better support after release

The Guardian Thu, 08 Oct 2026 16:30:22 GMT

Pavan Dhaliwal responds to an article on the early release of prisoners. Plus a letter from a prison officer who works in a men’s open prison

Regarding your article (Prisoners thank Andy Burnham as they leave jail in first wave of early releases, 1 October), Michael Bogle’s story should make us ask a bigger question than whether prisoners are being released too soon.

Bogle, 38, has 100 convictions and has been jailed five times. He told the Guardian that he turned to shoplifting after becoming homeless, in order to eat. On leaving prison, he said that there was a risk he would shoplift again.

At Revolving Doors, we work on systems change with people whose lives follow precisely this pattern – repeated contact with the criminal justice system, often for relatively low-level offences, driven by combinations of homelessness, addiction, poor mental health, poverty and trauma.

We can keep arresting, prosecuting and imprisoning people like this. But after 100 convictions, surely we are entitled to ask whether doing the same thing for the 101st time constitutes a serious public-safety strategy. A prison place without stable housing, treatment and support on release simply sends people back through the same revolving door. Pavan DhaliwalChief executive, Revolving Doors

There has been much in the media on the early release of prisoners, how full our prisons are and sentencing. I work at the end of the line, in a men’s open prison. It is my personal and strong opinion that we need to look at children and how we are failing to care for them. This is where a criminal life often begins, through neglect, abuse, trauma, the witnessing of violence and rape in the home, and so on.

Many of the prisoners who I work with enter the care system at an early age, leave care without the support they need and end up in prison. For a large number of them, prison is the only life they know. I would urge anyone who is interested, and truly cares, to read Justice on Trial by Chris Daw KC. He suggests some radical solutions, which give hope that we might, one day, be able to prevent so many going to prison and, equally as important, reduce the number of victims of crime. Honouring Sylvia and Emmeline Pankhurst on stage and in political action

The Guardian Thu, 08 Oct 2026 16:29:58 GMT

As we approach the centenary of equal franchise in 2028, it is important to build on the rights that were won by the suffragettes, writes Helen Pankhurst

There was a proud Pankhurst in the audience in Leicester as Sylvia: A Musical Revolution began its national tour (Suffragette cities: blazing Sylvia Pankhurst musical hits the road – in pictures, 3 October). A blazing show indeed – and one that, 98 years after women gained the vote on equal terms with men, asks how much remains to be done, how to do it and how women can bridge their differences to advance their common cause.

As Sylvia Pankhurst’s granddaughter and Emmeline Pankhurst’s great-granddaughter, I honour both women. Their political paths diverged. I seek to reconcile their legacies through Centenary Action, the cross-party coalition that I lead, in a shared cause: dismantling the barriers to women’s participation, selection and retention in politics.

Also in the audience were Philippa, a relative of Emily Wilding Davison, and Peter, a relative of Alice Hawkins. The connections endure – and so does the activism. Remembering past sacrifices means protecting the rights won and building on those struggles as we approach the centenary of equal franchise in 2028.

As Emmeline said: “You must make women count as much as men.” And as Sylvia said: “Great is the work that remains to be accomplished.”Helen PankhurstConvener, Centenary Action

Search warrants used in Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor raids were unlawful, court rules

The Guardian Thu, 08 Oct 2026 16:23:23 GMT

‘Technical errors’ are embarrassing for Thames Valley police but unlikely to affect outcome of investigation

Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor has won his legal challenge against Thames Valley police over search warrants used to raid his home after they arrested him.

The former prince brought a judicial review of the legality of the force’s actions and those of the central criminal court, which granted the warrants.

On Thursday, Mr Justice Hilliard, sitting at the high court in central London, said Thames Valley police (TVP) had conceded that it obtained the search powers under the wrong statutory provision and ruled that the warrants were unlawful.

The episode is embarrassing for TVP but police believe it will not affect the success of the investigation.

The warrants were issued by an Old Bailey judge on 18 February and Mountbatten-Windsor was subsequently arrested the following day, on his 66th birthday, on suspicion of misconduct in public office.

The arrest followed information that emerged from the Jeffrey Epstein files. It was alleged that when Mountbatten-Windsor was the UK’s trade envoy he shared sensitive information with Epstein, a convicted child sex offender.

Police began searching the former Duke of York’s residence on the Sandringham estate and his former Windsor home, Royal Lodge, on the same day as his arrest. Documentary material and electronic devices were seized.

Hilliard said the search warrants were quashed but police had made an application, which would be heard next year, to retain the seized property on the basis that it would have been lawful to take it under a different statutory provision. Mountbatten-Windsor opposes that application.

The judge said: “The fact that the search warrants were quashed does not bring the investigation to an end or mean that the whole of the investigation is unlawful.”

A senior police source said: “It’s not going to bring the investigation to a halt or affect the chances of success.”

They added: “The news media might say the police messed up. But it was the judicial decision [to grant the warrant] that was incorrect.”

TVP have been in discussions with lawyers from the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) about the strength of their case and what evidence they would need for a prosecution.

A TVP spokesperson said: “The agreement that led to the quashing of the warrants relates specifically to a decision made by the court regarding the legal basis for these and is not a judgment on our ongoing investigation.

“We ensured the court was presented with all the necessary information and paperwork to inform their decision, following the correct legal processes throughout.

“We accept the position that the initial court’s decision to issue warrants under the specific piece of legislation used was incorrect and therefore these must be legally quashed.”

Hilliard told the court that the grant of a search warrant under section eight of the Police and Criminal Evidence Act (Pace) 1984 was conditional on the issuing judge being satisfied there were reasonable grounds to suspect that the material sought did not include items subject to legal privilege or special procedure material.

Special procedure material includes documents in possession of a person who acquired them in the course of any trade, business, profession or other occupation – for the purpose of any paid or unpaid office – who holds it subject to an express or implied undertaking to hold it in confidence.

The judge said the presence of legally privileged material was expressly envisaged in the application for the search warrants and that material was likely to be in the possession of Mountbatten-Windsor “who had acquired or created it in circumstances which would make it special procedure material”. He concluded that a lawful warrant could only have been issued under section nine of Pace.

Nick Vamos, the former head of special crime at the CPS, said: “Given the technical nature of the errors revealed today, I expect the crown court to rule in due course that the police can keep the material, or at least as much of it as they would have been entitled to seize in the first place, so they may not ultimately pay much of a price beyond today’s red faces.”

Late last year, King Charles stripped his brother of his right to be a prince and of his dukedom over his association with Epstein.

Mountbatten-Windsor receives an annual stipend, the amount of which has not been disclosed, from King Charles’s private funds, but a palace source told reporters it had been made clear this should not be used to fund the judicial review.

Valtteri Bottas has revealed the details of an incident-packed 418km bike ride including encounters with snakes, being chased by dogs and the eerie atmosphere of riding through the jungle at night as the Cadillac driver cycled between Malaysia and Singapore this week.

The 37-year-old is a keen cyclist and after a suggestion from his girlfriend, the Australian Olympic cyclist Tiffany Cromwell, he decided to take on the challenge of riding from the last round in Sepang near Kuala Lumpur to this weekend’s grand prix on the street circuit in Singapore, under his own steam.

He managed the journey, which the rest of the F1 paddock undertook in flights that last just over an hour, in four days of riding including off-road and gravel sections beginning on the Sunday after the race in Malaysia. He completed 56km on the Sunday, before putting in two big stints on Monday and Tuesday, both of 161km, before concluding with 40km to finish on Wednesday.

Speaking before this Sunday’s night race in Singapore the Finn, who has won 10 grands prix, described events that included leaping over a lizard en route.

“Saw some snakes, which I was a little bit worried about but actually they were pretty chill. They were just doing their thing,” he said. “I saw one cobra, saw one python just crossing the path in front of me. Saw some of those big lizards that you also see here.

“One was on the path, I had to jump over it with a bike. So I saw it like last minute. Got chased by one dog. Got stuck behind a group of cows on a small track. Eventually they moved away.”

He admitted it had been hard, but added that it was a unique experience. “What was the wildest part was the riding at night in the jungle. The noise in there is like … your mind starts to play games of what is out there. But then you just need to crack on and keep going. Riding with your lights at night, that was probably the most epic part in the forest.”

Bottas has taken part in cycling events when he is away from F1. Earlier this year he finished fifth in his age group in a qualifying event in Czechia for the Gravel World Championships, earning him a place in the competition which he is unable to take up because it clashes with the race this weekend.

Victor Montagliani has told Concacaf staff he intends to stand for re-election as the confederation’s presidentnext year, which will rule him out of going up against Gianni Infantino for the top job at Fifa.

The Canadian businessman is understood to have relayed the message to most of the 41 members of Concacaf, the North and Central American and Caribbean confederation.

Montagliani has been widely touted as a potential candidate to take on Infantino for the Fifa presidency, particularly among Uefa member associations, who are conscious a European candidate would have no chance of beating Infantino in a ballot of Fifa’s 211 members.

At a town hall meeting of Concacaf staff late last month, however, Montagliani is understood to have said that despite the Fifa governance crisis and calls for him to stand, he wants to continue serving members in the region.

Concacaf’s presidential election will take place in the first quarter of next year before the Fifa vote on 18 March in Rabat, with the similar timelines leading Montagliani to clarify his intentions to staff.

The 61-year-old was elected president on a reforming mandate 10 years ago after the corruption scandal that culminated in the arrest of then Concacaf president, Jeffrey Webb, after an FBI investigation. Webb admitted he had taken “bribes and kickbacks”.

Uefa will also hold presidential elections next year, with Aleksander Ceferin confirming his intention to stand at a meeting of Uefa’s 55 member associations in Berlin on Thursday. Ceferin had said in February 2024 that he would not run for a fourth term at the helm but the likelihood that he would, after all, continue had long been an open secret. Previously, changes to the Uefa statutes had been passed that meant his first term, which began midway through the standard four-year cycle, did not count towards the standard three-term limit.

It raises the prospect of Ceferin, who took the presidency in September 2016, holding power for more than 15 years in total. That is seen among most European FAs as a positive amid the turmoil engulfing football’s governance while putting to bed any perception that Ceferin, who would have had a number of proponents, might be tempted to challenge Infantino for the Fifa role

Montagliani and Ceferin are expected to continue working together to bring about governance reform at Fifa after the World Cup sell-off scandal, which will be on the agenda at next Thursday’s Fifa council meeting in Zurich.

Fifa’s council has not met since Infantino’s Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) plan was exposed in July despite repeated calls from members for an extraordinary general meeting, with the summit their first meeting since Fifa congress in Vancouver last March.

‘Entitled’ ex-police chief guilty of gross misconduct over affairs with junior officers

The Guardian Thu, 08 Oct 2026 15:11:42 GMT

Scott Chilton, who led Hampshire and the Isle of Wight police, barred from becoming a police officer again

A former chief constable showed a sense of entitlement, dishonesty and lack of integrity by having sexual relationships with two subordinate officers, including engaging in sexual activity while on call to lead major incidents, a misconduct hearing has ruled.

The panel found that the behaviour of Scott Chilton, 53, who retired as chief constable of Hampshire and the Isle of Wight before the hearing, amounted to gross misconduct.

Chilton was found to have had “consensual sexual relations” when he was a chief inspector or superintendent with a woman identified as Officer A, including while he was on duty. When he applied to be chief constable – and during his tenure – he “repetitively and dishonestly” denied this relationship.

The hearing in Eastleigh, Hampshire, was told that a consensual relationship with another woman, Officer B, began within weeks of Chilton becoming chief constable.

He was found to have “abused his position for a sexual purpose” and should have declared the relationship. When it came to light, he “behaved inappropriately” to Officer B, putting pressure on her to conceal what had happened.

Chairing the panel, Michelle Skeer of His Majesty’s Inspectorate of Constabulary and Fire & Rescue Services said Chilton’s behaviour showed “persistent dishonesty and lack of integrity”. She said his actions suggested he did not think the rules applied to him.

“He was in the highest position of trust as the most senior officer in the constabulary and ought to have known the foreseeable risk of harm by having a covert relationship,” Skeer said.

“He repeatedly lied by act and omission about both his relationships with Officer A and Officer B and he knew that this was wrong. His conduct was a serious, deliberate and sustained attempt to mislead … to subvert any negative impact on himself.”

Skeer said Chilton had been privy to confidential and sensitive information on colleagues, security and national policing matters. “There was evidence that he was discussing issues which he shouldn’t have been discussing with Officer B during WhatsApp message exchanges.”

She added that Chilton had attempted to bully Officer B into “keeping quiet” by asking her to “delete and double delete” their messages and not to go to events that his wife would attend, which showed the power imbalance between them.

She said Chilton had engaged in sexual activity with Officer A while on duty and in silver command, which meant he would have been the officer in charge if a major incident had occurred.

Skeer added that “his actions were driven by his own entitlement” and the “abuse of his position was for personal gain and ultimately his own sexual gratification”.

She said Chilton had acted in a domineering fashion towards his colleagues in an attempt to “control the narrative” in relation to responding to press inquiries about the allegations.

Attention also focused during the hearing on disciplinary proceedings against another prominent Hampshire police officer, the former DCI Roger Wood.

In February 2025 a disciplinary hearing concluded Wood had inappropriate relations with two junior colleagues and would have been dismissed had he not already resigned.

Before his case, Wood claimed to have “damaging information” about Chilton and during the proceedings stated that the chief had “had affairs”.

John Beggs KC, who presented the case against the former chief constable, said Chilton had discussed using the force solicitor to prevent Wood from speaking to the press, adding: “He was trying to use his position as a chief constable to advance his own best interests.”

Since Chilton became chief constable in February 2023, there have been about 20 misconduct cases in Hampshire in which officers were accused of various forms of sexual behaviour. About five of these have included behaviour against junior officers.

Chilton retired in April 2025 after a career spanning 33 years that included acting as a lead for the National Police Chiefs’ Council on national investigation standards and coordination.

At the start of the hearing, James Berry KC, representing Chilton, said his client would not be attending the hearing because of “medical issues”.

Chilton said in a statement that he admitted the second relationship but not the first. He said he accepted that by not disclosing that relationship he fell short of the standards police officers were judged by.

He added: “These were personal matters, rather than issues affecting policing or public safety, and at no point did this relationship influence policing decisions, operational matters or the discharge of professional responsibilities.”

He said his “deepest regret” was for his family “for the hurt caused by my poor judgment and actions”.

Chilton would have been dismissed if he had not resigned, the panel said. He has been placed on the College of Policing barred officers list, so he can never again become a police officer.

London, Manchester, Rome, Athens, Istanbul and Lyon will also get permanent franchises, topped up by four qualifiers from within European basketball’s existing structure.

The London franchise is understood to have attracted several bids in excess of $1bn from some eye-catching investors including the former Chelsea chair Todd Boehly, a consortium involving the former Tottenham chair Daniel Levy and MSP Sports Capital, as well as Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund.

Buss Sports Capital, the US investment group that sold its 17.8% stake in the Los Angeles Lakers to Joshua Kushner this year, is believed to have submitted an offer for the Manchester franchise, but City Football Group (CFG) has not bid despite having close links with the NBA, which has agreed to set up a new global academy in Abu Dhabi as part of a $300m partnership.

While the NBA has not committed to a timeframe, it is understood it hopes to announce the identity of the new franchise owners this year.

“We’ve got people who are well-capitalised investors who don’t own any basketball franchise, but they want to get into basketball,” Tatum said at last week’s general assembly of European Football Clubs.

“We’ve got existing basketball clubs in the ecosystem that have submitted bids and we have football clubs, some that have their own basketball teams today, and some that don’t and want to get involved in basketball.”

The level of the bids indicates that the NBA has succeeded in winning over some of Europe’s biggest football clubs and powerful US institutional investors, but it is continuing to encounter resistance from within basketball.

At a meeting at Lake Como this week, the EuroLeague clubs voted to reject the NBA’s initial offer of investment in favour of pursuing their plans to expand from 20 to 24 clubs, although NBA sources insist talks will continue.

“Our vision for basketball is to bring everybody with us – EuroLeague, the governing body, Fiba and the clubs – to revamp the European basketball scene,” Tatum said. “One of the things that we’ve learned from European football is the power of the pyramid. In football every single club understands the clear pathway to play at the top level. That doesn’t exist in basketball.”

The NBA’s decision to seek a partnership with EuroLeagues rather than go it alone was taken during the summer, when it settled on a hybrid model representing Europe and North America’s sporting cultures.

In a structure that echoes football’s toxic and swiftly abandoned European Super League (ESL), NBA Europe will have 12 permanent members, with four temporary members admitted annually.

While the mechanism for promotion is to be confirmed, NBA sources say there will be two entry routes: the top two ranked sides from a new second-tier European competition called the Basketball Champions League, and two finalists in a separate tournament for all of Europe’s domestic champions.

In another nod to greater upward mobility, the highest ranked non-franchise club that reaches the nd-of-season playoffs would keep their place in NBA Europe the next season, with the other three sent back to the play-in competition, so there would probably be a regular turnover of entrants outside the permanent 12.

While there are billions of reasons that big European football clubs want a slice of the NBA, there are suspicions that some may have ulterior motives.

Sign up to Soccer Desk

Jonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer.

after newsletter promotion

Several sources involved in the discussions said Real Madrid’s president, Florentino Pérez, seems particularly invested in NBA Europe, eager to establish the principle of a semi-closed league in Europe in case the prospect of a breakaway football league returns.

Ironically, Pérez had previously cited EuroLeague, which has 13 permanent voting members supplemented by seven additional clubs on an annual basis, as a model for the ESL. NBA Europe sources insist the proposed new competition would be more open, by providing a direct mechanism for all domestic champions to qualify.

Real formally withdrew from the ESL only last year, four years after the project collapsed, and their commercial partner A22 continues to pursue Fifa and Uefa in the courts for allegedly abusing their dominant position by banning clubs from signing up.

The Madrid commercial court and Spain’s high court of justice have both ruled in Real’s favour over the past two years, with Pérez seemingly determined to keep the club’s options open.

“Florentino has been very involved in NBA Europe,” a senior source at a EuroLeague club said. “He wants it to happen quickly and is constantly asking for updates.

“The Super League may be dead for now, but it’s not difficult to imagine a world where the biggest Champions League clubs demand permanent qualification and try to restrict access. A semi-closed Champions League would protect them from domestic failure, so NBA Europe could be very useful.”

Despite the club staying out of the auction, the Manchester City issue remains a potential complication for the NBA, however, as CFG are 50% owners alongside Oak View Group of Manchester’s biggest arena, the 23,000-capacity Co-op Live, which has been earmarked as the most likely venue. A regular-season NBA game between San Antonio Spurs and New Orleans Pelicans will be staged there in January.

“We want to bring on partners who are going to invest in basketball development,” Tatum said. “Academies, indoor arenas. When you think about all of Europe there’s probably only a handful of what I would consider world-class indoor arenas. These arenas provide an economic engine to cities, but we don’t have that in Europe. And so that is the investment that we’re looking to create.”

Tatum has close relations with CFG, whose chair, Khaldoon al‑Mubarak, has been a basketball fan since attending a Boston Celtics’ game while studying at Tufts University in the 1990s.

Al-Mubarak has played an important role in forging a relationship between the NBA and Abu Dhabi’s department of culture and tourism, culminating in a nine-year partnership that for the last four years has led to NBA pre-season games in Abu Dhabi.

That deal will remain in place despite the fallout from Manchester City being found guilty by an independent commission of more than 100 charges of financial cheating, although the NBA may be slightly relieved that the club is not part of the franchise bidding process.

Can hope save the planet? An endangered parrot that is beating the odds can help us find out

The Guardian Thu, 08 Oct 2026 15:05:53 GMT

A new global biodiversity report strikes an encouraging note. But we cannot rest on our laurels – and resilience is key

The new Living Planet Report is out. Published every two years, it assesses the health of the natural world and, historically, it’s made for gloomy reading.

Take 2024’s report, which showed global wildlife populations had plummeted by 73% in 50 years and that ecosystems were being pushed toward collapse.

After reading it, I retired to a dark room and drank gin, but every time I popped my head out, there was more bad news: heatwaves, floods, wildfires and mass coral bleaching.

So, when this year’s edition dropped, I braced myself. But there was a plot twist. Biodiversity is still being pummelled, but not everywhere. According to the new report, conservationists have prevented the extinction of 32 birds and 16 mammals since 1993, and the numbers of wild tigers, elephants and sea otters are stable or growing. The energy sector has historically been extremely damaging to the planet, accounting for about 75% of global greenhouse gas emissions. But the report notes we have passed a positive tipping point in the energy system, with the transition to renewables snowballing and coal use declining in many wealthy countries.

I can therefore see why the report is titled The Science of Hope.

But pegging it on hope is a bold move. People who write about the natural world, myself included, face a difficult choice. Focus on the bad news, and risk shouting into a void where people simply don’t want to listen. Focus on the good news and risk peddling “hopium” – stories that dull the pain briefly but do little to spur action.

The report, however, isn’t talking about your average kind of hope. It’s talking about a geeky kind of hope rooted in psychological research.

The American psychologist Charles “Rick” Snyder spent decades studying hope and came up with a surprisingly practical definition. Hope, he argued, starts with a goal but also requires pathways, or ideas about how to get there, and agency: the belief that you can make a difference. To this, the Living Planet Report adds another ingredient: resilience – the capacity to keep going when progress stalls. Or, as British anarchist punk band Chumbawamba famously put it: you get knocked down, but you get up again.

We can illustrate this point by looking at New Zealand’s kākāpō, the world’s fattest, greenest, least-able-to-fly parrot. When non-native predators drove the kākāpō to the brink of extinction, conservationists didn’t waste time wishing its numbers back up. In the mid 1990s, they moved the remaining birds to predator-free islands, and when recovery was slow, they changed tack.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

They experimented with hand-rearing, foster mothers and artificial insemination. They fitted the birds with smart transmitters and monitored them almost obsessively. When new technology came along, they embraced it: the genomes of every living bird have now been sequenced to inform decisions about who should breed with whom.

This is what real hope looks like. It’s not the same as optimism – the expectation that things will work out. Nor is it wishful thinking. And it’s certainly not “hopium”, which can make the problem seem smaller than it is. Real hope has its sleeves rolled up and is prepared to get messy. It leaves room for uncertainty and failure but refuses to believe that there’s nothing left to do. That’s why the opposite of hope isn’t despair. It’s inaction.

Scientists who have studied hope have found it matters what we’re hopeful about. A 2023 meta-analysis found that people who felt hopeful about their ability to make a difference were more likely to engage with the climate crisis – from seeking information and supporting climate policies to taking everyday action to reduce their environmental impact. Those whose hope rested on the belief that the climate crisis wasn’t really a problem were less likely to engage.

In other words, useful hope needs to be grounded in reality. And that requires knowing what we’re up against. This was why the Starmer government’s decision not to publish the full national security assessment on global biodiversity loss is so frustrating. The public has since seen an abridged 14-page version. But the detail – and any devil within it – likely remains hidden.

Produced by the Joint Intelligence Committee, it asks a stark question: what would ecosystem collapse mean for the UK?

The answer is bleak: threats to national security and prosperity, havoc wroughtwith food and water supplies, a surge in irregular migration and even more geopolitical instability around the world.

To find a way through the climate crisis, we need both a clear view of the problem and the determination to tackle it. How can we find the right pathway if we don’t have the full map?

In 1995, there were just 51 kākāpō. Today, there are 324, a remarkable turnaround for such a slow-breeding bird. Conservation plans are still evolving, and the species isn’t out of the woods yet. But at least it has a fighting chance.

That’s the kind of hope we need: pragmatic, resilient and open to revision. We need our governments to be honest about the scale of the challenge we face. Because when they withhold information, they don’t just rob us of knowledge. They also rob us of hope.

Helen Pilcher is a science writer and the author of Life Changing: How Humans Are Altering Life on Earth and This Book May Cause Side Effects

Willem de Kooning review – the artist’s lifelong rebellion against himself is thrilling to watch

The Guardian Thu, 08 Oct 2026 14:35:10 GMT

Rijksmuseum, AmsterdamMarking a century since the Dutch artist stowed away to New York, this vast retrospective gloriously showcases the abstract expressionist’s fierce boundary-pushing

Willem de Kooning was the last great artist who really knew how to draw. More precisely, if less provocatively, he was the last truly transformative painter to have been schooled in the academic tradition that produces what is still recognised, by most people, as “good drawing”. Accurate in the sense of a photograph but, like a filter on your cameraphone, also subtly tidying up the world to meet the ideals of classical proportion. “Draw what you see and not what you think,” the young De Kooning was told. Raw personal emotion had no place – a far cry from what this master of abstract expressionism was to become.

The intense labour required to build a connection between eye, brain and hand so quick as to be instinctive is illustrated by the charcoal still life Dish With Jugs. Made when De Kooning was in his mid-teens, and so minutely rendered that you might mistake it for a sepia photograph, the catalogue estimates that it took 600 hours at the Rotterdam academy to complete. The aim of this exercise was not to produce a single picture so much as to ingrain a way of seeing and reconstructing the world to the point that it becomes inescapable.

This brilliantly researched exhibition makes a compelling case for the success of that training. Setting a handful of standout paintings among a wider selection of drawings illustrates the artist’s lifelong rebellion against rules so thoroughly internalised that he could push fiercely at their limits without entirely breaking them. The battle is thrilling to watch.

De Kooning’s formative training is apparent in an early drawing of the dancer Juliet Browner and a marvellously deft portrait of the artist’s wife, Elaine. The influence of Ingres – the Pelé of academic drawing – on these works has often been remarked upon, not least by rival New York painters for whom De Kooning’s superior draughtsmanship was a source of suspicion (too prissy, too European). And it seems that the immigrant artist placed himself under pressure to unstitch the aesthetic conventions of the old world and rework them into something more appropriate to the new: irreverent, free, immediate, expressive.

It is important to note that De Kooning’s education was not limited to the academy. A working-class kid, his evening classes had been subsidised by the design firm where he worked in the day; after stowing away to the US at 22, he scraped a living as a sign painter and commercial illustrator. These lessons made their way into his art, and the difficulty of synthesising them might explain the struggles of his early career (he didn’t have a solo show until he was nearly 44) and how revolutionary the breakthrough was when it did arrive.

Central to that achievement was that he made no distinction between drawing and painting (the tradition being, in simple terms, that you draw the outlines and paint the space between them). In Queen of Hearts, a harbinger of women to come, he drags charcoal sticks across wet paint to create soft edges, sanding down and painting over layers like a housepainter. The big bang arrives in the seminal work on paper completed in 1949, an arrangement of white sparks against a black ground that calls to mind comets dancing through the night sky. But De Kooning was no starry-eyed mystic: at the bottom edge, transforming those white sparks into liquid spurts, is a scrawled cock and balls.

Excavation, a knockout masterpiece, likewise appears at first as an abstract pattern of interlocking shapes only to reveal itself as a maelstrom of screaming faces and dismembered body parts. Completed in 1950, it conjures both Europe’s mass graves and an orgiastic ecstasy of bodies dissolving into each other. Sex and death, heaven and hell, the end of the old world and the birth of the new. In one of many intelligent arrangements, Excavation is paired with a drawing from four years earlier, the aptly titled Judgment Day.

It is a quirk of the exhibition that its most famous painting, Woman I, hangs in a separate gallery normally reserved for the museum’s treasures from the Dutch golden age. Not only does this icon hold its own against Vermeer and Rembrandt, but she is also unexpectedly at home. Scandalous when first exhibited, the accusation that this cartoonish, charismatic and wild figure defames all womankind by its “monstrosity” seems now to rely on some mid-century assumptions about how women should be represented. Whatever you think about Woman I, she could never be mistaken for a submissive sex object or a Stepford wife.

De Kooning’s relentless attacks on convention, which is to say on himself and everything else, took their toll. A series of black-and-white works, made in Rome in the late 1950s, mark the end of his imperial phase. While these vaguely calligraphic graphic signs illustrate a point about the convergence of painting and drawing, they feel to me slapdash and derivative of Franz Kline. From here, this exhibition does little to overturn the conventional wisdom that De Kooning struggled over the next two decades to scale the same heights. There are standouts – notably the irrepressible Clam Diggers, a woozy portrait of two women standing in shallow water rendered in ice-cream colours and buttery textures, and a gorgeously fleshy painting from the mid-70s that advertises the painter’s occasionally overlooked gift as a colourist. If the paintings are hit and miss, the drawings from this period reveal that, even hindered by alcoholism and a chaotic personal life, De Kooning could always rely on his line.

That line holds to the end. The show closes with an astonishing painting from 1985, during the period when De Kooning’s cognitive decline was increasingly apparent. Sinuous blue and black lines curve across a mottled white ground, weaving a pattern suggestive of bodies and yet emptied of desire. It is serene, strange and straightforwardly beautiful, as if everything that the artist had struggled to pack into his work had been boiled down to basic principles. He is back to fitting the world to a pleasing form. The difference is that it is no longer a boilerplate inherited from the classical tradition, but shaped by his experiences and entirely his own. He doesn’t need to think about it. The battle is over.

Willem de Kooning at Work is at the Rijksmuseum, Amsterdam, from 9 October to 17 January

Manchester United offer JJ Gabriel new deal but risk losing prodigy for £350,000

The Guardian Thu, 08 Oct 2026 14:10:04 GMT

Teenager almost certain to leave despite fresh offer

Compensation for move to European rival would be low

Manchester United have made JJ Gabriel an official scholarship contract offer, but remain at risk of losing the teenage forward for as little as £350,000.

The prodigy, who turned 16 this week, stunned the club when he asked for his registration to be cancelled last month, setting in motion a scramble among Europe’s elite clubs for his signature.

Under Premier League youth rules, Gabriel would have been able to leave for a rival for nothing in January if the club had not offered him a formal scholarship for next season. The Guardian can reveal that the offer has now been lodged with the player.

Whether he accepts it or not – and it appears unlikely he will stay at Old Trafford – any Premier League club must now negotiate a fee directly with United for the player. If one is not reached, compensation will be set by a Professional Football Compensation Committee tribunal.

At a tribunal, United would expect to receive in excess of £3m, plus a clause in the deal granting them 20% of his next transfer fee. In a previous tribunal for a high-profile academy player, Liverpool were required to pay Chelsea £2.8m up front – with an additional £1.2m in performance-related add-ons – for Rio Ngumoha, and a 20% sell-on clause was inserted in the deal.

A United team photograph released this week featuring Gabriel briefly raised fan hopes of a reconciliation. But a breakdown between his representatives and the club means the forward – who has been at United since he was 11 – is now almost certain to leave.

He was permitted under Premier League rules to sign a pre-agreement after his 16th birthday, but his camp were not prepared to enter discussions after a disagreement over first-team minutes.

His next move is yet to be decided, though it is believed he favours a move to Europe, where compensation would be significantly lower. Real Madrid are favourites to sign him, with Barcelona, Bayern Munich and Paris Saint-Germain all monitoring developments.
