Russian attack on bus kills at least 30 people near Ukraine frontline

The Guardian Thu, 08 Oct 2026 14:00:05 GMT

Zelenskyy says Kremlin deliberately targeted ‘ordinary public transport stop’ in Kramatorsk, with 18 wounded

A Russian missile strike on a bus in the eastern city of Kramatorsk has killed at least 30 people, officials have said, in one of the worst attacks by Moscow on Ukrainian civilians this year.

The regional prosecutor’s office in the Donetsk region said on Thursday the vehicle had been hit at 10am by an aerial bomb. “As of now, the death toll from this morning’s attack has risen to 30. Eighteen people were wounded,” it said, adding that all local public transport had been suspended.

Images ​posted by police ‌showed bodies ‌strewn across a street littered with debris, as well ‌as a charred shell of what appeared to be a bus. A second bus had also caught fire, officials said. The strike targeted an area next to a dental clinic on the city’s Yuvileina Street.

Three people had also been killed by shelling in the village of Bilenke, outside Kramatorsk, they added. Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the Kremlin had deliberately targeted an “ordinary public transport stop”.

Some of those killed could not be identified because of the severity of their injuries, Ukraine’s president added. He said the number of victims could “sadly rise”, as doctors fought to save the lives of those wounded.

He said: “This strike will not go unanswered. Russia is trying to destroy all life in Donbas, and a response from the world is a must. A forceful response – exactly as the Russians deserve for all the deaths they have brought. May all those killed rest in peace.”

The bombing follows a gruesome Russian strike on Wednesday on a five-storey block of flats in Pryluky in the northern Chernihiv region. The building collapsed, entombing those inside. At least 22 people were killed, including five children, aged between one and eight.

Visiting the scene with Ed Miliband, the British foreign secretary, Zelenskyy urged the US to expand Starlink satellite internet coverage so that Ukraine could hit targets inside Russia such as launch sites. So far, Donald Trump and Elon Musk have refused Kyiv’s request.

Miliband said there was “no clearer sign of Putin’s evil, evil intent and strategy in this conflict” than this week’s murderous attacks. He said: “Putin once said that he was going to win on the battlefield. He is trying to win by terrorising civilians.”

Writing earlier on social media, Zelenskyy called on western allies to take “concrete steps” to boost Ukraine’s depleted air defences, amid a round-the-clock Russian onslaught in recent weeks featuring ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones.

“Supplies of anti-ballistic capabilities, ammunition for our combat aircraft, and investments in interceptors – all of this is directly helping save lives every day. Important talks with our partners will take place today and tomorrow,” Zelenskyy said.

Kramatorsk and neighbouring Sloviansk form part of a “fortress belt”. They are the last two big cities in northern Donetsk under full Ukrainian military control. Russia has been trying to capture them for more than a decade, after a brief period in which Russian forces occupied Sloviansk in 2014.

The cities are home to thousands of civilians, as well as Ukrainian soldiers. In recent months, roads have been festooned with nets to protect traffic from marauding enemy drones. These defences offer little protection, however, against aerial bombs.

“These are not ‘the consequences of war’, nor dry statistics. These are people killed by the Russian army,” the Donetsk regional governor, Vadym Filashkin, said ‌on Telegram after Thursday’s strike. “Russia comes to Ukrainian land with death.”

He added: “The Russians are deliberately targeting civilians. For them, a bus full of passengers is an attractive target precisely because a single strike can kill as many people as possible.

“Russia deliberately flouts every conceivable rule of warfare and the norms of international humanitarian law. It selects targets where it can inflict the greatest suffering on civilians.”

There was criticism of the White House’s policy of engaging with Vladimir Putin, whom Donald Trump has invited to December’s G20 summit in Miami, Florida. The Kremlin has yet to say if Russia’s leader will take part.

The former US ambassador to Moscow Michael McFaul said on social media that Russia was guilty of terrorism. “There is no other word for it. Putin is running a terrorist state. That officials from my country call this terrorist a nice guy is deeply embarrassing for me.”

Putin has demanded Ukraine cede the rest ​of ​the eastern Donbas region still under its ​control. Kyiv refuses to hand over its territory, believing Russia will take any concessions and carry on fighting.

I’d spent a lot of time on my dad’s film sets, so it was fun to be on someone else’s. I still like to visit film sets. I’m never jaded – I’m still impressed by movie magic.

Khaldoon al-Mubarak: the tightrope walker who made rare misstep over City charges

The Guardian Thu, 08 Oct 2026 12:19:02 GMT

Manchester City’s chair is key to the project of making Abu Dhabi a secure world power but his next move may be the sale of the club

No one better understands the precarious tightrope Abu Dhabi walks when it tries to balance its relationships with western Europe while weighing the complex geopolitics of the Gulf region than Manchester City’s chair, Khaldoon al-Mubarak. He was eight when his father, ambassador Khalifa Ahmed Abdel Aziz al-Mubarak, left the family’s Paris apartment for work on 9 February 1984, and was assassinated on the street by a Palestinian terrorist.

And no one outside the emirate’s royal family could be more wrapped up in the project of making and maintaining Abu Dhabi as a significant and secure world power and the dominant member of the United Arab Emirates, a nation state still only 55 years old. His paternal grandfather, Ahmad bin Abdul Aziz al-Mubarak, was chair of Abu Dhabi’s Sharia judicial department and senior adviser to Sheikh Zayed bin Sultan al-Nahyan, the founding president of the UAE. As such, Ahmad bin Abdul Aziz was the James Madison of the UAE (the founding father, not the Spurs player) in that he crafted the Islamic legal framework of the new nation in the 1970s.

Khaldoon’s father was assassinated by a group led by Abu Nidal which, according to the CIA, was “the most dangerous and effective of all terrorist groups [and] the best organized of the radical Palestinian terrorist groups” before the emergence of Hamas. The murder was justified in a phone call saying that the UAE “had expelled Palestinian and Arab residents and was linked with American imperialism”. In essence, they were accused of being too soft on the west, not radical enough for Palestinians.

Both al-Mubarak’s grandfather and father have streets named after them in Abu Dhabi, with his father honoured as a martyr of the state. It is fair to say the City chair has honoured the family tradition as chief adviser to the UAE president and Abu Dhabi ruler, Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed al-Nahyan, for whom he first worked after graduating from Tufts University in Massachusetts. Given his father’s martyrdom, the royal family is said to have looked out for al-Mubarak as a quasi-adopted son. According to a source in the Financial Times, al-Mubarak is “diplomatically in charge of the UK file as well as the China file … and he’s the main liaison with the US administration” and has diplomatic immunity in the UK. That said, he appears to have made a rare misstep with his belligerent tone on Manchester City.

According to Manchester City’s lawyer Simon Cliff, it was al-Mubarak who dictated the aggressive, confrontational stance City have taken with football authorities. As far back as 2014, when City were fighting their first Uefa charge, Cliff wrote, according to leaked documents first published by Der Spiegel: “Khaldoon says he would rather spend £30m on the 50 best lawyers in the world and sue them [Uefa] for the next ten years than agree a financial penalty.”

He backed down on that occasion, along with the co-accused Paris Saint-Germain, both clubs agreeing a small fine and minor transfer restrictions with Uefa. It is extraordinary that City kept fighting thereafter, whereas the Qatar-owned PSG accepted their punishment, cosied up to Uefa – with the club’s president, Nasser al-Khelaifi, becoming chair of the European Club Association (now European Football Clubs) and chief opponent of the breakaway Super League – and built the most exciting and successful team in Europe, bringing admiration for the Qatari brand from observers willing to ignore human rights abuses. Al-Mubarak, in fighting to the end with City, appears to have broken an ambassador’s cardinal law: don’t embarrass your boss. Should City lose their appeal against an independent commission’s finding that they were guilty of multiple breaches of financial rules, al-Mubarak may be instructed to organise the sale of the club.

“I’m sure that’s the case with Man City,” says Christopher Davidson, author of Abu Dhabi, Oil and Beyond. “More than that, I’ve been told by some [in Abu Dhabi] that it will be the case. I can’t see any reason why they would stick around and try to rebuild the reputation after this. It’s embarrassing the royal family now. I can’t think of any example where things have gone wrong [for Abu Dhabi] and they’ve just kept plugging money into it. I think they’ll play out the appeal – nothing to lose with that – but once that’s done, it’s all about how to get out before the owners are declared unfit, a far worse outcome. There are very clever people involved in Abu Dhabi who I’m led to believe will very strongly counsel this needs to be a quiet retreat because the longer they stay in the game, the more damaging it is and it will unravel any kind of soft power Abu Dhabi managed to gain.”

In June al-Mubarak said “these sorts of jewels, you don’t sell” and that there was “only intention to keep growing this”. As for the wider threat to UK-Abu Dhabi relations, Davidson believes it is overstated. “Some of the reporting perhaps has portrayed Abu Dhabi as a bit monolithic. There are entire big and growing sections of Abu Dhabi state economy that are outside al-Mubarak’s remit. Some of Abu Dhabi’s biggest investments in the UK in recent years have been in renewable energy and the windfarms of Scotland from Masdar energy, which is chaired by Sultan al-Jaber, who’s another key lieutenant of the ruler.”

Davidson also cites the International Holding Company (IHC), which has huge biotech, shipping, healthcare and retail investments in the UK, including the Ivy restaurants, and is chaired by Sheikh Tahnoon bin Zayed al-Nahyan, deputy ruler of Abu Dhabi and brother of the UAE president and Sheikh Mansour. “It’s inconceivable that these investments would be withdrawn,” says Davidson.

In May this year the UK signed a free trade agreement with Bahrain, Kuwait, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the UAE which it said could be worth £3.7bn a year to the UK economy. “The UAE was a major force behind getting that and it was a major accomplishment on both sides, so there’s no prospect any of this is going to be interfered with,” Davidson says.

Al-Mubarak will probably emerge from this fiasco largely untarnished, because City are a tiny part of his portfolio. “He can’t possibly have known what’s going on in every part of his empire,” says Davidson. “My gut feeling would be that it’s the layers below him. It’s all about your legal counsel. I think the Qataris had very clever people working for them. This has been a case of poor advice being given to the senior Emiratis involved, a misreading of UK politics and a misreading of the Premier League and its bigger picture as a rules-based institution.

“I think the statements al-Mubarak has made, including the one early last summer that ‘We will not sell’, are the product of poor advice delivered to him and ultimately to Sheikh Mansour. It may be important to us in the UK but Man City has been a peripheral project [for Abu Dhabi].”

Can Sánchez convince Spanish voters he is their best hope for fairer housing?

The Guardian Thu, 08 Oct 2026 12:16:06 GMT

Recent death of 87-year-old woman likely to focus attention on crisis in run-up to election at end of November

Europe live – latest updates

Even before María del Carmen Abascal died on Wednesday night, a mere fortnight after her eviction from the Madrid flat where she had lived for most of her life, the frail 87-year-old woman had become the enduring face of Spain’s housing crisis.

Her plight – and the wider issue it embodied – had led to street demonstrations, the creation of a protest camp in the middle of the Spanish capital, and spurred the socialist-led government to propose emergency measures to facilitate and protect access to housing. When rightwing and far-right parties voted down those measures in congress last week, the prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, responded by announcing a snap general election for the end of November.

Abascal’s death now looks set to focus even more attention on housing in the run-up to that election and, in particular, on what her lawyer has called “the shameful violence of these types of evictions and the evident impact and consequences they can have on people’s health”.

With more than 42% of Spaniards identifying access to housing as their main worry and with rents having risen by 80% over the past decade, the most pertinent question may be: why has it taken the eviction of an octogenarian and the accompanying protests to shake Spain’s political class into action? To which the answer could be that, despite years of protests against overtourism and gentrification, the tipping point had not been reached. Now, arguably, it has.

On Thursday, Spain’s state centre for sociological research published polling that showed that 76.3% of those surveyed were in favour of the state intervening in the market “as much as necessary to guarantee everyone’s access to housing”, while 79% believed housing should be prioritised as a constitutional right.

Sánchez’s socialist-led government is keen to persuade voters that it is the only political force that cares about rents and tenants’ rights – hence the emergency measures, which have been redrafted into two new decrees after their defeat in parliament last week. The 21 measures include facilitating renting or buying a new home; extending eviction protections for vulnerable residents; prohibiting speculative real estate purchases, and granting tax breaks to property owners and tenants who pay on time.

“These are measures that, if I may say so, are a matter of simple common sense; a matter of humanity,” the prime minister said on Tuesday. “They unite small property owners and tenants while standing up to vulture funds, precisely because they target only those who view housing merely as a commodity for speculation.”

The measures come almost three years after the prime minister promised to build 184,000 affordable public rental homes. His government has also sought to address soaring housing prices by introducing a law allowing authorities to cap “disproportionate” rent prices in some areas.

Those who had voted down last week’s decrees, Sánchez said, had done so despite studies showing the measures enjoyed “cross-cutting support that transcends ideology”, adding that the public was in favour of regulating “a dysfunctional market”. He is now hoping that at least one of the decrees will be passed by congress’s permanent council, a special body that operates when parliament is not in session. Its approval could go some way to convincing voters that his administration is taking the housing issue seriously.

Others disagree. Alberto Núñez Feijóo, the leader of the conservative People’s party, which voted down the measures last week, has said it is a bit late for Sánchez, who has been prime minister since 2018, to suddenly appoint himself Spain’s housing champion.

“Housing has been the big failure of this government but will be the success story of the one that follows it,” he said on Monday. Feijóo, whose party is leading the polls, added: “When a prime minister has been in power for eight years, it’s hard to blame others for what he’s failed to do.” The PP has promised to address the crisis by building 200,000 homes a year, lowering taxes and cutting down on bureaucracy.

However, the PP’s decision to side with the far-right Vox party and the rightwing Catalan pro-independence Junts party to fell the measures has left it looking less than committed to the issue of the day. Sánchez and his allies will be hoping that fact will not be lost on voters as the election campaign kicks off and as trade unions prepare a general strike over housing for 11 November.

Mindful, perhaps, of the distance between his words and his party’s voting history in congress, Feijóo called for people not to manipulate Abascal’s death to suit their own purposes.

“No campaigning, no political parties, no partisan ends, no more bricks in the wall,” he said on Wednesday night. “When a person dies there should be nothing but respect.”

And yet, despite the primacy of housing as an issue, Feijóo opted to start his campaign in Spain’s North African territory of Ceuta, where at least 141 people died as tens of thousands tried to cross over from neighbouring Morocco at the end of July. The Spanish government’s handling of the mass crossing, which saw about 80,000 people enter Ceuta, has been criticised at home and abroad. Speaking in the territory on Wednesday, Feijóo promised that its safety would be at the “top of [the] in-tray” if he became prime minister.

Vox, meanwhile, has responded to Absacal’s death by posting footage of a TV interview in which she said she held Sánchez responsible for what had happened to her. The far-right party accused the socialists of using “the suffering of an elderly person to stage a campaign to hide the government’s responsibility in the housing disaster”. It also suggested that Sánchez had visited “ruin and death” on Spain in the form of the floods that killed 230 people in Valencia two years ago, last year’s nationwide power cut, the deadly train crash in southern Spain in January, and recent events in Ceuta.

Free land for those who will build social homes on it. Is this the radical solution to the UK’s housing problem?

The Guardian Thu, 08 Oct 2026 11:56:45 GMT

A bold south London initiative to give land to community groups rather than private developers could transform the system

Lewisham council, in southeast London, is developing ambitious plans to transfer public land to community groups in an attempt to get new social housing built in the borough. According to papers tabled at Wednesday’s council cabinet meeting, the local authority is devising a new housing strategy, which includes giving packages of public land worth up to £2m each to community-led organisations such as housing co-operatives, on the condition that they build social housing.

The Green-controlled council is further considering placing any land it gives away through the programme into community land trusts, legal instruments that lock in permanent affordability. They may also provide low-interest loans to help developments get started, and pre-approve planning permission to speed up construction. It is hoped that the proposals will take effect within a year. Together, they form the most radical suite of solutions to the housing crisis any local authority is currently putting forward. If adopted elsewhere, the approach could transform the construction of social housing not just in Lewisham, but across the entire country.

Today three in four new British homes are built by for-profit property developers. The rest are erected predominantly by housing associations, with just a paltry few built by local authorities. Unlike in comparable European economies, almost no new UK homes are being built by community organisations. To get new social housing built in their area, therefore, councils are reliant on private developers building a proportion of homes for social rent as part of larger master plans. But developers frequently use their strong bargaining position to haggle down the amount of social housing they actually deliver.

“There’s a limit to how much social housing we can realistically get private property developers to build,” says Daniel Dream, cabinet member for inclusive regeneration, planning and housing delivery in Lewisham. “We’ve got to get more creative about how to deliver social housing.” Dream, a key architect of Lewisham’s evolving new strategy, says the current system of councils haggling with developers is broken and will never produce enough social housing to meet need. Instead, he hopes to use public land to empower community-led organisations to build essential housing for themselves, or as he puts it: “enabling community to deliver community”.

Selling off public land is a fraught business even for well-meaning councils. Under a 1972 law, public bodies are obliged to accept the highest price they are offered, regardless of the buyer’s intentions. Wealthy property developers can therefore typically swoop in and outbid community groups for land, even when the community groups have far more interesting, sustainable and socially valuable ambitions. In September, for example, Somerset council voted to sell a site in Frome to the London-based investment firm Newcore Capital rather than to local community developers who had plans to build homes, workspaces, a riverside park and a lido.

However, the 1972 law has a loophole. If a local authority is selling a site worth £2m or less, the council can choose to sell it to whomever it likes, and at whatever price it pleases, even giving it away for free, provided doing so provides positive benefits for the area.

The new strategy could be especially useful in helping support more ambitious housebuilding on tricky small sites. In London a “small site” is defined as a piece of land that is under 2,500 sq metres, about the size of nine tennis courts. These plots are too modest for major developers to take an interest in, so often just sit empty. However, the potential to better use vacant small sites is enormous. The architecture practice RCKa estimates there is enough land stuck in small sites to build 850,000 new homes in the capital alone. It recently conducted a survey of Lewisham identifying space for up to 9,700 new homes across more than 3,000 potential small sites.

Improved use of small sites can also create better homes. As the research project Small Sites London shows, modest developments are generally more likely to produce high-quality housing that makes a positive contribution to its local neighbourhood than the swathes of anodyne towers put up by mainstream developers on larger sites.

Lewisham has a long history of successful projects proving the potential of community participation in housing. Beginning in the late 1970s, families on the council housing waiting list were offered the opportunity to build their own homes using an innovative construction system devised by the German architect Walter Segal. In 1997, London’s first black housing co-operative finished building Nubia Way. In 2024 a community land trust completed Church Grove, a block of 36 permanently affordable homes. But more recently the borough’s reputation for housing leadership has waned. In June, The Filigree, a major new residential and commercial development in central Lewisham, was announced joint winner of the Carbuncle Cup, an award for Britain’s worst new building. These plans to revive ambitious community-led housing could not come sooner.

Lewisham’s housing target is 30,376 homes over 15 years. Community-led development won’t be able to meet that target alone, but it marks a clear break with the failing system of squeezing piecemeal benefits from major speculative developments. If successful, the approach could better empower the council and its constituents – and if introduced nationwide, it could catalyse a genuine revolution in social housing construction everywhere.

Phineas Harper is a writer and curator

Supermarket shake-up: why Asda or Morrisons could vanish within a decade

The Guardian Thu, 08 Oct 2026 10:26:10 GMT

Talks between Sainsbury’s and Morrisons have set industry tongues wagging, with analysts saying the market is ripe for change

Tesco lifts profit forecast and says shoppers are resilient

They may be two of the most recognisable brands in Britain, with a combined 188 years serving shoppers, but industry watchers agree that either Asda or Morrisons – or both – could disappear within a decade.

This week, it emerged that Sainsbury’s and Morrisons – the UK’s second- and sixth-largest supermarket chains – had held merger talks between last November and February, before the larger player decided to walk away.

News of the potential deal has relaunched speculation that the UK grocery market is now ripe for consolidation and revealed that the Sainsbury’s boss, Simon Roberts – who has been in post for six years – is at least willing to consider the possibility of buying one of his troubled rivals.

Sainsbury’s, which has 600 supermarkets and almost 900 convenience stores, has until recently been seen as wary of trying to revive merger talks with its rivals after its bid to buy Asda for £7bn in 2019 was blocked.

However, industry experts say Asda and Morrisons’ owners have held informal talks with each other – and both with Sainsbury’s team – and predict that talks could restart.

“The three of them, one way or another, are talking to each other,” one said. He suggested that a combination of Asda and Morrisons could happen but was likely to be a weaker deal than a Sainsbury’s takeover of either, as both businesses struggle with costs and interest on debt piles.

The industry has undergone significant change since the collapse of the Sainsbury’s-Asda deal. While riding the wider retail trends towards online shopping and convenience stores, the supermarket groups have been jockeying for market share.

Aldi is poised to overtake Asda to become the UK’s third-largest supermarket, with less than 1 percentage point separating them. Aldi is rapidly opening stores while Asda has struggled to find growth since a £6.8bn, debt-fuelled takeover in 2020 and heavy price competition from the discounters and from its bigger rivals Tesco and Sainsbury’s.

Another big change could emerge this month when the UK’s competition watchdog is due to publish its final ruling on whether Aldi and Lidl should now officially be classified as “large grocery retailers” like Tesco, Sainsbury’s, Asda and Morrisons.

In August, the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) said it had found provisionally that Aldi and Lidl no longer qualified as “limited assortment discounters” as they now carry a “full range” of groceries and operate stores larger than 1,000 sq m (10,700 sq ft) across the UK.

The change means the German-owned discounters are now taken into account when assessing competition in different locations.

This is the strongest hint yet that the CMA has changed its stance blocking the Sainsbury’s buyout of Asda on the basis that shoppers would be worse off.

It also indicates that the CMA’s “balance of competition” – its estimation of the impact of a deal based on drive times for customers around stores – has shifted, meaning Sainsbury’s might have to dispose of dozens fewer stores to gain regulatory clearance for a merger. A figure of 150 was suggested when it tried to buy Asda.

Clive Black, an analyst at Shore Capital and Sainsbury’s broker, says the CMA preliminary ruling indicates “the shape of the pitch has adjusted a little” and “the change encourages another chapter of consolidation”.

It is a step-change from 2019 when analysts accused the singing former Sainsbury’s boss Mike Coupe and his board of directors of “arrogance” and “folly” for pursuing Asda. Now they say that consolidation is almost inevitable.

That comes amid what is seen as a more welcoming regulatory environment backed by the UK government’s growth agenda combined with the appointment of Doug Gurr, a grocery industry veteran who has spent time at Asda and Amazon, to lead the CMA.

One analyst described Sainsbury’s as the “kingmaker” in any industry consolidation as it uniquely has the resources to snap up a rival without the market dominance to immediately prevent any deal.

Analysts agree it is unlikely to face significant competition if it opts to buy Morrisons or Asda – Tesco is too big to buy a rival, while Marks & Spencer and Waitrose appear unlikely to have the financial firepower or desire to pursue such a deal.

Amazon should not be ruled out as a player in consolidation, according to one analyst, who said the online specialist might be prompted into action by any of the supermarkets announcing plans to merge.

“The last cards are coming on to the table,” he said, suggesting that Amazon might consider buying Asda, Morrisons or even Sainsbury’s, now that it had effectively disposed of Argos which may have caused competition concerns for Amazon.

However, Amazon has not fared well with its dip into high street retail. Last year, it decided to close all 19 of its Fresh stores, with plans to convert five of them into shops under its Whole Foods Market brand.

As analysts at Bernstein put it: “We believe that scale is the most important source of advantage in grocery retail, and the combined market share of Sainsbury’s and Morrisons would improve Sainsbury’s ability to take on Tesco.”

The logic of a deal for Morrisons’ American private equity owner is clear. Clayton, Dubilier & Rice has few options for an exit, four years on from its £7bn acquisition of the Bradford-based chain. Private equity bidders are not likely to be lining up, as there is little room for a another debt-fuelled buyout, while pursuing a stock market flotation would require a compelling growth story to lure investors but which is now absent.

The heavy debts taken on to fund CD&R’s acquisition in 2022 have left Morrisons struggling to compete as interest rates have risen, pushing up costs, while competition has toughened as pinched households look to save costs on their grocery bill.

Clearly, the CD&R adviser and former Tesco boss Terry Leahy is unlikely to let Morrisons go cheaply – with price demands ultimately understood to have led Sainsbury’s Roberts to walk away from any deal.

However, Morrisons has fallen back to be the UK’s sixth-largest supermarket with an 8.4% market share, just behind Lidl on 8.7%, according to the latest data from the industry analysts Worldpanel by Numerator.

Asda’s owners, led by the British investment firm TDR Capital, may also welcome a tidy exit although they are likely to be happier to wait, having largely made their money selling off various parts of the grocer’s assets, industry insiders say. Under the returning boss, Allan Leighton, there are nascent signs of a turnaround if the owners are willing to sit tight and he does not appear keen on reviving talks with Sainsbury’s.

For Sainsbury’s, the appeal is cost-savings derived from larger scale. The combination of Sainsbury’s and Morrisons would hold 23.6% of the UK market and add 500 supermarkets and 1,600 convenience stores to its portfolio – taking it closer to Tesco’s 27.8% market share. Buying Asda would take it to about 26.7%.

One industry expert said a combination with Asda was the “sweetheart deal” because it would not only bring larger scale but involve fewer stores serving the same customers in the south of the country.

The main benefit of any deal would come from cost-savings garnered from combining central operations, such as buying and property management, and aligning supplier terms.

Asda’s bigger supply chain brings greater potential savings and it is arguably a less complicated acquisition than Morrisons, which operates a large food processing business which Sainsbury’s would probably want to dispose of to a variety of specialist suppliers.

One issue is that businesses cannot seek pre-approval for a deal from the CMA, so launching a formal takeover offer for either Morrisons or Asda would involve an element of risk – consuming management time, and costly fees for bankers and lawyers.

As one industry expert says, “the critical argument is the role of the discounters” and the CMA’s rulings do not always follow the expected path. “It’s a lottery,” he said.

Analysts at Bernstein also say that “despite the benefits of a possible deal, the risk of distraction for Sainsbury’s would be high”.

The industry insider says: “Sainsbury’s is best served by being patient” as Asda and Morrisons are likely to continue to struggle. “There comes a point when the CMA has no choice but to let something happen as [Asda and Morrisons] can’t compete. You could argue that is already the case.”

This article was amended on 8 October 2026. An earlier version said that Sainsbury’s is unlikely to face significant competition if it opts to buy “Sainsbury’s or Asda”; that should have said Morrisons or Asda.

My latest discovery? You can eat the skin of a kiwifruit – and the benefits are myriad

The Guardian Thu, 08 Oct 2026 10:00:17 GMT

It turns out all that time spent peeling and paring was entirely wasted. Now I’m gobbling them like apples and putting the extra fibre to good use

Every day’s a school day, honestly. How on earth did I get to just short of my 60th birthday before finding out that you could eat the skin of kiwifruit? Astounding, just astounding. What a revelation. It’s odd, because of all fruit skins, it’s probably the one that looks least appetising. Nice clean oranges and bananas almost beg to be troughed, skins and all, yet we know this is a no-no. But it turns out that all of this small, hairy, boringly coloured object can go down the hatch. Admittedly, I have been slicing the ends off first, but I might start eating them, too.

The first time is the hardest. You need to set aside years of prejudice against that hairy skin that you’ve been so painstakingly removing. Mind over matter. Initially, I sliced my kiwis longways and then each half into four. Now, I’m just eating them like apples. Sometimes three bites, usually two, occasionally just the one. I promise you, a lifetime’s fear of the fur evaporates in an instant. At least, for me it did. I have to report that when I talked my mum into giving it a try, she gagged alarmingly and swore at me with some venom as she fought to expel bits of skin from her mouth. Perhaps it’s not for everyone, after all.

The health benefits are many, apparently. Plenty of furry fibre (I’m sure the furry type is the best) and all kinds of nutrient blah as well. This wasn’t the appeal for me, so much as the dispensing of the faff, all the peeling and paring. That said – and I apologise for oversharing – increasing the furry fibre intake made short shrift indeed of a recent bout of constipation. Highly recommend.

The kiwifruit’s trade association needs to get this out there – the easy eating, that is, not the laxative effect. I think it’s possible it doesn’t even know. In Lidl in Stourbridge this week, I saw some badged up as “easy peelers”. What? No need! If there had been anywhere to give them a wash, I’d have commenced an eat-it-whole demonstration there and then. Seriously, this is marketing gold. My kiwi consumption has gone from every now and then to every other hour. Once the word gets out, all that pent-up demand will be unblocked. Get yourself out there and panic-buy, while stocks last.

Adrian Chiles is a broadcaster, writer and Guardian columnist

Trump’s latest attacks on the press exude desperation

The Guardian Thu, 08 Oct 2026 10:00:16 GMT

Trump seems to invent ugly new variations on his press-bashing theme almost every day

When you hate the mainstream press as much as Donald Trump does, nothing gets in the way of the punishment fantasy.

Not court rulings. Not public opinion. Not even the dreadful consequence of less media coverage.

And certainly not any awareness of how the first amendment is supposed to function in American democracy.

This week, his revenge tour took yet another turn.

He barred one of his most disfavored media organizations – Politico – from boarding Air Force One, where it was supposed to provide “pool coverage” to the rest of the press corps as Trump traveled to Nebraska for a campaign stop on Monday afternoon.

That move was met with a strong show of solidarity by several media outlets, who decided not to fill the Politico spot.

And the White House was defiantly delusional, claiming that Trump will “continue to grant an unprecedented level of access to the press”.

This latest chapter came with the usual blast of venom at the mainstream media, though not specifically aimed at Politico.

“The New York Times and many other Artificial Media Outlets should be arrested for their dishonesty and disservice to our Country,” he posted on Truth Social.

The episode follows Trump’s effort in mid-September to ban Politico, CNN and MS Now from the White House. Those organizations quickly sued, charging that Trump’s action was unconstitutional.

Trump-appointed judge Timothy Kelly came down on the side of the media, issuing a temporary restraining order that ordered the White House to reinstate the press badges that had been taken away.

And since then, CNN has been kept off Air Force One repeatedly, using the rationale that access to the White House is one thing, but access to the president’s plane is another.

“The law is absolutely clear,” Ted Boutrous, the first amendment lawyer who is representing the three news organizations said in a statement. “The harm to our clients, the first amendment and the public as a whole is profound.”

The Trump administration’s position is that traveling with the president is a privilege not a right.

The fight is not over, since Kelly will conduct a hearing later this week over the media outlets’ request for a preliminary injunction – a stopgap measure to protect press access in advance of a possible trial.

Trump, of course, has been picking fights with individual journalists and entire news outlets for years. At this very moment, there are court fights involving the Associated Press, the Wall Street Journal, the New York Times and Disney, which owns ABC News and a number of local ABC affiliates.

So far, there’s been a rare display of support among news organizations that are normally each other’s competition. Columbia Journalism Review called it “a striking and heartening show of solidarity from the White House Press Corps”.

When the three outlets were kicked out of the White House last month, the other networks in the press pool decided not to replace CNN in the rotation, thus suspending coverage for a time.

Peter Baker of the New York Times noted that for the first time in his 30 years covering the White House, “the president will not have a network TV camera covering his everyday official actions and travels”.

What’s more, about 50 media organizations backed up the lawsuit by the three who had been singled out by filing an amicus brief.

It’s hard to understand exactly how less coverage and this constant squabbling benefits Trump, but apparently, he is making a different calculation.

His anti-press actions get a lot of attention, which is the very oxygen he requires to breathe. It doesn’t matter that much of the attention is negative.

Meanwhile, he has entered a phase of saying and doing ever more outrageous things, like his statement this week at a rally that his war in Iran was necessary to protect the world. Trump appeared to suggest that Iran could “take out” Los Angeles and San Diego if it develops a nuclear weapon which prompted California’s Democratic governor, Gavin Newsom, to call the president “deranged and dangerous”.

Trump exudes a sense of desperation these days, with the midterm elections only weeks away and his approval ratings underwater.

His war against the press is something of a reflex for him – it’s what comes naturally, especially when he doesn’t like the shape of reality.

The press corps’ newfound solidarity is encouraging. It’s been a long time coming from a group that, in the past, has responded to this president’s constant abuse with deference and dinner invitations.

Trump seems to invent ugly new variations on his press-bashing theme almost every day.

Standing together will be a necessity in the weeks and months ahead.

Margaret Sullivan is a Guardian US columnist writing on media, politics and culture

Indiana Fever and the Magasphere: a WNBA team’s dangerous path to popularity

The Guardian Thu, 08 Oct 2026 09:00:15 GMT

Teams have always symbolized division within America. And the Fever have come to prominence during a time of dark political intensity

It’s over for now, but no professional sports team spent more time receiving and drawing attention to itself than did the Indiana Fever this season. The Fever has broken, the team eliminated by the defending champion Las Vegas Aces for the second straight season, but Indiana succeeded in being the WNBA’s canary in the coal mine, embodying both the obvious and unintended consequences of rapid growth, while also allowing themselves to be a season-long distraction: part-time professional basketball team, part-time right-wing culture war centerpiece. Less than a decade ago, Atlanta and Minneapolis were praised for their unified political stances. Today, Trumpism has replaced social justice as the defining characteristic of the league – and as the curtain closed on the 2026 WNBA regular season, Indiana stood at its epicenter.

The Fever were the most polarizing team in professional sports, known less for their basketball than their culpability in pulling the league from its old cultural identity as a Black/queer league into its current climate of political divisiveness – a calculated and dangerous path to popularity. This season, there was the basketball of the WNBA, and then there was the Indiana Fever, the league’s Maga-friendly option.

Their two most recognizable players, Caitlin Clark and Sophie Cunningham, were in a constant state of churn, always in the news, always embroiled against an other, symbolizing and pandering to America’s fractures. Their best and longest-tenured player, Kelsey Mitchell, hasn’t been able to concentrate fully on basketball the past two seasons as the Clark-Cunningham sideshow devours the oxygen and may end her time in Indiana that began as the second overall pick in 2018.

Clark remains the league’s biggest name and its chief avatar – mildly reluctant or willing pawn, but an avatar nevertheless. She is an avatar for the money at a time when broadcasters and venture capitalists are making their bets on women’s sports. She represented a certain type of hope, that the day had arrived where women’s team sports would enjoy the same visibility as female stars such as Serena Williams and Lindsey Vonn.

She was an avatar of weaponization, the speculator’s proof that the WNBA is doomed by its own hand for not recognizing her overall importance to its future, a future bizarrely framed as bright only if Clark succeeds – an odd framework for sports, where the final score and holders of the trophies determines who wins.

Most obviously and explosively, Clark was an avatar for whiteness, a Christian, hetero whiteness that holds the pervasive belief that it is straight, white America – already the overwhelming and unchallenged dominant cultural and financial force in this country – that is under assault. Any struggle Clark showed on the court – a foul call, a non-call – was treated as if it were an urban crime statistic, unmistakable proof that Black people had even turned basketball lawless. The opportunistic and racist White House and the Trump administration repeated this fiction. Republican members of Congress earlier this season insinuated Clark was being discriminated against by the league because she is white. The Congressmen threatened the WNBA with a Department of Justice investigation if the league did not take steps to protect her. Clark and the Fever did little to dispel the notion.

Whenever Clark did succeed, her partisans saw it as proof of how much better the league would be if only it stopped persecuting her. Through Clark, and how she navigated playing basketball in a league largely comprised of Black women – even as Breanna Stewart, Paige Bueckers and a host of other white women thrive without incident – was how the government (as well as many fans and journalists) framed the state of women’s professional basketball. She is half of what all the fuss has been about.

The other half is Cunningham, who spent much of the season building the scaffolding for her second act by driving a wedge into heart of the league, positioning herself at the center of the attention-fueled culture war against trans women, being the blonde, blue-eyed foil to the league’s unruly Black women, and providing an entry point for the bros, their money and misogyny to show up, for men such an Enes Kanter Freedom to do what they have always done to women’s sport – find a way to denigrate it and be rewarded with attention. While it was all very tired and calculating, framed as speaking her truth, designed to reach the very group of white male sports fans that have either criticized or ignored women’s sports but are now bringing their toxicity to the tent under the guise of “growth,” Cunningham has been the subject of more attention than she’s ever had in her decade-long career, with public appearances and lengthy profiles. She knows exactly to whom she is talking, and why.

The Fever carrying these burdens – or wearing them proudly until having to answer for them – is how Clark’s career has shifted from starting her first season a phenom joining a team that hadn’t had a winning season in seven years to ending her third in daily controversy, with her as the signature, aggrieved face of Maga’s team.

With the avatars mercifully tabled, Clark emerged as an excellent player with enormous upside and serious deficiencies. She is a volume scorer but not yet a great one – her career field-goal percentage is just 42.3, below the league average, and for all her dazzle, her career three-point percentage is a below-average 34.2. She shot 36.1% from three this season, below the Fever team average of 38.6%. She is an adept playmaker whose true skill may be less in creating offense for herself and more in controlling the tempo of the game and involving her teammates. She was second in the league in assists and first in turnovers, fitting considering she constantly has the ball – similar to James Harden in a way. She is an apathetic defender.

As a basketball presence, she is wholly unlikeable. She does not play the game with her teammates as much as beyond them – a common affliction of many superstars that in victory is touted as a virtue but looks selfish following first-round defeats. She does not appear to play the game with joy or intensity, but carries a childish outrage, not only confronting officials on virtually every trip downcourt, but sprinting to berate them in dead-ball situations. Clark plays with grievance, an entitled grievance that recalls the White House grievance, the same grievance shared by much of the white electorate that uncoincidentally claims her as their champion – they’re all unfairly under attack.

For all the criticism, WNBA officials have actually shown remarkable restraint toward her. She exaggerates most calls and outwardly flops on others to steal calls – call it European gamesmanship, but the true nature of flopping is to receive something undeserved and is the worst example of immoral basketball. Even during timeouts Clark finds a way to spar with someone, be it a cameraman or an assistant coach.

Like Cunningham, however, Clark has mastered the key component of the so-called attention economy – she sees to it the camera is always on her. A more professional Clark, with fewer outbursts and deeper concentration on basketball would lower the temperature on the league, her team, herself, and would probably win her more trips to the foul line – but there was virtually no evidence this season that is what she wants.

Superstar petulance is nothing new, and if Stephanie White doesn’t return as coach, it won’t be the first time a star player will be accused of getting the coach fired. Nor is it the first time a sports team has reflected a national political mood or been pulled into its vortex. Usually reflection marks triumph – Black and Jewish America loved the Dodgers because of Jackie Robinson and Sandy Koufax just as the Yankee teams of Tony Lazzeri, Frankie Crosetti, Joe DiMaggio, and Phil Rizzuto made them beloved in Italian-American homes.

Sign up to WNBA 30

A limited run women’s basketball newsletter dedicated to the league’s historic 30th season.

after newsletter promotion

Teams have also symbolized division. In the 1980s, the Boston Celtics were often considered white America’s team because of Larry Bird, the high number of white players the Celtics routinely signed, and the perception that the Celtics did not play with the flamboyant Blackness that defined the rest of the league, which allowed white fans to see themselves in their no-nonsense, blue-collar ethic.

Despite the presence of James White, Dont’a Hightower, the McCourty twins and Stephon Gilmore, the late-stage Brady/Belichick Patriots were adopted by certain white supremacists because the Patriots were led offensively by a handful of white players – Tom Brady, Rob Gronkowski and Julian Edelman. The supposedly colorblind whites had found their ideal.

None of those examples, however, have existed within the combination of today’s dark political intensity where the federal government has positioned itself as the legal guardian of whiteness and the precarious political footing of the league. The nation has effectively closed its borders to everyone except white South Africans, while Cunningham encourages the right to use the WNBA for anti-trans fodder and the DOJ believes Clark needs its protection.

In a feeble attempt to distance itself from the obvious racism, the Fever periodically made bland, unconvincing statements – there’s no room for hate in the game – but their actions undermined their sentiments. Cunningham knows exactly who her fans view as the enemy, which fires to stoke on her podcasts, which dog whistles to sound. As does Clark, for her constant on-court histrionics elicit the right sympathy from the right people. They both know exactly what they’re doing.

The season over, the Fever closed 2026 not by celebrating their best record since 2015, or by marking the first time since the 2009-2012 season the franchise posted three-straight 20-win seasons and have momentum as a potential title contender, but with more grievance. General manager Amber Cox read a ridiculous, gaslighting statement blaming outside media for the odious reputation of Fever fans. “The attacks on our fan base have no basis in reality, and must stop,” she read from the podium. Mitchell’s own words painfully contradicted Cox, as did rival players around the league.

Maybe they just want it this way.

Here’s what connects the Cornell alleged rape case to those before: accused men not being held to serious account

The Guardian Thu, 08 Oct 2026 07:00:13 GMT

There was progress after #MeToo, but not enough. Certainly not enough to shift the assumptions that still protect men and denigrate victims

If the past is another country, and there is nothing so poignant as the innocence of recent history, then there is a third category of engagement with the era directly preceding our own, encapsulated by the line “that didn’t age well”.

I found myself thinking about this in relation to news of the seven male students accused of gang-raping a 20-year-old woman two years ago in their fraternity house at Cornell University, and now facing a civil suit brought by their alleged victim. Apparent failures by Cornell and the local district attorney to act appropriately at the time have triggered another round of commentary about the “death of #MeToo”, not least with the looming anniversary on 15 October, the date in 2017 when the hashtag first went viral. But the period I find myself thinking about predates even that, when it seemed as if these questions of consent had been largely resolved.

“Campus rape” – a category of sex crime historically taken even less seriously by the criminal justice system than regular rape – has always flushed out complacencies among those who otherwise consider themselves liberal.

So it was in 2015, when it seemed to many liberal observers as if, after almost eight solid years of President Barack Obama in the White House, a crucial line had been crossed; conservatism had lost, liberalism had won, and the biggest threat to female students on campus was the temptation to overpunish men for minor transgressions, thanks to the sheer force of the pendulum swing to their side.

This was the notion of “liberal overreach”, in which a popular president and a comfortably dominant political order allowed for what, in hindsight, looks like a load of decadently counterintuitive takes, accusing the left of going too far.

Two things pertinent to the Cornell case happened that year: Valerie Jarrett, the Obama adviser tasked with co-chairing a White House panel on women and girls, came up with the idea of using civil rights legislation known as Title IX to prosecute sexual assault cases on campus. And, in January that year, a 22-year-old woman was sexually assaulted at a frat party at Stanford University in what would become known as the “Stanford swimmer case”. As with the Jane Doe at the centre of the Cornell rape allegations, Emily Doe had been drunk when the sexual assault occurred and much of the debate would centre on her ability to consent.

The reason for bringing this up is twofold. First, Stanford’s Title IX process had yet to be introduced when Emily Doe was assaulted in 2015, but her experience foreshadowed just how inadequate the new internal complaint system would become for handling serious felonies on campus.

Second, the conversation around Emily Doe’s own culpability was a stark reminder that the Obama era had ushered in neither a brave new dawn of understanding around consent, nor a period in which innocent male students were at risk of persecution. Instead, the details of the case ran along age-old lines in which a man, Brock Turner, after being discovered assaulting an unconscious Emily Doe by the bins at the back of the fraternity house, was found guilty of felony sexual assault and sentenced to six months in jail, of which he served three.

While the assailant was spoken of glowingly by the judge as a champion swimmer, his victim was dragged through the mud, a narrative that only changed when Chanel Miller, who would later dispense with her anonymity, read out her victim impact statement in court. “You don’t know me,” she said, addressing Turner directly, “but you’ve been inside me, and that’s why we’re here today.”

If looking back at this case brings on a dismal sense that nothing changes, it also allows us to celebrate a little progress. After an initial flurry of whataboutery, it seems to me the Jane Doe in the Cornell case has been subject to considerably less public scepticism than Miller was a decade ago. The problem remains the utter pointlessness of Title IX as a mechanism for punishing serious sexual assault – two of Jane Doe’s alleged assailants were expelled from Cornell, two were suspended, one defendant was issued a persona non grata, and two were barred from campus – and some lingering fallacies about the role played by alcohol.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

Espousing a popular view, in his 2019 book Talking to Strangers, Malcolm Gladwell, over an entire chapter, presented the crime against Miller as a tragic misunderstanding between two people – a “transparency failure on steroids” – which wouldn’t have happened had alcohol not been present. This is true.

Also true, but omitted from Gladwell’s analysis, is that it wouldn’t have happened if Brock Turner hadn’t been male; if parents didn’t raise their darling boys differently to how they raise their girls; if the criminal justice system prosecuted sexual assault with the enthusiasm it brings to, say, motoring offences; if “campus rape” was taken seriously as a category of crime; if two-thirds of the rapes and sexual assaults that occur in the US didn’t go unreported; if the conviction rate for those that are reported was higher than about 8%.

It would seem to me that the pivotal disinhibiting agent in the sexual assault of Chanel Miller, and in the alleged assault of the latest Jane Doe, wasn’t drugs or alcohol, but entitlement, misogyny and a well-founded assumption on the part of the men accused that they would never be held to serious account.

Emma Brockes is a Guardian columnist

Is Fury v Joshua about meritocratic sporting excellence or just algorithmic celebrity power?

The Guardian Thu, 08 Oct 2026 07:00:13 GMT

This long-awaited fight is happening exactly as intended: at the sweet spot where commercial potential meets a genuine absence of jeopardy

The 1912 Olympic marathon was held in a brutal Scandinavian heatwave, and before long Shizo Kanakuri of Japan was flagging. His journey to Stockholm had been debilitating; he had barely trained and struggled to sleep. At around the 16-mile mark he finally gave in. Exhausted and disoriented, he stumbled off the road and into a garden party, where – according to his bemused hosts – he sat and drank orange juice for an hour.

The next day, deeply ashamed at his failure to complete the race, he quietly took a boat back to Japan. In Sweden the mystery of the “disappearing runner” took on almost mythical proportions. Kanakuri’s name was on the country’s missing persons list for more than 50 years.

In the 1960s, a journalist tracked him down to Kumamoto in southern Japan, where he worked as a geography teacher. At great expense, Swedish television flew him back to Stockholm and ferried him to the spot where he had abandoned the race.

So it was that in March 1967, Kanakuri finally completed the 1912 Olympic marathon in a time of 54 years, eight months, six days, five hours, 32 minutes and 20.3 seconds. None of this, of course, was of the least sporting consequence. But it was a nice story, generating substantial interest, and the newspapers could fill their column inches, and the broadcasters could fill their schedules, and perhaps ultimately this was all that mattered.

All of which brings us, by a similarly circuitous route, to Tyson Fury v Anthony Joshua, a heavyweight fight that is often wrongly described as happening several years too late, long after the 38-year-old Fury and the 36-year-old Joshua have passed their fighting peak, years since either man has beaten anyone of world-class pedigree, a delay that makes Mayweather v Pacquiao look impromptu.

In fact Fury v Joshua is happening exactly as intended: at the sweet spot where commercial potential meets an absence of genuine jeopardy. Make this fight in 2021 and both men are putting titles, the undisputed crown, an entire fighting legacy, at terminal risk. Make it in 2031 and not even the combined bullshit wattage of Frank Warren, Eddie Hearn, Dana White and Turki al-Sheikh could persuade the public that this was anything other than a fairground sideshow.

No: it has to be now, before anyone stops caring. Like a market trader extracting maximum price for a fruit on the very brink of going rotten, this is the fight business operating on God-tier mode. “We will get it on at the right time,” Joshua once said. That was in April 2016, when a fight with Fury would have been worth a fraction of the £150m it is worth now. When it comes to boxing, absence makes the purse grow fatter.

That this is often regarded as a minor annoyance, a glitch in the system rather than a fundamental existential-level malfunction, is just one of the reasons for boxing’s slow drift towards mainstream irrelevance. Virtually every other sport on earth operates along the principle that at some point the best will meet the best, and assembles structures and rules and governing bodies that compel this into being.

Boxing is pretty much the only sport in the world where this is not true, which raises the germane question of whether it can really be considered a sport at all, at least in the modern, codified sense.

Naturally Fury has spent the past few weeks (Months? Years?) desperately trying to pin the blame on Joshua for not getting the fight made. In Fury’s tale of the tape, he has been ready and waiting this whole time. With the exception of the two and a half years he spent out of the sport dealing with a combination of doping charges, substance abuse, and mental health crises.

Or the subsequent two and a half years he spent battling Deontay Wilder, not just in the ring but in the courts. As frequently thrilling as that trilogy of fights was, even at the time there was a sense we were missing out on something even greater; that as one rivalry was playing itself out, there were others suffering as a result.

Then there were the retirements: around five in total, depending on how you count these things. It feels pleasingly nostalgic now to recall that Fury first quit boxing in 2013 (“1000000%, no matter what, ill never fight again”), then again in 2016, again in 2017 (“THE END”), again in 2022 (“the truth, the gospel truth, nothing but the truth, I’m done, no amount of material assets or money will make me come back”), and most recently from 2025 to 2026. I’m no expert in contract negotiation. But if you’re trying to establish yourself as a bona fide sporting and business partner, maybe stop retiring every few years?

Cowardice will always be too strong a word for anyone who steps between those ropes and risks their health for our titillation. But it is a shame that a fight that could have defined an entire generation of British boxing is happening only when the stakes are so low. For all the biblical hype that will doubtless accumulate under the wheels over the next two months, what does this fight actually tell us? What gets settled or rewritten? Is it actually in anybody’s interests for anything to be settled or rewritten, given the potential for an even more lucrative rematch sometime in late 2027?

Prizefighting owes its success to the ability to hold two ideas in its orbit at once. First, the sense of sporting ultimacy, the idea that what we are watching is a kind of pinnacle of raw human endurance, the very best fighting men and women on the planet. And second, the sense of vaudeville and pantomime, the deliberate and often provocative packaging of a product for entertainment and consumption.

Boxing has always been at its greatest when each has been in the service of the other. A Christmas cracker requires the colourful wrapping and the bit that bangs in the middle. Remove either and the whole concept falls apart.

But for years now, these ideas have been breaking in opposite directions. What we essentially have now is a sport increasingly rearranging around the two disparate poles of meritocratic sporting excellence and algorithmic celebrity power.

In the former, Moses Itauma is one of this country’s best-kept sporting secrets, and an all-British world title clash between Daniel Dubois and Fabio Wardley is feted as one of the greatest fights of the decade but generates virtually zero wider recognition.

In the latter, the internet pest Jake Paul is one of the sport’s most bankable names, the greatest heavyweight of his generation, Oleksandr Usyk, is fighting a kickboxer, Floyd Mayweather Jr is in talks about coming out of retirement to fight Mike Tyson, and Conor Benn and Chris Eubank Jr keep rematching for the next 10 years.

Which world does Fury v Joshua belong to? Which half of the marathon are we being invited to watch? I want to believe – and so do Netflix – that Fury can still be the force of old, rather than an increasingly monotonous provocateur. I want to believe in the Joshua of the 2010s, unscarred and optimistic, this beautiful man of beautiful clean lines. I want to believe this is sport. But deep down, I think we all know the answer.

Stockpile food – and wash your hands: is that really how to prepare for environmental catastrophe?

The Guardian Thu, 08 Oct 2026 05:00:10 GMT

The UK state is dumping its responsibilities on our doorsteps, while green-lighting policies that lead us closer to crisis

Would you mind fixing the NHS? And while you’re at it, could you please build an anti-missile system in your garden? Then regulate the banks, replace the water mains, tax the very rich and use the proceeds to rebuild our schools. Well, come on people: what are you waiting for?

I exaggerate, but this isn’t very far from the approach taken by the government’s Prepare campaign. Crucial functions, way beyond the scope of individual action, are dumped on our doorsteps while those in power fail to act. As a result, our national resilience is arguably lower than at any time since the second world war. At the Labour conference last week, Andy Burnham promised “a Britain where people feel the country has got their back again”. To make good on that pledge, he will have to change almost everything.

It’s not that the advice offered by Prepare – a government campaign designed to promote readiness for emergencies – is irrational. But when the state is absent or working against us, households and communities cannot fill the gap. The campaign tells us, for example, to conserve water during droughts by turning off the tap while brushing teeth, or taking a shower instead of a bath. For sure. Every citizen should do their duty. But the government has at the same time declared datacentres “nationally significant infrastructure projects” that can be forced through the planning system, despite two startling facts. The first is that even Water UK – the body representing water companies, those paragons of environmental responsibility – has said there isn’t enough water to support the new datacentres. The second is that, as a freedom of information response reveals, the government has no idea what they are being used for. You could be turning off your taps so the water can be used to nudify celebrities.

Talking of droughts, the government’s National Risk Register seems seriously out of whack. It estimates the risk of a drought with a moderate impact occurring in the next five years at just 0.2-1%. What?? It also estimates the risk of heatwaves with a “significant” impact – by which it means between 200 and 1,000 deaths – at only 1-5% over the next five years. The government estimates there were 2,877 heat-associated excess deaths in England during this year’s hot weather in May and June. There were a similar number of deaths in the heatwave of 2022.

But never mind: the Prepare campaign advises that “if you live in a home that is more likely to overheat … contact your local council, your letting agency or Citizens Advice to find out what help and support they can provide”. Good luck with that. In the meantime, the “future homes standard” is at last due to come into force in March 2028, but thanks to lobbying by the building sector, according to some practitioners it still won’t deliver new homes matched to the climate challenges we face. And local authorities have been blocked from demanding anything better, thanks to the same corporate pressure.

Survive floods, the Prepare campaign tells us, by “packing a ‘grab bag’ of essentials in advance”, moving “valuable items upstairs” and making “changes to your property to reduce the damage flooding can do”. But one in nine new homes are being built in areas at risk of flooding according to data from Aviva, and a recent high court judgment reveals that the law prevents local authorities from blocking such developments, even if they fail a crucial safety test.

These are not the starkest examples of public exhortation colliding with government failure. The Prepare campaign tells us to help stop the spread of avian flu by washing hands “with soap and water” after feeding wild birds. Fine. But at the same time, at the behest of lobbyists, the government is pushing a “poultry sector growth plan”. This will multiply the number of super-incubators of avian flu: namely the factory farms rearing chickens. As the Scientific Task Force on Avian Influenza and Wild Birds points out, poultry farms are where highly pathogenic bird flu first arose. Through their growth and intensification, the spreading of their manure on fields and its runoff into rivers, we could scarcely devise a better formula for generating new variants of the virus and the attendant ecological disasters. Oh hang on, we could: the shooting industry is still allowed to breed tens of millions of pheasants and partridges in similar conditions each year, then release them into the countryside to mingle with wild birds. But do wash your hands.

You’re also advised to “reduce your exposure to air pollution”. How? The government is allowing new homes to be equipped with wood-burning stoves, building huge and arguably pointless new roads and consulting on radically delaying the transition to all-electric vehicles. All, once again, in response to lobbying.

As for food resilience, the Prepare campaign scarcely mentions it, except to say we should stock some “non-perishable food that doesn’t need cooking” in our homes. Last week, a group of anonymous senior food executives warned that, in the face of “material reductions in yield, quality and reliability of supply”, their industry was “defaulting to quick-fix crisis management” rather than taking a strategic, long-term approach. “At present, we are seeing companies either consistently lobby against necessary regulations or stay silent,” they said. The result is a likely failure to address an existential threat.

There was much in Burnham’s speech that delighted me, especially his listing of deregulation as one of the five great evils putting Britain on “the wrong path”. That’s a break with 47 years of policy, in which all governments have dismissed essential public protections as “red tape” that must be cut. The Tories were still at it in their own conference this week – telling us, in effect, they are here to burn it all down. But, like Keir Starmer, Burnham has tied his own hands by pledging to “stick to our fiscal rules”. These rules did not come from government. They were developed by Westminster junktanks and pushed into being by the media. As Larry Elliott has argued persuasively, they are unnecessary and self-defeating.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

The threats to our resilience are the same as the threats to our democracy: what Burnham called “that sense of the powers-that-be pulling against the people, not with them”. We’ve had five decades of lobbyists shaping policy, with devastating consequences for our ability to withstand crises. Willing to play our part as we may be, we cannot do the work of government.

George Monbiot is a Guardian columnist

This article was amended on 8 October 2026. The illustration was replaced as an earlier version had said to take baths instead of showers, rather than vice versa.
