A death, a plagiarism scandal and a quest for revenge: the bizarre tale of Otto Z

The Guardian Thu, 08 Oct 2026 04:00:09 GMT

After his mother died, Otto became convinced he’d been wronged by the forensic investigators – and that one of them was a fraud. The truth was even stranger

On a balmy, quiet evening in June 2020, Otto’s elderly mother, Doria, was fading in her Munich apartment. As she lay with her eyes closed, her pale face, framed by her white hair, was calm.

Otto, masked, gloved and draped in a sterile apron, dozed in a chair beside her. Otto, who sometimes goes by the name Rainer, and whose last name is only known as “Z” because of Germany’s strict privacy laws, was a doctor who had cared for his mother for years, ever since she had suffered a stroke and moved in with him. He described the course of that night to me. He woke to the sound of her short breath and tried to sit her upright. Her eyes were shut, and her lips pursed. She stopped breathing. Otto reached for his phone to call for help, but then Doria opened her eyes and stared into his. She smiled, drew one last deep breath, shut her eyes again, and lay still.

Otto sank into his chair. As a doctor, he had seen death many times, but his own mother’s passing sent him into shock. He felt frozen, watching the windows glisten in the fading light. He was 66, and his brother and father had died years before. He had no friends. He had given all of his time, energy and attention to his mother’s care, and now that his task was suddenly over, he had no one to turn to. He mourned in solitude, with an impromptu ritual. He lit candles and set metal plates at the four corners of her bed. He sat beside her and thought about her soul.

Once the rite was complete, Otto picked up the phone and called a funeral home. He knew the procedure: as a doctor, he could issue his own mother’s death certificate. After he hung up, Otto waited. It was the last calm moment he would experience for many months.

After he called the funeral home, Otto told me, he waited beside his mother all night and into the next afternoon before he heard a knock at the door. He was surprised to see that, rather than doctors, the two men in the hallway were police officers. They wore bulletproof vests and carried guns. He invited them inside, where they scanned the rooms. He directed them to his mother’s bedroom and followed close behind, but the officers stopped him and asked him to take a seat.

While the officers inspected his mother’s body, Otto sat in his office. Forty-five minutes passed, and then he heard someone else enter the flat without knocking. A tall, stylish woman approached and introduced herself as a coroner from the Munich Institute of Forensic Medicine, before walking off to the bedroom.

Otto knew that a coroner – as opposed to a doctor or nurse – is only sent to the scenes of suspicious deaths. He followed her to the bedroom, where she had begun inspecting his mother’s body. Otto wasn’t easily rattled, but he told me that the way the coroner handled Doria threw him off. He found her elegant attire unprofessional, given the circumstances, and her bedside manner lacking. He said that he tried, however, to remain polite and helpful. As she went about her work, he offered his recollections from his mother’s final hours and an account of her long illness, which he had documented minutely over the years. Otto informed the coroner that he was a doctor, but it seemed to him that she was uninterested. She turned to the police officers and, without explanation, told them that this was a matter for law enforcement, before leaving the flat. Otto told me he wondered why nobody was listening to him, the grieving son, the doctor?

More armed police officers arrived and searched the rooms. A commissioner approached Otto and told him to gather his things, as they needed to conduct their work uninterrupted. Sleep-deprived and grief-stricken, Otto was ushered on to the street and ordered not to return. He drifted along Munich’s wide, lamplit streets. As darkness fell upon the city, Otto told me he felt that he “didn’t understand the world any more”.

He checked into a hotel, but found it intolerable to sit in his room. Later that night he wandered back to his flat and found the door sealed with police tape. He was desperate to check in on his mother and thought she might still be inside. He broke the police seal and entered the dark rooms, which were a chaotic mess, as if burglars had turned it over before fleeing the scene. He entered the bedroom. His mother was gone.

Otto went back to his hotel but still found it impossible to sleep. He returned to his flat a second time at about 2am, and this time he found several police officers stationed there. They spotted him and put him in the back of a police car. He was taken to the Institute of Forensic Medicine, where doctors extracted samples from him: hair, urine and blood. When they had finished, Otto was taken back to the police station and found himself alone in what he described as a tiny, windowless cell with only a mattress, a stainless steel toilet and bars on the door.

The next morning, two officers questioned him. How did he care for Doria? Why did he document her condition so precisely? Had he given his mother a concentrated saline injection? Only then did Otto understand: the police believed he had murdered his mother.

After two nights in jail, or possibly three (his memory of this time is confused), Otto was released and allowed to return to his flat. While it was a relief to be home, he told me he still didn’t understand why he was under suspicion. He had not yet been formally charged with any crime. Otto wrote to the head of the Institute of Forensic Medicine, Prof Matthias Graw, to ask if his team had discovered anything suspicious while inspecting Doria’s body. Eager to prove his innocence, Otto offered to send Graw all of his day-to-day notes on Doria’s health. He suggested, boldly, that they co-author a paper about the cause of her death.

Graw never answered Otto’s emails, and Otto fell into a depression. He told me he began blaming himself for his mother’s death. Had he made a mistake? Overlooked some critical detail? Was there some way he could have saved her? Over the years, he said, he had taken her to see 19 different specialists to ensure that she received the best care. He made sure she exercised and spent time each day in the fresh air. He had tried his best, hadn’t he?

Doria was his whole world. Before the pandemic he used to take her into the city centre each night, where she was a favourite among the buskers for her generous tips. In her younger years, Doria had been an avid traveller, and Otto had taken her, in a wheelchair, on one last holiday to Italy. Now she was gone. Otto’s despair grew until he was unable to eat or sleep.

In January 2021, the authorities dropped their investigation into his mother’s death, and Otto was cleared of any wrongdoing. But he still couldn’t get over her death. He checked himself into a psychiatric treatment centre, hoping to quiet his mind.

Through therapy and exercise, Otto slowly regained his strength. Meanwhile, he had received a copy of the results of his mother’s toxicological report, signed by Graw and two of his institute’s specialists, but he was too disoriented to examine them carefully. Months passed. It was mid-summer, after Otto had moved back into his apartment, when he finally sat down with Doria’s medical files and the report.

With two PhDs and decades of experience in medicine and chemistry, Otto knew how to interpret lab reports. He told me that something seemed off. Data seemed to him to have been highlighted selectively. Other details seemed to him to have been glossed over. In the toxicological report, he said he spotted a chemical compound – commonly associated with exposure to cold – in her bloodstream. In his telling, an impossible, unspeakable idea crept into his mind: could his mother have somehow still been alive when she was taken away and stowed in the mortuary’s freezer? Could she have actually died at the Institute of Forensic Medicine, under the coroner’s care? And if so, how? The report also mentioned unusual traces of a substance contained in the autumn crocus flower, a poison called colchicine.

Otto began researching the Institute of Forensic Medicine. He started with its director, Prof Matthias Graw, and discovered that decades earlier, when Graw was a doctoral student at the University of Hamburg, he had written his dissertation on a certain naturally occurring poison found in the autumn crocus flower, called colchicine – the same poison found in Doria’s blood. Otto told me that a dark theory took shape in his mind: what if the institute had tried to frame him, to cover up the fact that they had actually killed his mother?

He did not go to the police – who, he reasoned, must work closely with the head of the institute of legal medicine. He would take the matter into his own hands. Hoping to perform his own examinations, Otto again wrote to the institute and requested access to his mother’s remains. Once more, his letter received no reply. In his apartment, hunched over his computer, Otto dug deeper into Graw, looking for evidence of negligence or criminality in the records of the man who oversaw his mother’s autopsy. He scoured scientific literature to research colchicine, the poison in which Graw was an expert.

By mid-February 2022, Otto had on his desk a book, dated 1982. Its title was Colchicine – 100 Years of Research. One of the chapters – its experiments, findings, tables and conclusion – was nearly identical to Graw’s dissertation, published five years later. Otto was convinced that he had in his hands the evidence he needed to bring Graw down.

At the end February 2022, a man named Stefan Weber was sitting in his office on the outskirts of Salzburg when an intriguing email landed in his inbox. The message claimed that Graw, the head of the Institute of Forensic Medicine at the University of Munich and one of the most respected forensic scientists in Germany, had plagiarised his doctoral thesis.

This was the kind of message Weber lived for. Fifty-six years old, baby-faced, broad, energetic and unrelentingly serious, Weber is the German-speaking world’s most-feared plagiarism hunter. His investigations have previously targeted Austria’s former labour and family minister Christine Aschbacher, who stepped down after Weber claimed her master’s thesis showed “never-before-seen depths of gobbledegook, nonsense and plagiarism”, and the German politician Annalena Baerbock, whose once-promising bid for the chancellorship was torpedoed when he investigated her book. The New York Times has called Weber the “undisputed terror of academics, politicians, [and] celebrities”.

Weber does not go out of his way to be liked. A former communications professor, he failed on eight occasions at eight universities to attain tenure. His colleagues in academia often found him brusque and inflexible. He told me he was hated because of his insistence on high standards.

Weber dresses in black and conducts his affairs with extreme scrupulousness. Fearing diabetes, he fasts for long periods. He spends his days in almost complete solitude, moving between his office, the library and the copy shop. He receives numerous requests for investigations each month, mostly from law firms and private individuals who want him to look into an applicant, competitor or colleague. Weber told me he charges up to €350 an hour for his work. He frequently pillories both public figures and obscure academics on his blog, where he also rails against “the Wokistan ideology” and has written: “Rightwing extremist must be understood as a title of honour!” In his spare time, he writes lofty books of philosophy and theory, with titles such as Language, Humanity, Universe.

The email, sent by one Otto Z, claimed that Graw’s entire career was “built on deception”. From Otto’s description, the colchicine book would have been an easy source to pilfer. It had been published in East Germany at the height of the cold war, which meant that it most likely wasn’t known to western academics when Graw published his dissertation. It was also, in plagiarism-hunter parlance, “grey literature”: informal material that isn’t peer-reviewed and therefore lies outside the reach of digital research platforms. Without Otto’s tip-off, it would have been impossible for Weber to discover the book’s existence.

Weber accepted the case and, with the help of an assistant, got to work researching the book. The archive of the East German publisher had been lost after reunification, and the book had never been cited by another source. Weber went searching for a physical copy. At the library, the elderly archivist told him they didn’t carry it. After consulting her databases, she informed him that no other library in the world did, either. But she found a single copy on eBay, for $220, and soon Weber held the book in his hands: a bright red hardcover. When Weber sat down to read it, he discovered that the red book told an incredible story nearly lost to history.

It was a record of an academic symposium held in 1981 at a hospital in the small Romanian city of Târgu Neamţ. Present were eminent experts on colchicine – biologists, pharmacists, zoologists – who gathered to present their work. Their lectures and conversations were assembled into chapters that chronicled the history of their niche field of research. Since at least the first century, the autumn crocus has been known to be toxic. Since the sixth century, the toxin responsible, colchicine, has been used to treat gout. Throughout the 20th century, new uses for colchicine were discovered: its ability to disrupt microtubules, for example, helps scientists study cell division, disease mechanisms and drug toxicity.

More surprising than any discovery presented at the symposium, however, was the guest list. Experts came from both sides of the iron curtain. At least two Americans were present: zoologist John Julius Biesele and obesity researcher Jules Hirsch. Had these westerners risked their reputations, careers and possibly their freedom to take part?

Perhaps the explanation had something to do with the symposium’s host, Elena Ceaușescu, the eccentric and ruthless wife of Nicolae Ceaușescu, then-dictator of Romania. Adding a bizarre twist to Weber’s investigation, Mrs Ceaușescu was, herself, an infamous academic cheat. Despite only completing elementary school, she believed that she was “born a great chemist”, and coerced the Polytechnic Institute in Bucharest into awarding her a PhD in chemistry. Throughout her husband’s reign, she forced Romanian chemists to produce work under her name. Had she somehow blackmailed western scientists into attending her conference? Or could they have been spies sent by the CIA to gather intelligence?

When Romania’s Soviet-backed regime collapsed in 1989, Elena Ceaușescu, along with her husband, was executed by firing squad. Weber’s research turned up no other references to her groundbreaking conference. By 2022, most of its attendants had also passed away. The conference seemed destined to remain a footnote in the history of science. But poring over the pages of Colchicine, Weber was soon convinced that one man had not overlooked the book: Matthias Graw.

After cross-referencing the red book and Graw’s dissertation, Weber and his assistant concluded that nearly 80% of Graw’s work was not original. Two of his thesis’s central chapters and many whole sections were word-for-word copies, with images and tables reproduced wholesale.

On 6 June 2022, Weber finally filed his report. In the 70-page document, which he sent to several media outlets, he claimed that Graw had plagiarised deliberately and with intent to deceive. “The case smells of severe scientific misconduct,” he declared in his blog. “The head of a forensic medicine institute … obviously has a corpse in the basement himself.”

Graw was on holiday in northern Norway when word reached him. On 20 June 2022, a reporter from the investigative magazine Der Spiegel contacted the University of Munich’s Institute of Forensic Medicine, asking if Graw would like to comment on allegations that he had plagiarised his thesis. Graw, a stern man of 66, told me through his lawyer that he remembered being baffled by the call. He explained that he had gone on holiday and left his laptop behind in Munich, about 1,500 miles away. Without it, he couldn’t possibly respond to each of the many accusations, which were anyway baseless. Soon after, the legal department of Graw’s employer, the University of Munich, called Graw to say that they could not support or represent him, as they had to maintain impartiality until the end of the investigation.

Der Spiegel broke the story on 1 July 2022 with an article headlined: “Serious plagiarism allegations against Munich forensic pathologist”. The Munich-based Süddeutsche Zeitung quoted Weber saying that Graw should be suspended while the allegations were investigated. Then came the tabloid Bild, which reported that several lawyers were calling for all the institute’s reports published under Graw’s directorship – thousands – to be reviewed, and the cases re-examined, potentially causing an “earthquake in the Munich judiciary”.

There were calls for Graw to resign. His underlings at the institute began speculating about his successor. The German government asked him to step down from his position as vice-president of the Society for Forensic Medicine. Finally, Graw’s alma mater, the University of Hamburg, opened an inquiry. If its investigation corroborated Weber’s report, Graw’s doctorate would be rescinded. He would lose his office, tenure and pension.

While Weber waited for the results of the Hamburg inquest, in late August he was surprised to read a follow-up story in Bild. Without alerting Weber, Otto had granted the paper an interview in which he claimed that Graw had stolen a gold tooth from his mother during the autopsy. In the article, Otto also claimed that his mother, Doria, was a Jewish Holocaust survivor – which immediately evoked a parallel between the gold tooth theft and the Nazi concentration camps. It was Weber’s policy never to investigate his clients’ motives. He was only interested in the truth, not in hearsay or petty grievances. But reading the article, he began to wonder whether Otto’s interest in Graw might go beyond academic integrity.

Three months after opening their investigation, the University of Hamburg’s panel of ombudsmen finished their internal inquiry. Graw’s detractors expected his disgrace to be complete. But the story was to take a new, unexpected twist.

The university team did not agree with the conclusions of Weber’s report accusing Graw of plagiarism. In fact, they pointed the finger in an entirely new direction. In the university’s view, it wasn’t Graw’s dissertation that was fraudulent. The panel had examined the red book on colchicine, which Graw had supposedly plagiarised for his thesis. And in their expert opinion, it was the red book that was fake.

Weber was stunned. He began looking into the university inquiry’s claims. First, it stated that the publisher’s address listed on the copyright page didn’t correspond to any real location in the former German Democratic Republic. Second, a certain technical term was translated awkwardly into English. And third, the text cited a 1983 source, which was impossible for a book printed in 1982 and based on a 1981 conference.

This evidence struck Weber as weak. It could all be the result of sloppy socialist-era publishing, rather than proof of a forgery. And why would anyone go to such lengths to destroy Graw’s reputation as to create an entirely fake book with such an elaborate backstory?

Still, Weber felt his abilities as an investigator had been called into question, and he set out to crush the accusations. He began by contacting Otto, who had first sent him a pdf scan of the red book, before Weber’s librarian found a print copy on sale on eBay. He asked where exactly he had first found the red book. Previously, Otto had explained that he had seen it cited in a patent, then happened upon the volume he had in his possession at a Serbian flea market. Weber asked, which flea market? And could he provide the patent where it was cited?

Otto, who had previously been helpful in all of his interactions with Weber, became evasive, then angry. Without answering Weber’s questions, he insisted that the University of Hamburg had performed a sham investigation designed to clear Graw’s name. Then, turning conspiratorial, he flooded Weber’s inbox with hundreds of pages of documents chronicling his mother’s death and his reasons for believing that Graw had mishandled her remains.

Weber tried to make sense of Otto’s behaviour by working through the twists in the story on his blog. “If [this is a] forgery, then all this is as unlikely as researchers finding out tomorrow that the Earth is flat,” he wrote on 6 October 2022. Weber saw only two options: either the academic elite had conspired to protect Graw by conducting a shoddy investigation, or Otto had forged the book with the intention of using Weber as a pawn in a shockingly elaborate scheme to sabotage Graw. He announced that if the latter was true, he would renounce plagiarism hunting for ever.

Weber cleared his schedule and turned his attention to the red book. He looked through old GDR phone books for the name of the translator – but no person under that name seemed to live in East Berlin at the time. Weber brought the book to an antiquarian, who claimed that the volume’s cloth bookmark was unusual for that era of East German publishing. A graphic designer informed him that the book’s primary font, Scotch Modern, was only released in 2008. Finally, Weber tracked down the photographer responsible for a key photo of the autumn crocus, who told him that he had uploaded the picture to Wikimedia Commons in 2005.

Weber realised he had been duped. On 13 October, he publicly apologised and revoked his accusations against Graw in a blog post that called the affair “a disaster for plagiarism research”. Then, in a new blog post titled Chronology of a Failed Character Assassination, he set out to document how the book had been produced.

Graw was perfectly sure he had not copied his PhD dissertation, but in a recent phone call, he told me how unsettling the accusations had been: “One thing was clear: the plagiarism hunters had been commissioned by someone, but the question was who, and why?” He spent months trying to calm people in his circles, convincing them he’d done nothing wrong. When he received a pdf of the red book he was supposed to have plagiarised, he was struck by how many glaring errors it contained – and how many people had overlooked them.

During this time, Otto had initiated a series of civil proceedings against Graw, accusing him of copyright infringement. In August 2022, Graw read the interview with Otto in Bild, in which Otto further accused him of stealing a gold tooth from his dead mother. It was then he realised that Otto, the bereaved son, was behind the plot to destroy his career. In October, Graw filed a criminal complaint against Otto, asking for a police investigation of the whole affair.

On 8 November 2022, police burst into Otto’s apartment. Officers found extensive literature on colchicine and several of Graw’s scientific papers. They seized correspondence and data-storage devices containing sprawling documents in which the name “Graw” appeared more than 28,000 times. Otto’s laptop contained folders named Graw and Dissertation, and images of the autumn crocus flower. Investigators also found correspondence with a Pakistani ghostwriter and a contract with a Serbian printer. Out of these disparate ingredients, it seemed, Otto had carefully assembled the red book.

As investigators pored over Otto’s records, a picture emerged of his past, his mother’s final days and his strange, obsessive quest for revenge. Though he had lied about practically everything else, Otto was, in fact, a doctor – albeit one with a chequered clinical history. After practising in the US, Switzerland and Germany, he settled in the UK, but concerns raised by a pharmacist about “bizarre” prescriptions he’d written had prompted a review by Lambeth primary care trust and an investigation by the General Medical Council. In 2010, he had been barred from practising medicine in the UK, but by then, he had returned to Munich to focus on just one patient: his mother.

Otto believed that movement was key to improving Doria’s health. He insisted that Doria walk every day, even when she was so exhausted she could barely get out of bed. He brought her down into the streets and observed as she hobbled along the pavement. He told me that he would leave marks on the buildings to track her progress, and took her to her favourite park bench. “Come on, Ma!” he remembered saying to cheer her on. “Just another three metres!”

For years, he monitored her day and night, noting signs of progress or deterioration. Every day, he inspected her urine and weighed her faeces to make sure she was getting enough nutrition.

After Doria died, Otto called the funeral home, asking for her to be picked up as late as legally possible, 36 hours after her death. When the company asked for a death certificate, Otto issued one himself, noting “rigor mortis” as a sign of death. It was then that the funeral company got suspicious and alerted the police, who sent a patrol unit and a coroner.

When the coroner arrived, Otto’s erratic behaviour and desire to share his copious records of his mother’s health made her suspicious, too. “Extremely odd behaviour of the son; questionable medical treatment; extremely poor condition of care,” she noted in her report. Noting “indications of an unnatural death”, she ordered an autopsy. The examiners’ prevailing theory was that Otto had accidentally killed his mother with an overdose of insulin, then covered up his mistake by administering a glucose injection to stabilise her vitals.

In the weeks after the coroner issued her report, Otto launched legal action against her, including for invoicing irregularities, but his suit was dismissed. Police opened a manslaughter investigation against Otto for the death of his mother, but dropped the case after the autopsy. Graw told me he didn’t perform the autopsy himself. His name was on the report merely as the institute’s director. The report found no conclusive evidence that Doria’s death was unnatural.

During those long, uncertain months, Otto became tormented by trying to recover his mother’s corpse and discovering the exact cause of death – wondering whether it was due to a mistake he had made. He wrote to Matthias Graw to suggest they co-author a paper on the conditions that led to Doria’s passing, and recommended they perform an invasive brain exam, called a histology, which he later described in court as entailing “a circular cut with a butcher’s knife, then pulling the skin off and going at it with a saw”.

Graw said he never received the letter, but if he had, he wouldn’t have responded to Otto for the same reason that Otto was kept in the dark about the examinations of his mother’s body – the ongoing criminal investigation forbade any contact with a suspect. Otto seems to have become obsessed with Graw, the keeper of his mother’s remains, and his fixation gradually twisted into a conviction that he was hiding something sinister.

Barred access to Graw, Otto sought to learn everything he could about the man and find a fatal flaw. He fixated on Graw’s dissertation on the poison colchicine, hoping to undermine the foundation of the doctor’s entire career. He launched a flurry of bizarre proceedings against him, claiming that the doctor had failed to recognise inconsistencies in the colchicine levels in his mother’s blood, and accusing him of using the “flesh of the Jewish woman Mrs Z” for experiments.

On 1 March 2024, the Munich public prosecutor concluded its investigation and charged Otto with document forgery, copyright infringement and multiple counts of defamation and fraud. The case came to trial in early 2025. The prosecution argued that Otto had attempted to “completely obliterate the livelihood” of Graw by commissioning the creation of the red book, inventing the 1981 conference on which it was based, and listing the book on eBay in order to fool Stefan Weber into carrying out his plan. Carbon dating corroborated these claims – the paper on which the book was printed was produced no earlier than 2015. When the furore failed to cost Graw his job, the prosecution claimed, Otto had fed the press the gold tooth accusation.

During the trial, Otto repeatedly claimed that his mother was a Holocaust survivor. Reporters for Die Zeit, the weekly magazine that published an extensive article on the case, contacted every organisation that documents survivors of the camps, and concluded that her name does not appear in the records.

On 6 March 2025, Otto was sentenced to two and a half years in prison. The court cited his “almost unprecedented criminal energy”. Otto appealed against the court’s decision. When convicted, he was offered a suspended sentence if he confessed, but he maintained his innocence, claiming he and his mother were the victims of a string of bureaucratic errors, then a conspiracy to cover them up. Finally, in July 2026, he confessed to commissioning the red book and agreed to pay €210,000 in damages to Graw. He received a two-year suspended sentence.

When I spoke to Graw recently, he told me he was satisfied with the outcome and hoped for peace and quiet now. But he was still coming to terms with the case, which had consumed the past few years of his life. He remained baffled by Otto’s motive in targeting him – he hadn’t performed the autopsy or started the investigation, and his institute’s report was the reason why Otto had been exonerated. He lamented that Otto had never explained, or apologised.

He complained that “some of the media had no interest in investigating the allegations and carried stories before giving me a chance to respond”. And while, as a scientist, he was bound to test hypotheses before publishing them, “plagiarism hunters didn’t even check whether the source was genuine at all”. (Despite his vow, Stefan Weber has not retired from plagiarism hunting, but he has sworn to never again work with “grey literature”.)

At trial, questions were raised about Otto’s mental health, but he refused to submit to psychiatric evaluation. According to experts called by the court, the assiduous attention to detail with which he carried out his forgery seems to rule out a full psychotic breakdown or a schizophrenic episode, but he may have experienced temporary delusions brought on by grief.

Otto dismisses mental illness allegations as attempts to discredit him. He told me he has bought a house in Serbia to transform it into a memorial dedicated to his mother. With the slow, reverent precision with which he does everything, he has been attempting to retrace the steps of Doria’s entire life. In this memorial exhibition, he said, he will show she was a Holocaust survivor, and detail the true sequence of events that led to her death.

Microsoft Is Suspended From Green Card Program as Trump Officials Widen Fraud Drive

The New York Times October 08, 2026

U. S. Immigration Crackdown

Advertisement

Supported by

Vice President JD Vance singled out the tech firm as he and other officials accused an array of companies and universities of abusing the visa system.

By Erica L. Green

Reporting from Washington

Vice President JD Vance announced on Thursday that Microsoft would be suspended from using a visa program that allowed foreign workers to permanently reside in the United States after an investigation found that the tech giant had “abused” the system.

Mr. Vance made the announcement in a news conference where he and other Trump administration officials made a slew of allegations that American companies and universities were committing visa fraud. Microsoft, they announced, is just the largest of several technology companies to face such a suspension, and schools including Harvard and Yale are now under investigation.

Mr. Vance took aim at the embattled H-1B visa program, which allows companies to hire skilled foreign workers in hard-to-fill jobs. The Trump administration has sought to overhaul the program, including imposing fees for the visas, claiming that it has unfairly allowed companies to sideline Americans and hire foreign workers. Mr. Vance has called the program “broken” and said he would support eliminating it.

Mr. Vance said on Thursday that companies like Microsoft had been using the H-1B visa program to exploit the Labor Department’s permanent labor certification program, known as PERM, which allows H-1B visa recipients to obtain a green card and potentially stay in the United States indefinitely.

Officials said that other companies suspended from PERM would include Adobe and several large information technology outsourcing firms. Mr. Vance said the suspension would “last as long as it needs to.”

The announcement on Thursday, which included officials from several agencies, was the latest attempt by the administration to seize on purported fraud to argue that exploitation of the country’s immigration system — and not President Trump’s policies — has been depriving Americans of jobs, wages and paths to prosperity.

“The Department of Labor is taking historic action by shutting down the pipeline of systemic fraud, the fraud that has flooded our country with foreign labor at the expense of American workers,” said Keith Sonderling, the labor secretary. “It begins with universities and companies that have turned into visa mills, promoting foreign workers that have lied about their qualifications to take jobs from our beloved American workers.”

But the administration has not always provided evidence to match its fraud claims. And several of its targets on Thursday disputed its assertions.

Mr. Vance directed his harshest criticism at Microsoft, saying that there had been “no company in the United States, unfortunately, that has abused this system more.”

Mr. Vance said that in the past year, the company had laid off 6,000 American workers, while it benefited from 6,300 H-1B visas and nearly 3,000 green cards. He referred to the visa holders as “indentured servants” who were paid a fraction of what their American counterparts would be.

“In other words, if you do the math, for every worker that Microsoft laid off, they replaced that worker with one and a half foreign indentured servants,” Mr. Vance said. “Now that is a scandalous system that we’ve allowed in this country for far too long.”

“And so our message to Microsoft is: You’re a great American company, but you’ve got to hire great American workers,” he added. “You cannot lay off American workers and then replace them with foreign indentured servants.”

In a statement, Microsoft challenged some of Mr. Vance’s claims.

The company said the “vast majority” of its employees in the United States are citizens. It said that of the roughly 6,000 H-1B applications it made last fiscal year, 80 percent were to extend or change the status of existing Microsoft employees. The remaining applications were for people already legally in the country who then joined Microsoft, the company said.

“They are not new arrivals to our country,” it added.

Microsoft said its pay is among the highest in tech and among H-1B filings.

“Microsoft succeeds as a global technology leader by developing the world’s best technology work force,” the company said. “We do this by strengthening this country’s talent pipeline, hiring American workers and attracting the best talent from around the world.”

On the academic front, Mr. Vance maintained that universities were employing foreign graduate students as research assistants at lower wages, and suggested that the visas were being overused and sucking up federal funding.

Anthony D’Esposito, the inspector general of the Labor Department, announced that the agency was launching investigations into several universities for potential abuses of the J-1 visa, a cultural exchange program that allows foreign students to work and study in the United States.

“Subpoenas have been served, investigations are underway, and nobody will be getting a free pass because their name is carved into an expensive building,” he said.

The schools under investigation are Harvard, Yale, Stanford, Arizona State, Brown, M. I. T., the University of Pittsburgh, the University of California, Davis, and the California Institute of Technology.

Stanford said in a statement that it “complies with all applicable visa laws, including those relating to J-1 visas,” and “will cooperate with the investigation.”

Brian Clark, a spokesman for Brown University, said in a statement that the university had received the subpoena “for various records pertaining to foreign labor programs administered by the U. S. government, and we will respond promptly and directly.”

“Brown’s international scholars, students and employees make essential contributions on our campus, including to teaching and research that advances American innovation, competitiveness and economic vitality,” Mr. Clark said.

Arizona State University, noting that it educates more science, technology, engineering and math majors than any other university and employs one of the largest technical and scientific workforces in the country, said that it “has hired the talent needed to perform these functions and done so in complete compliance with existing United States policy and law.”

The H-1B program has long been the target of bipartisan calls for changes, but has become a centerpiece of Mr. Trump’s immigration crackdown agenda. Economists have maintained that the visa holders boost American productivity and raise wages even for American workers.

Mr. Vance, pressed on how the use of the certification program amounted to fraud, said that companies were misrepresenting that they were bringing in workers with “hyper-specialized and hyper-capable” skill sets.

Mr. Vance said that there was a difference between bringing in foreign workers like the tech tycoon Elon Musk, “who wants to come in and build something great in the United States of America,” versus an accountant at a lower wage.

“You’re not bringing in a genius to build a great American corporation,” Mr. Vance said. “You are committing fraud against the American people and against this visa program.”

Hours after the announcement, President Trump awarded Satya Nadella, Microsoft’s chief executive, the National Medal of Technology and Innovation at a summit in Washington where Mr. Musk and other tech executives also were honored.

Mr. Nadella came to the United States for graduate school and joined Microsoft in 1992. Two years later, he wrote in his memoir, he turned in his permanent residency for an H-1B visa so that his wife could immediately join him in the United States. (At the time, he said, the spouses of green card holders faced a long wait for visa approval.) Both eventually gained citizenship, and he rose through the ranks to revive Microsoft from a yearslong slump. It is now worth almost $4 trillion.

In awarding Mr. Nadella the highest honor in technology on Thursday, Mr. Trump said it was “so well deserved,” and that Mr. Nadella had turned Microsoft into “an early leader in superintelligence.”

Karen Weise contributed reporting from Seattle, Alan Blinder from Atlanta, Vimal Patel from Denver and Mark Arsenault from Boston.

Erica L. Green is a White House correspondent for The Times, covering President Trump and his administration.

Pentagon Draws Up New Iran Strike Plans as Trump Hesitates

The New York Times October 08, 2026

War in the Middle East

Advertisement

Supported by

The U. S. military has drafted options for three days of strikes, but in recent months the president has repeatedly vetoed plans to restart the war.

By Julian E. Barnes and Eric Schmitt

The reporters have been covering the U. S.-Israeli conflict with Iran.

The U. S. military is preparing options to restart major combat operations against Iran, even as President Trump continues to show ambivalence about restarting the war, according to American officials.

Three aircraft carriers will soon be in the Middle East, a massive assembly of force, and the Pentagon, on Mr. Trump’s orders, has developed plans to strike Iran’s drone and missile arsenal, energy facilities and other military sites.

But Mr. Trump has repeatedly decided not to relaunch heavy combat operations against Iran. And the U. S. military response to Iran has been more muted in recent weeks, despite Iran’s escalating attacks on oil tankers.

In a social media post on Thursday, Mr. Trump said that he would not attack Iran before the midterm elections, and that the two countries were “having productive discussions.”

In recent months, officials said, Mr. Trump’s national security team and the Pentagon have made five proposals to him for major operations against either Iran or the Houthis, an Iranian-backed militia based in Yemen. Each time, Mr. Trump vetoed the plans.

But Mr. Trump has once more ordered up strike options. Senior national security officials, led by Vice President JD Vance, discussed plans at a meeting last Friday at Camp David. The plans center on a short, intense campaign lasting about three days, according to people briefed on the proposal.

The strikes would focus on Iran’s missile and drone arsenal, much of which Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps has rebuilt since the early phase of the war. Other targets could include Iranian energy facilities and Revolutionary Guard command posts and headquarters.

The latest plans were earlier reported by Axios.

Officials have backed Mr. Trump’s assessment that some progress is being made in diplomatic talks, which have continued through mediators. The talks have continued to get hung up on the issue of Iran’s nuclear program. American officials want to reach a deal on Iran’s nuclear ambitions first, while Iranian negotiators insist that those discussions must come last.

Over the months, Iran has become a tougher opponent as its military tactics improved. Taking down Iranian missiles has required more interceptors than earlier in the war, posing challenges to America’s already taxed arsenal of munitions. Armed with satellite imagery from Chinese companies, Iran has also been able to more effectively target U. S. bases, according to people briefed on the intelligence.

Since September, the time of the last significant exchange of retaliatory attacks, Iran has struck at least 13 ships, according to a monitoring group run by the British Navy. Intelligence reports have put the number higher, at nearly 20, according to people briefed on the information. None of those attacks generated a major U. S. response.

While oil exports from the Middle East are up, Iran’s increased attacks have spooked shippers and raised questions about future energy shipments.

Throughout the summer, the U. S. military regularly retaliated after Iranian attacks on international shipping. But the far less robust response since then reflects Mr. Trump’s hesitancy to restart the war in full, officials say.

U. S. commanders are also concerned about the increasing difficulty of stopping Iranian attacks against bases where American troops are stationed, and energy facilities and other civilian infrastructure in the region.

On Thursday, in his social media post, Mr. Trump insisted that none of the oil passing through the Strait of Hormuz was coming from Iran. That is debatable, according to people briefed on intelligence reports. Iran allows some vessels to pass that have paid fees or that potentially carry some of its oil. Iran also has its own dark fleet of tankers, according to current and former officials.

Chinese companies have paid fees to Iran to transit the strait, and Iran has long secretly blended its oil with Iraqi oil to avoid sanctions. The Treasury Department on Thursday sanctioned 17 vessels that it said were part of Iran’s shadow fleet smuggling oil.

Even members of Mr. Trump’s inner circle are increasingly skeptical that military action will change Tehran’s calculus or plans. Some of these officials believe that the Trump administration’s campaign of economic pressure is working and just needs more time to force Iran to make meaningful concessions.

Even before Mr. Trump’s said there would be no strike before the November vote, officials had predicted that he would wait until after the Israeli elections, on Oct. 27, and the U. S. midterms the following week to decide whether to attack.

But U. S. military commanders are ready to begin larger operations in the coming days, in case the president shifts again.

The Theodore Roosevelt carrier strike group left San Diego last week and will join the George H. W. Bush and the George Washington carriers as early as the end of October. Each strike group includes other warships carrying attack helicopters and Marines. It will be the first time since 2003 that three aircraft carriers will be in the Middle East.

At the end of the month, there will be more than 20,000 sailors and Marines afloat, along with hundreds of aircraft. But the high troop level will be only temporary. The George Washington is expected to return to its base in Japan soon after the Roosevelt arrives next month to replace it.

Despite the force buildup, it is hardly certain that Mr. Trump will give a green light to any new attacks even after the election. Senior U. S. officials are worried about further depleting the global arsenal of defensive weapons to defend bases in the Middle East, as well as the U. S. ability to intercept Iranian attacks.

Still other officials in favor of resumed operations note that Iran’s economy continues to weaken, and a short, intense barrage could intensify Tehran’s problems, especially if it hurts Iran’s ability to control the strait, according to current and former officials.

The United States has continued to take out Iranian drones and cruise missiles. But it has not attacked Iran’s dark tanker fleet or conducted retaliatory strikes inside Iran.

At the beginning of the war, the U. S. military in most cases fired two interceptors at incoming Iranian missiles, focusing on the most dangerous volleys.

But American officials now say Iran’s improved tactics and targeting have forced the United States and its regional partners to fire more missiles to thwart salvos aimed at American bases in the region.

American commanders say they still have reserves of interceptors as the war has drained stockpiles, and U. S. Central Command, which oversees military operations in the Middle East, has pulled in weaponry from Europe and Asia.

Reporting was contributed by Jonathan Swan and Alan Rappeport in Washington; David E. Sanger in Cambridge, Mass.; and Farnaz Fassihi in New York.

Julian E. Barnes covers the U. S. intelligence agencies and international security matters for The Times. He has written about security issues for more than two decades.

Eric Schmitt is a national security correspondent for The Times. He has reported on U. S. military affairs and counterterrorism for more than three decades. Contact him securely on Signal: @ericschmitt.36.

How a U. S. Diplomat Suppressed and Altered Reports Critical of Israel

The New York Times October 08, 2026

Trump Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

TIMES EXCLUSIVE

A top aide to Ambassador Mike Huckabee skewed information to portray the Netanyahu government in a favorable light, according to multiple officials and documents obtained by The Times.

By Natan Odenheimer and Adam Rasgon

Natan Odenheimer and Adam Rasgon interviewed more than a dozen U. S. officials and reviewed dozens of State Department records for this article.

In late March, at the height of the Iran war, Israel quietly approved more settlements in the Israeli-occupied West Bank than it ever had at one time.

Staff members at the United States Embassy in Jerusalem saw the move as potentially flouting one of President Trump’s explicit red lines for Israel — no annexation of the West Bank — and drafted an urgent report intended for policy makers in Washington.

That memo never reached Washington. It was quashed by David Milstein, a top aide to Ambassador Mike Huckabee, according to three U. S. officials briefed on the process.

This was no isolated incident.

Since taking up his post in April 2025, Mr. Milstein, 36, has repeatedly suppressed or significantly revised embassy reporting on Israeli activities to present the Netanyahu government in a favorable light, according to a dozen people who work with or interact with Mr. Milstein in both Jerusalem and Washington:

As settler violence in the West Bank surged in the spring, for instance, he stymied embassy reporting suggesting that the Israeli government was failing to take action, according to the three officials. Instead the embassy sent a cable to Washington, viewed by The New York Times, praising Israel for “cracking down” on the attacks.

When members of Congress pushed for accountability over the killings of Palestinian Americans by Israeli settlers and security forces, he suppressed a detailed report that the embassy staff had written, effectively stonewalling lawmakers’ efforts to gain information, according to multiple officials briefed on the matter.

Soon after arriving in Jerusalem, Mr. Milstein began insisting on approving communications from the embassy section that handles Palestinian affairs, multiple officials with direct knowledge of the process said. The flow of cables plummeted from several a week to a few a month, as some staffers refrained from writing reports for fear that Mr. Milstein would block or rewrite them, these officials said.

Mr. Milstein’s interventions go far beyond those of any recent predecessor, several officials said. They and others said they were speaking out of concern that officials in Washington were getting a distorted view of Israeli actions through core diplomatic channels.

Mr. Milstein’s efforts have helped insulate Israel’s right-wing government against potential blowback from a Trump Administration that has been its closest ally.

Among the most contentious issues on which Mr. Milstein has intervened is the accelerating expansion of Israeli settlements in the West Bank.

It’s an inflammatory subject that has soured Israel’s relationship with some of its longtime allies. Last month, Britain, Canada and France announced sanctions on Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank in response to the Israeli policy on settlement expansion. Britain accused some settlers of “ethnic cleansing.”

It is unclear to what extent Mr. Huckabee is aware of his adviser’s actions. Both he and Mr. Milstein declined requests for an interview.

The ambassador, a longtime advocate for the Israeli settlement movement, has denounced specific attacks by settlers, calling them “Israeli terrorists,” but he has played down settler violence more broadly, saying it is being carried out by a small group.

Mr. Huckabee is required to sign off on most cables and significant decisions, but officials said Mr. Milstein sometimes acts on his own. The ambassador has also sometimes worked in concert with Mr. Milstein to suppress or recast information, these officials said. But in several cases when he believed Mr. Milstein had gone too far, they said, Mr. Huckabee has reined him in.

Earlier this month, after an article critical of Mr. Milstein for inviting wedding guests to give him money appeared in Politico, Mr. Huckabee posted on social media that he had “absolute confidence” in his aide, whom he said possesses “impeccable integrity.”

Mr. Milstein is a familiar figure in right-wing circles in the United States and Israel, and has organized meetings between Mr. Huckabee and some top Israeli officials. But he is not well known in either country, and his role as a gatekeeper of information sent to Washington has drawn little attention.

His effort to shape embassy reporting was first reported a year ago by the online magazine of the Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft, a Washington think tank that advocates de-escalation and U. S. military restraint.

But fresh reporting by The New York Times unearthed documentary evidence and previously unreported instances of Mr. Milstein’s effort to skew information to the benefit of the Netanyahu government, which has continued throughout this year.

The Times interviewed 15 U. S. officials for this article, including many in Washington, all of whom worked with Mr. Milstein in some manner. The Times also talked to nine former diplomats who provided context on the role and responsibilities of senior embassy officials. All spoke on the condition of anonymity for fear of reprisal. The Times also obtained or reviewed dozens of documents, cables, memos and other internal communications.

The people who spoke to The Times were career government officials and political appointees, including strong supporters of the United States-Israel relationship. Most said they were speaking out of concern that Mr. Milstein’s actions are undermining standard diplomatic work, expressing worry that, in some cases, they contradict the president’s stated policies.

The concern extended to senior administration officials in Washington, including in the White House, who have expressed frustration to colleagues over some of Mr. Milstein’s actions, according to four officials, who have either witnessed or been briefed on the dissatisfaction.

It is not clear whether Mr. Milstein’s interventions have affected White House policy. But since Mr. Trump declared a year ago that he would not allow Israel to annex the West Bank, he has said little about the issue beyond briefly reaffirming in February that he opposed annexation, even as Israel was extending more control over the territory.

In response to questions sent to the embassy about Mr. Milstein’s actions, Mr. Huckabee did not address specific instances cited by The Times. He wrote in a statement: “The elements of the story The New York Times is trying to assemble are so lacking in fact that it ranks up with other Times farcical endeavors.” He added: “I personally and categorically refute the elements of your proposed ‘story.’ ”

Asked about The Times’s reporting on Mr. Milstein, the State Department provided the following statement: “The entire team at State remains focused on advancing President Trump’s America First agenda.”

The White House referred The Times to the State Department.

Mr. Milstein is the stepson of the right-wing radio host Mark Levin — a close ally of both Mr. Trump and Mr. Netanyahu. That relationship is well known in Washington and the embassy, and has been a factor in how he is treated, officials in both Jerusalem and Washington said.

As an adviser to Mr. Huckabee, Mr. Milstein is one of the most senior officials in the embassy, acting as a chief of staff of sorts to Mr. Huckabee. The ambassador has empowered him to oversee much of the mission’s portfolio, particularly the West Bank and Gaza.

Previous ambassadors to Israel have had political appointees as senior advisers who, like Mr. Milstein, tried to influence the reporting back to Washington. And Mr. Milstein’s responsibilities include reviewing and amending information sent to Washington.

People who interact with Mr. Milstein professionally, however, say he goes to unusual lengths to frame Israel in a positive light. He has blocked reporting from being sent, rewritten cables to deliver a different — sometimes opposite — message from the original, and delayed approving drafts until the topic was no longer relevant, these officials said.

In the summer of 2025, for instance, dozens of Palestinians seeking food were killed near the distribution sites run by the Gaza Humanitarian Foundation, backed by Israel and the United States. American diplomats in Israel drafted a cable, viewed by The Times, warning that the foundation’s distribution process was chaotic and deadly and risked more “mass casualty events.”

Mr. Milstein rewrote the cable to declare GHF’s operation a success while overlooking the mass casualties, according to people who saw the cable and were briefed on the editing process.

Troubled by glaring discrepancies between news coverage and the embassy’s official reports, White House and State Department officials seeking a clearer picture of events bypassed standard channels at least twice to communicate directly with embassy staff, according to two officials briefed on the outreach and an internal communication from late this summer seen by The Times.

Veteran American diplomats said that withholding or twisting the information sent to Washington should raise serious concerns.

“The embassy ought to tell Washington everything — the good, the bad and the ugly,” said Dan Kurtzer, who was the U. S. ambassador to Israel under President George W. Bush. “If they’re not doing so, they are damaging the policy-making process and possibly undermining the president’s policies.”

Mr. Milstein also questioned several colleagues on whether they were “pro-Israel” or “pro-Hamas,” according to four officials, who found the question inappropriate and said it made some people fearful of speaking freely.

A conservative and longtime Republican, Mr. Milstein served as an aide to Senator Ted Cruz of Texas from 2013 to 2018 before relocating to Israel to study at a Jerusalem yeshiva, a school for Jewish religious studies. In 2020, he landed a job as an assistant to David M. Friedman, Mr. Trump’s ambassador to Israel between 2017 to 2021.

During the Biden Administration, Mr. Milstein worked for Gov. Ron DeSantis of Florida, handling outreach to pro-Israel voters.

In April 2025, Mr. Milstein was back at the embassy in Jerusalem after Mr. Trump was elected to a second term.

In February, Nasrallah Abu Siyam, 19, was trying to stop settlers from stealing livestock when one of them shot him dead in his West Bank village.

He was the ninth American citizen of Palestinian or Turkish heritage killed in the West Bank by Israeli settlers or soldiers in four years. Weeks later, seeking an update on the investigations into the killings, 30 members of Congress led by Senator Chris Van Hollen, Democrat of Maryland, sent a letter to Secretary of State Marco Rubio demanding answers from Israel.

In response, officers in the embassy compiled a report that was completed in March detailing the status of each investigation, according to multiple officials briefed on the process.

Its central findings suggested that, in most cases, investigations had made little progress, that some cases had been closed, and that no one had been charged in any of the killings, these officials said. Instead of forwarding the report, Mr. Milstein argued that the embassy should send a letter saying that Israel was properly handling the investigations, two officials briefed on the discussions said.

On May 4, Paul D. Guaglianone, a State Department official, sent a letter responding to Mr. Van Hollen, saying that the embassy, which had reduced staff because of the Iran war, was focused on security cooperation with Israel and protecting Americans against Iranian attacks. (The intense fighting had wound down nearly a month earlier, after a cease-fire was struck on April 8.)

The letter, provided to The Times by Mr. Van Hollen’s office, said the embassy was working with Israel to “ensure accountability for these deaths.”

The response did not reassure Mr. Van Hollen.

“If you don’t get accountability, you endanger more American citizens,” he said in a phone interview.

In February, the Netanyahu government passed a measure that made it easier for Israelis to buy land in the West Bank, a move widely condemned internationally as speeding the way to annexation.

Any formal Israeli annexation of the West Bank, which Israel captured in the 1967 Arab-Israeli war, would carry immense consequences. But in embassy discussions, Mr. Milstein portrayed the government’s announcement on land purchases as a domestic matter with little significance to the outside world, according to two officials.

An embassy report sent to Washington, reviewed by The Times, said the Israeli policy was meant “to address humanitarian needs” of Israeli settlers, without detailing those needs.

A similar intervention occurred in April, when top Israeli military commanders publicly warned that West Bank settler violence could set off a new Palestinian uprising. Embassy staffers tried to alert Washington to those warnings, but Mr. Milstein prevented the reports from being sent as drafted, according to three officials.

In a cable viewed by The Times on which he is listed as the first author, Mr. Milstein praised Mr. Netanyahu’s “unprecedented new initiatives to combat” rising violence in the West Bank. The report’s title read, “Government Cracks Down on Escalating West Bank Violence.”

David M. Halbfinger and Isabel Kershner contributed reporting from Jerusalem.

Natan Odenheimer is a Times reporter in Jerusalem, covering Israeli and Palestinian affairs.

Adam Rasgon is a reporter for The Times in Jerusalem, covering Israeli and Palestinian affairs.

The Wave of Student Protests Roiling France

In Pictures & Video

In Pictures & Video

Protesters in Nantes, France, clashed with the police on Thursday as part of a wave of demonstrations across the country. Credit... Stephane Mahe/Reuters

By The New York Times

Protests by high school students have rattled France in recent weeks, with hundreds of school blockages, large demonstrations and violent clashes with the police.

The students are protesting overcrowded classrooms, teacher shortages and decrepit buildings. The French government is scrambling to address their frustrations, which erupted amid a heated political climate ahead of a presidential election in April and have threatened to swell into a broader wave of grievances.

More than 700 police officers and more than 300 students and school staff members have been injured, some of them seriously, according to the government. Some high schools were set on fire or ransacked, and hundreds more were damaged, according to the education ministry.

The government has tried to assuage students’ anger, in part by pledging to create emergency plans to address school staffing shortages. But deteriorating public finances have left officials without much wiggle room to address the students’ complaints, and concessions have done little to calm the protesters.

The police used tear gas on young protesters in Paris on Thursday.

U. S. S. Abraham Lincoln Returns Home After Long and Grueling Deployment

The New York Times October 08, 2026

War in the Middle East

Advertisement

Supported by

The aircraft carrier, whose crew endured food shortages, spent much of its nearly 11-month deployment in combat without a day off.

By Jan Ransom and John Ismay

Jan Ransom reported from San Diego, and John Ismay from Washington.

The aircraft carrier U. S. S. Abraham Lincoln, whose crew endured food shortages and mental health struggles prompted by a near-record 322-day deployment in support of the Iran war, returned on Thursday to its home port of San Diego.

Friends and family members of the crew gathered on the pier to greet the ship. They had come with signs and banners, toting American flags, and were clad in red, white and blue.

Many arrived before dawn, then erupted in thunderous cheers as the hulking vessel entered San Diego Bay with sailors in white summer uniforms manning the rails — and again when the ship docked shortly after 3 p. m. Eastern.

Family members expressed relief at the sight of their loved ones returning home after such a long and grueling assignment.

“It was nerve-racking when he went days and weeks without communication,” said Lashonda Jones, whose 20-year-old son, Jaysean Jones, is a boatswain’s mate, responsible for maintaining the ship. She sent him Bible scriptures and motivational text messages to keep his spirits high.

By longstanding Navy tradition, sailors whose spouses gave birth during the deployment were expected to be among the first to step off to meet their sons and daughters. That included 21-year-old Eduardo Morales, whose 5-month-old son Emmanuelle was on the pier early Thursday with Mr. Morales’s wife, Legna Morales.

“It’s been really hard going through labor by myself,” said Ms. Morales. “Being far away for so long, and not being there with us, not knowing the baby yet — he cries.”

The deployment for the Lincoln’s 5,000-member crew began before the war, when it left San Diego on Nov. 21, 2025. It spent almost a month at sea before pulling into the naval base in Guam for a brief stop for supplies.

The Lincoln nearly broke the record for longest carrier deployment since the Vietnam War.

The Gerald R. Ford set that record with a 327-day deployment. But unlike the Lincoln’s, the Ford’s crew was able to disembark in ports across the Mediterranean and Caribbean before steaming to the Arabian Sea before the start of the war.

The Lincoln and other ships began experiencing logistical problems after Iran destroyed the Navy’s main Middle Eastern hub in Manama, Bahrain, in response to the United States and Israel launching the war on Feb. 28.

With Iran’s ballistic missiles able to hold all ports around the Arabian Peninsula at risk of attack, the Navy’s warships in the region began to experience shortages of food, fuel and other goods as the service moved its supply hub to the British-owned island of Diego Garcia about 2,200 miles away.

The first indications of problems came from family members of Lincoln sailors, who sent reporters photos of meager meals served on the ship while supplies were running low. Many families tried to send their loved ones care packages to make up the difference, only to have their mail lost, destroyed or delivered months late.

The reports rankled Navy leaders, who downplayed the problems.

In a social media post in August, the Navy’s acting secretary, Hung Cao, accused reporters of presenting Lincoln’s sailors as “victims.” Six days later, the carrier left the Arabian Sea to begin its journey home after another carrier, the Japan-based U. S. S. George Washington, took its place.

The next month, in response to questions from Democratic lawmakers, Mr. Cao acknowledged that eight sailors from the Lincoln strike group had tried to take their own lives. One jumped overboard, and another tried to do so before being stopped by shipmates.

When asked in August about the reported problems aboard the Lincoln, Mr. Trump dismissed the concerns raised by the families of crew members. When pressed about whether he was worried about the crew’s mental health and whether he thought the deployment had gone on too long, the president said, “No. No. No.” He added that the deployment — then more than eight months long — had not been “nearly long enough.”

Some family members gathered on the pier Thursday said the challenges aboard the ship were real — including the rationing of food.

“It was pathetic,” Victoria Tozzi, whose son enlisted after high school to help fund his college education, said of the portions of food. “It looked gross, and he was like, ‘yeah it’s pretty bad.’”

When she learned that Iran had launched attacks at the ship, and that the missiles and drones had been intercepted, she asked how he was doing.

“He said, ‘Everybody is just on edge,’” she said.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, who flew to the Lincoln from San Diego on Wednesday to ride the ship for its final stretch, acknowledged the lengthy deployment in remarks to the crew on Wednesday. But he criticized reports of logistics problems as overblown. He also awarded the crew the Presidential Unit Citation, the highest decoration that can be given to a unit of the Navy or Marine Corps for valorous service.

“There were a few folks in the media who tried to turn the U. S. S. Abraham Lincoln into some sort of a symbol — a symbol of dysfunction or a symbol of low morale or a symbol of a failed mission,” Mr. Hegseth said, speaking into a microphone before a crowd of sailors. “And what I look out at right here and when I talk to your leadership — and I’ve had a chance to talk to a number of you — I know it is the exact opposite.”

The war with Iran has placed the Navy’s fleet of 11 nuclear-powered aircraft carriers under tremendous strain. Two carriers, the John C. Stennis and Harry S. Truman, are unavailable because of the refueling of their nuclear reactors. Another five have already played a role during the war. In July, the Ford entered a shipyard for long-delayed maintenance, and the 50-year-old Nimitz is scheduled to be decommissioned next year.

That leaves only the Dwight D. Eisenhower, the Carl Vinson and the Ronald Reagan as potentially available to deploy should the war, which is now in its eighth month, continue.

The pace of operations for the Lincoln and its crew during their extended deployment was unrelenting, as the ship played a major role in the air campaign over Iran. In August, a Navy official said that the ship launched more than 10,000 sorties and dropped more than 1.5 million pounds of ordnance during the conflict.

Aircraft aboard the Lincoln also played a key part in enforcing Mr. Trump’s blockade of Iranian ports.

In early May, an F/A-18 Super Hornet launched from the Lincoln fired its 20-millimeter cannon at the rudders of an Iranian-flagged tanker, the M/T Hasna, disabling the ship as it attempted to pass through the blockade line. A month later, another Super Hornet from the Lincoln fired a precision-guided munition into the engineering spaces aboard the Palau-flagged tanker M/T Marivex in the Gulf of Oman as it steamed toward Iran. The ship’s 24 crew members were rescued by an Omani military helicopter.

In his remarks Wednesday, Mr. Hegseth said the extended deployment was worthwhile, crediting the crew with demonstrating enormous resilience.

“What makes the U. S. military and the U. S. Navy and all these sailors different is that you adapt and that you are resilient and you overcome,” he added. “You finish the mission nonetheless. Yes, it’s hard. That’s why you’re here, and you do difficult and hard things. But you believe in your heart in that mission.”

“My heart only swells with pride just standing in front of all of you,” he added.

In all, the Lincoln’s crew spent nearly nine and a half months at sea without a break until the Lincoln pulled in to Pattaya, Thailand, on Sept. 2 for five days of rest.

On Sept. 18, the Lincoln reached U. S. soil during a brief stop in Guam. The crew was allowed to get off the ship so long as they stayed on the naval base there.

Now, back on the mainland, the crew will get a bit more time off.

When a warship returns from a lengthy deployment, about half the crew typically takes two weeks of leave. The other half maintains a Monday-to-Friday workweek, but can then go home. After those two weeks are up, the groups swap, and the other half goes on leave.

Jan Ransom is an investigative reporter for The Times focusing on the criminal justice system, law enforcement and incarceration in New York.

John Ismay is a reporter covering the Pentagon for The Times. He served as an explosive ordnance disposal officer in the U. S. Navy.

Trump’s Speech Is Getting Filthier

The New York Times October 08, 2026

Advertisement

Newsletter

By John McWhorter

Opinion Writer

President Trump has been especially potty-mouthed lately. In his second term, he has used significantly more profanity in public than in his first, according to an analysis by The Washington Post in May. Just last week we were treated to him telling interviewers from Time, “You haven’t asked me one positive question” — but dropping an F-bomb to modify “positive” — and at a rally in Ohio calling Democrats “dumb son of a bitches” and saying he was “working my ass off.”

At that same rally he made another gluteal reference of a more pugnacious nature when he said that a Republican victory would “shove it up” Democrats’ something or other.

Some have argued that the uptick in Trump’s lexical filth is a symptom of cognitive decline, a disinhibition suggestive of dementia. I doubt it. The increase in his use of profanity is what you would expect, given how language works.

When we use language, we often want to get and keep people’s attention. But the words and expressions we use to do that can lose their force over time. They require freshening up. This is how you get nonsensical words like “irregardless,” where “regardless” alone should do the trick but the “ir-” gets tacked on for added punch — the extra rhythmic oomph of “irrespective.” “Advance warning,” “close proximity” and “final outcome” are similar cases: redundancies from a logical point of view, but useful for vividness.

Trump has always been fond of “damn” and “hell,” which were part of his populist shtick from the outset. So we would have predicted that he would progress to more piquant profanity.

In this way, Trump’s public speech retraces the evolution of popular profanity over the past hundred years. In the early 20th century, religion-related terms like “hell” were people’s “hit your thumb with a hammer” words. A woman having repeated trouble with her glasses in the 1929 film musical “Glorifying the American Girl” keeps saying “damn it!” — as did film stars in blooper reels from that era. But by the 1960s, things had changed. My parents’ “hit your thumb” profanity of choice began with an “s.” To me (born 1965), that is a tad tame, and I go for the F-bomb, which is common among people my age and younger.

Profanity is all about escalation. “Damn” is reinforced as “goddamn,” with “bull” modifying the S-word and “mother” serving an analogous purpose for the F-bomb.

That said, it’s highly unlikely that Trump will turn up the volume much more when it comes to bad words. In English, profanity comes in three stages of shock value. Stage 1 is blasphemous words. “Damn” and “hell” were once considered such strong drink that in the 19th-century opera “H. M. S. Pinafore,” the captain prides himself on never saying “damn” (or hardly ever, he admits). Today, in our less pious age, those are mild expletives at best.

Stage 2 is sexual or graphic words about the body, and Trump revels in those. We will recall a notorious comment of his about grabbing women by a certain body part and his scatological characterization of countries such as Haiti and El Salvador. But these sorts of words, which are used publicly today much more than in the past, now qualify more as salty or tasteless than genuinely taboo.

Stage 3 is racial and other slurs against groups. Though Trump has been accused of using the N-word, he has long avoided using slurs in public. We can, of course, expect him to push the envelope. Indeed, just this week he used an anti-transgender slur when referring to Annie Andrews, the Democratic nominee for the Senate in South Carolina. But it’s notable that Andrews, who has expressed support for transgender youth, is not transgender herself. I’m willing to bet that Trump wouldn’t use that slur in public to refer to a transgender person like Sarah McBride, the congresswoman from Delaware, just as I wouldn’t expect him to use a homophobic slur to publicly attack a gay opponent.

Today, it is such words that qualify as truly profane. We often think of slurs as distinct from swear words, but it’s an indication that they are, in fact, today’s profanity that even someone as heedless of etiquette, decorum, restraint and reflection as Trump has tended to avoid them.

Because the Stage 1 and Stage 2 words are now more naughty than profane, Trump uses them to thumb his nose at propriety. In this, he is like an 11-year-old, snapping towels at people in the locker room — and snapping them ever more to get a rise out of the people looking on.

Yet he does not typically risk Stage 3 profanity. Amid his staggering megalomania and chronic logorrhea, Trump, if only for pragmatic purposes, maintains a twinkle of — of all things — decorum.

John McWhorter (@JohnHMcWhorter) is an associate professor of linguistics at Columbia University. He is the author of “Nine Nasty Words: English in the Gutter: Then, Now and Forever” and, most recently, “Woke Racism: How a New Religion Has Betrayed Black America.” @JohnHMcWhorter
