French Students Take to the Streets as Government Seeks Way Out of Crisis

The New York Times October 08, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Mass protests over decrepit schools and absent teachers are in their third week, with more planned. Officials have failed so far to quell a movement drawing many adult supporters.

By Catherine PorterMark Landler and Ségolène Le Stradic

Reporting from Paris

Chanting, marching and clashing at times with the police, French students protested for the second day this week on Thursday as officials looked for ways to ease a crisis that has threatened to swell into a nationwide wave of grievance.

Although officials estimated that the protests were smaller than the ones on Tuesday, they were still large and boisterous, as thousands of young people railed against overcrowded classrooms, a shortage of teachers and decrepit facilities. The mass demonstrations, sometimes joined by labor unions, parents and teachers, began more than two weeks ago, forcing hundreds of schools to close, and more are scheduled for next week.

Thomas Droit, a 22-year-old law student, said that in his five years of study at CY Cergy Paris University, he had “never seen a protest of this magnitude.”

The protest, he said, was about a “convergence of struggles” — a phrase that has gained traction in the protests — from all parts of society. He cited his own concerns about the government’s plan to freeze housing benefits for students and to make foreign students pay higher university fees.

“And personally what angers me is that high school students have been severely repressed,” he said.

Many protesters said they were outraged by videos they had seen online of police violence against high schoolers, some of whom had thrown debris and launched fireworks at officers.

“We are used to seeing police in France beat people, but they are normally adults. These are kids,” said Kerra Underwood, 20, a psychology student who was among the protesters who flooded into the Place de la Bastille, a main square in Paris. The crowds chanted “justice nowhere, police everywhere,” and a demand of the current president: “Macron, resign.”

The police scuffled in the square with protesters who threw plants, chairs and benches toward officers. Officers with riot shields charged toward some of the protesters and fired tear gas, sending people running.

Orian Loupescande, 20, a business student, who was crying from tear gas, blasted the police response, saying that students had come to demonstrate peacefully. “It’s shocking because it means we don’t have the right to protest,” he said.

The demonstrations have come at a fraught moment for France. The country will hold a presidential election in April, and polls indicate a far-right candidate, Marine Le Pen, has a plausible path to victory to succeed the current president, Emmanuel Macron.

In front of the Lycée Turgot, a public high school in Paris, Zoé Baby-Coutousis and May Souai, both 15, said they were protesting in solidarity with their peers in the suburbs where there are higher levels of unemployment, poverty, immigration and teacher absenteeism.

“We’re all supposed to have the opportunities,” May said. Their school had problems, too, they said. The days were too long, teachers were absent in some classes and the building was not equipped to deal with climate change, they said.

French officials said were listening to the students’ concerns. The education minister, Édouard Geffray, met with representatives of three major student groups on Thursday. After the meeting, Mr. Geffray said that they had discussed the state of school buildings across the country, the unfairness of the university application system, absent teachers and the importance of dialogue and democracy in schools.

Mr. Geffray has also pledged that there will be no job cuts in schools, in an effort to address student complaints about a shortage of teachers. But the government won’t unveil its new education budget until Nov. 12, which has left many students frustrated.

Later, Mr. Geffray said the government would deploy 3,000 substitute teachers over the next few days to the high schools where they are needed most.

The French government, in the throes of a financial crisis, has offered students little remedy beyond suspending classes so they can voice their complaints.

The demonstrations could grow in size next week, when one of France’s main teachers’ unions has called on high school teachers and university professors to take part in a third day of nationwide protests. On Tuesday, when union activists joined the students protesters, the demonstrations drew an estimated 266,000 people across the country, and 71,500 in Paris, according to the Interior Ministry. The unions estimated the crowds were more than twice that large.

Just over 150 high schools were closed across France on Thursday, compared to 900 on Tuesday, according to the education ministry. Students have barricaded some of them, and a handful have been set on fire. The police have made thousands of arrests since the protests began.

Some students have compared the mood to May 1968, when mass demonstrations, street battles and nationwide strikes transformed France. But so far, the protests have been more tightly focused, and not as ideologically potent, said Julian Bourg, a history professor at Boston College.

“That said, each major French protest movement does raise the possibility that the demands of a specific cohort may lead to more generalized protest and a broader political crisis,” he said. “That is the echo of 1968.”

In a speech to the nation on Wednesday, the French prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, sought to assuage student anger. He pledged to fill vacant teaching positions and to identify urgent problems in school buildings, among other priorities. He also called on students and teachers to hold discussions in schools about how to improve the state of education.

“Young people’s anger doesn’t come out of nowhere,” Mr. Lecornu said, as he urged students to “choose their path and look to the future with confidence.”

On Thursday, some of the student protesters dismissed Mr. Lecornu’s remarks as a delay tactic.

“His speech motivated us to keep blocking our school until the government stops refusing to listen to us and responds to our demands,” said Augustin Lassaab, 17, who was protesting in the Place de la Bastille. “We will not stop.”

Giulia Imbert, Zane Irwin, Aurelien Breeden and Michael Levenson contributed reporting.

Catherine Porter is an international reporter for The Times, covering France. She is based in Paris.

Mark Landler is the Paris bureau chief of The Times, covering France, as well as American foreign policy in Europe and the Middle East. He has been a journalist for more than three decades.

Ségolène Le Stradic a reporter and researcher for The Times, based in Paris.

Trump Administration Considers Using Ships to Deport Immigrants

The New York Times October 08, 2026

U. S. Immigration Crackdown

Advertisement

Supported by

Journeys to destinations including El Salvador and Venezuela could take days and cost millions. Officials cautioned that discussions are still preliminary.

By Hamed Aleaziz

Reporting from Washington

The Trump administration is considering using ships, including a 500-foot training vessel and ferries, to deport migrants to Central and South America on journeys that could take days and cost millions of dollars, according to two U. S. officials.

The discussions over recent weeks are still preliminary, but officials have identified possible ships, including the Training Ship Golden Bear, a maritime academy vessel docked in California, said one person who spoke on the condition of anonymity because of the sensitivity of the plan. Defense Department officials have also reached out to companies about ships in Europe, the official said.

A different official, from the Department of Homeland Security, which oversees deportations, cautioned that the plan was still hypothetical and that no decisions had been made.

It is not clear why officials are entertaining such an unusual plan, considering the logistical challenges, high cost and checkered history of deportations by sea. The plan could, however, offload some deportation costs from Homeland Security to the Defense Department.

“D. H. S. is assessing all our resources, to maximize efficiency and continue to deliver on President Trump’s mission of securing the homeland for all Americans,” the Homeland Security Department said in a statement. Secretary Markwayne Mullin, the statement added, “is 100 percent focused on ensuring the needs of our department are met while being the best possible steward of taxpayer dollars.”

What you should know about anonymous sources. The Times makes a careful decision any time it shields the identity of a source. The information the source supplies must be newsworthy, credible and give readers genuine insight.

The Defense Department did not comment on the proposal.

The plan would represent another escalation of the Trump administration’s evolving strategy for carrying out mass deportations using all available means. Those drastic steps have included flying people abroad using military planes, sending migrants to unfamiliar and often dangerous third countries, and housing people in Guantánamo Bay, Cuba. The administration has also embraced policies to deter immigrants from coming to the United States and persuade them to self-deport.

“What ICE is functionally contemplating is prison ships,” said Claire Trickler-McNulty, a former top official at Immigration and Customs Enforcement during the Biden administration. “That raises serious concerns at every step. Moving people through international waters and past other countries’ territory for days at a time raises hard questions about which laws apply and who has jurisdiction if something goes wrong.”

She added that “holding hundreds of people on a ship is also an enormous operational and safety challenge.”

Ms. Trickler-McNulty said that during her time at the Homeland Security Department, including as a career official in the Obama and first Trump administrations, agency staff considered various ideas to deport people, such as using ships or trains. But they never pursued them seriously, she said.

The journeys to countries like El Salvador, Honduras and Venezuela would take days by sea and require a large number of security personnel. It is unclear whether migrants would be detained for the duration of the trips or what their sleeping arrangements would be.

The U. S. government has estimated that using ships could cost millions of dollars per trip, whereas deportation flights are substantially cheaper. It is also unclear whether other countries would agree to such a plan.

The Golden Bear served as a training ship for the Cal Poly Maritime Academy, a school for those seeking careers at sea, as a key part of the school’s educational program. The vessel ended its 30-year run with the school this summer. It is not clear under what authority the ship could be used for deportations by the federal government.

“For three decades, Golden Bear has served as a floating classroom where thousands of cadets transformed classroom knowledge into practical experience at sea,” a July announcement from the school read.

Such a plan would also conjure memories of a controversial 1950s campaign in which hundreds of thousands of Mexicans were deported in a large-scale deportation drive referred to as Operation Wetback. The campaign, named for a slur for Mexican immigrants, included expelling people by sea.

In August 1956, chaos erupted aboard one of the ships near the Mexican border city of Tampico. The New York Times reported that 40 passengers jumped from the ship and that five drowned.

The Mexican government had shut down the operation by September, citing poor weather. The Times reported, however, that the “prevailing opinion” was that it was because of the incident near Tampico as well as “alleged unsatisfactory facilities on ship and maltreatment of involuntary passengers.”

John Ismay and Jazmine Ulloa contributed reporting.

Hamed Aleaziz covers the Department of Homeland Security and immigration policy for The Times.

Why Anne Carson, the New Nobel Laureate, Is the Easiest Difficult Poet

The New York Times October 08, 2026

2026 Nobel Prizes

Advertisement

Supported by

AN Appraisal

Carson has mind-boggling range and formal audacity, our poetry columnist writes, but however much she toys with obscurity she remains too hilarious to be intimidating.

By Elisa Gabbert

Elisa Gabbert is the Book Review’s poetry columnist. Her collections of poetry and essays include, most recently, “Normal Distance” and “Any Person Is the Only Self.”

I like the way Anne Carson begins “Men in the Off Hours” (2000): “I like the way Thucydides begins his account of the hostilities between Athenians and Peloponnesians that we call the Peloponnesian War.”

This was the seventh book by Carson — the Canadian poet who won the Nobel Prize in Literature on Thursday — but the first I encountered, assigned to read it in a poetry workshop in college. My professor might as well have assigned us to be baffled and amazed.

And I was. What was this, this sentence, in what looked like an essay from every angle, from the (mock?) scholarly title (“Ordinary Time: Virginia Woolf and Thucydides on War”) to the block quotes to the unfolding thesis: War warps time, but differently for everyone, for children and old people (“Time embraces youth, youth embraces war”), women and men (“Even in the off hours, men know marks”). Yet it is short, for an essay — six pages that cover two millenniums — and is followed by an epitaph, a four-line poem.

The fourth piece in the book, “New Rule,” is a page of tercets about a squirrel (“I saw a squirrel jump and skid./Is this scary? he seemed to say”) and being jilted (“Not enough spin on it, said my true love/when he left in our fifth year”).

“Do you fear the same things as/I fear?” the speaker asks the squirrel. “A snail is a snail,” Carson writes in that first “essay” — is fear fear?

The fifth, called “Sumptuous Destitution,” is in couplets, kind of; every other line is a quote from one of Emily Dickinson’s letters to Thomas Higginson, followed by a loud citation, their full names spelled out each time: “(Emily Dickinson letter 319 to Thomas Higginson)” etc. These citations are longer, as lines, if they’re lines, than Carson’s own lines. One sentence is broken into five small parts (“‘Sumptuous destitution’/is a phrase/scholars use/of female/silence”), further broken up by ED’s interruptions. And is that even true?

Here, in these few pages from the middle of her career, we get a microcosmic sense of almost everything Carson is capable of and interested in. She has mind-boggling range and formal audacity, the power to bring out the poemhood in any prose genre (a story, a lecture, a play) and to complicate the poemhood of poems (what are lines?).

She mixes everything together in a casual defiance suggesting literature is always and never true, an art of fact. She translates meaning not just across language but across gapes of time, making ancient texts sound just-spoken. (Here is Elektra, in her “Orestes”: “Yes well, so it goes.”) She has an ever-present humor that can modulate from bitterest, dry-rag-dragging-on-dry-wood wit to full comedy. She likes to write about animals, gender, grief and suffering, human folly, love and war. She may be the easiest difficult poet, toying with obscurity but too hilarious to be truly intimidating.

Carson’s first book, “Eros the Bittersweet,” published in 1986, was a version of her doctoral thesis, a work of criticism. Her second was the first that could reasonably be read as poetry: “Short Talks,” released in 1992. Each piece in it is a prose block that takes on a single supposed subject: “Short Talk on Ovid.” “Short Talk on Rain.” If these are talks, they’re the shortest conceivable talks, several sentences each that could be voiced during the period most speakers spend opening their water bottle and taking a sip. These ironic little fictions or nonfictions could almost be labeled jokes, à la the one about walking backward: “My mother forbade us to walk backwards. That is how the dead walk, she would say. Where did she get this idea? Perhaps from a bad translation.”

In aggregate they constitute an argument about how to talk: say as little as possible, as densely as possible, to justify speaking on a topic at all, whether it’s hopes or trout or Van Gogh: “When he looked at the world he saw the nails that attach colors to things and he saw that the nails were in pain.” Be the most fascinating person in the room for a couple of minutes.

A classicist by training, Carson achieved a new level of fame with her verse novel “Autobiography of Red” (1998), which imagines the winged monster Geryon from Greek myth as a gay teenager. The poem is composed in alternating short and long lines:

Geryon’s mother turned to knock her cigarette ash on the sink then faced Geryon again. He was seated at the kitchen tablewith his camera in front of his face adjusting the focus. He did not answer. He had recently relinquished speech.

This see-sawing has the effect of a constant reminder, an alarm always waking you up: Novel or not, this is a poem. Don’t be lulled into a prose state of mind.

Carson’s recent work is as playful as ever, as funny and sad and perplexing. “Wrong Norma” (2024) has the everything’s-possible quality of “Men in the Off Hours.” There’s a sestina with a scholarly appendix, a translation of a speech from Symposium, a new short talk, a tiny speculative crime novella (“Thret,” Parts I-III) in which the narrator befriends a helpful carrion crow named Short Pants: “Short Pants had a good sense of coda.”

These 15 pages make a strong introduction to Carson’s whole thing, the sketch that holographically projects all of tragicomic life. “I have always felt stunted by my own loneliness,” Carson writes, toward the end of Part II, “but now this strikes me as inaccurate, or the answer to a question that has not been asked. What do answers answer anyway.”

Looking back on 25 years of readership, I find I can’t overstate the influence Carson has had on me. Those first 10 or so pages were sufficiently rich in beauty and shock to change a young poet wanting change. She seemed, then and now, to offer an entirely new model of what a poet could be, what a poetry book could contain. And her body of work demonstrates the dazzling scales a writer can achieve while staying basically the same, an isotropic infinite universe from a big bang.

Canadian Poet Anne Carson Is Awarded Nobel Prize in Literature

The New York Times October 08, 2026

2026 Nobel Prizes

Advertisement

Supported by

The writer joins a list of laureates that includes Toni Morrison, Samuel Beckett and Bob Dylan.

By Alex Marshall

Alex Marshall has reported on the Nobel Prize in Literature since 2019. This year, he prepared for 46 potential winners. Carson was thankfully among them.

The Canadian poet and essayist Anne Carson was awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature on Thursday by the Swedish Academy, which cited “her bold and inventive oeuvre that, in playful dialogue with the classical tradition, has created new forms for contemporary literature.”

She is the third Canadian-born writer to receive the honor, after Alice Munro in 2013 and Saul Bellow in 1976.

Upon learning of the prize, Carson said “Yikes,” according to her agent, Nicole Aragi.

Carson, 76, is best known for her translations of ancient Greek texts and for remixing them in a modern, playful voice. “Autobiography of Red: A Novel in Verse,” from 1998, turned a fragment of Greek poetry into a tale of a moody teenager’s destructive love affair, and “Red Doc>,” from 2013, a sequel of sorts to “Autobiography of Red,” concerned a road trip.

“Many toil in the interstices of genre,” the poet Daisy Fried wrote in a 2013 review of “Red Doc>” for The New York Times. “Carson’s palatable, popular, sophisticated and who-cares approach may have done the most and best work in the last two decades to stop people worrying so much about what’s poetry and what’s not.”

Sam Anderson, in a 2013 profile of Carson for The New York Times Magazine, said that the author’s work “can seduce even people who don’t like poetry.”

“Autobiography of Red” has sold nearly 100,000 copies across all formats in the United States, according to Knopf, the book’s American publisher.

Save to your reading list:

The Nobel Prize, literature’s key honor, is typically the capstone to a writer’s career. Past recipients have included the poets W. B. Yeats and Louise Glück, the playwrights Harold Pinter and Samuel Beckett, and the novelists Han Kang and Toni Morrison. More unexpected recipients have included Bob Dylan, in 2016, and Winston Churchill, in 1953.

The new laureate receives 12 million Swedish kronor, about $1.2 million, as well as a huge boost in reputation.

In recent years, the Swedish Academy has tried to expand the diversity of laureates after criticism that too many past recipients have been men. Since 2018, the academy has alternated between male and female laureates. Given that last year’s prize went to the Hungarian novelist Laszlo Krasznahorkai, critics had expected this year’s accolade to go to a woman.

And before Thursday’s announcement, bookmakers had two female favorites for the prize: Carson and Can Xue, the avant-garde Chinese writer.

Carson was born in Toronto in 1950, and her family moved several times around Canada because of her father’s job as a banker. She first became interested in ancient Greek language and texts in high school. “It just seemed to me the best language,” she told The New York Times Magazine in 2013.

Carson later studied at the University of Toronto and became a classics teacher at Canadian colleges, including the University of Calgary and McGill University, as her writing career took off. She has since held positions at colleges in the United States, including Cornell and New York University.

Among Carson’s key works cited by the Nobel committee are “Eros the Bittersweet,” her debut book-length essay from 1986 about the god of love, and “The Glass Essay,” a long poem from 1995 about unrequited love.

Save to your reading list:

The committee also singled out “Wrong Norma,” a poetry collection that earned her a National Book Award nomination in 2024. Its poems range through subjects including her father, snow and Roget’s Thesaurus, but Carson said there was no link between them. “That’s why I’ve called them ‘wrong,’” she said.

Tristram Fane Saunders, reviewing “Wrong Norma” for The Daily Telegraph, said the poems were “united only by the fact they’re all somehow uncompromisingly intelligent while being effortlessly readable.”

The Nobel accolade for Carson brought joyous responses from fellow poets, classicists and even Mark Carney, Canada’s prime minister.

Save to your reading list:

“As a classicist, poet and performer, Anne Carson has shown how the mysteries and absurdities of language and the eternal qualities of certain stories, possess us in the present,” Aragi, her agent, said in an emailed statement. “She is a writer of the great fires — love, fury, grief — but also of the quotidian. She amuses and shatters.”

Claudia Rankine, the poet, said in an interview that she was “extremely happy” that Carson had received the Nobel — adding that her students on the creative writing program at New York University would likely be, too, since they had just studied some of Carson’s work. ”There’s not a semester I don’t teach her,” Rankine said. “She is the person who has freed the imagination around writing and poetry in the past 30 years.”

In recent years, Carson and her partner, the artist Robert Currie, have split their time between Ann Arbor, Mich., and Iceland, where she has citizenship. Ragnar Kjartansson, one of Iceland’s most popular contemporary artists, said in a telephone interview that the pair acted “like cool teenagers” when in Reykjavik, the country’s capital, and spent their time attending and staging underground art and literary shows, supporting artists and hanging out with them in the city’s public baths.

“She means a lot to the scene here,” Kjartansson said: “She’s a force, and everyone’s really happy.”

Carson is a private figure. Her book jackets rarely feature an author photo and sometimes do not even have an author biography. She has rarely discussed her private life in interviews, although in an August 2024 essay in The London Review of Books, she said that she had Parkinson’s disease and that her handwriting had “disintegrated.”

“I used to take pleasure in writing in notebooks, shelves of them, day after day, year after year,” Carson wrote: “Now the upright strokes bend or break or go in all directions, vowels shrink to blobs, slant loses its smooth smart angle, it all looks embarrassing. I scrub out whole paragraphs in shame.”

She added that she had joined a boxing class to help with the disease’s symptoms.

Declan Spring, Carson’s editor at New Directions, her American publisher, said that he had tried calling Carson to congratulate her on the Nobel, “but I got a message that her phone is off.”

“She’s quite shy,” Spring said.

Finding champagne in Manhattan before 10 a. m. was not easy, but the New Directions president and publisher Barbara Epler managed to procure two bottles on her way to the office as she absorbed the news. Carson is “capable of incredible depth on difficult things, like grief and illness and love and loss,” she said. “It’s partly about her being a Greek scholar, but I think it’s just her nature.”

During a news conference to announce the award on Thursday, Ingrid Carlberg, the Swedish Academy’s permanent secretary, said that she had reached Carson earlier, and that Carson had sounded “very taken by surprise.”

It was a short call, Carlberg said: All the poet would say was that she was “in Iceland,” where she was “listening to the wind.”

Ronda Kaysen contributed reporting.

One of the joys of the Nobel for me discovering authors I might not otherwise be familiar with. In recent years, I've loved delving into Jon Fosse's mystical tomes and Abdulrazak Gurnah's migrant tales in the months after those authors became laureates. I'm looking forward to delving into Carson's catalogue soon.

For those unfamiliar with Carson, start with Plainwater, then Autobiography of Red, then The Beauty of the Husband. Then Eros the Bittersweet. Then read everything! I’ve been obsessed with Carson for 20 years and I’m so glad more people will know her work!

An Anne Carson Reader

The New York Times October 08, 2026

Want to read 0

Have read 0

Advertisement

Supported by

The Canadian poet won this year’s Nobel Prize in Literature. If you’ve never read any of her work, here’s where to start.

By Ash Wu

Anne Carson, the prolific Canadian essayist, novelist and poet, was awarded the 2026 Nobel Prize in Literature on Thursday. Over a career that spans more than four decades, Carson has built an oeuvre that draws on her education in classical literature and often refracts it through a playful lens.

Her writing threads a line from Greek antiquity to the present day, and interrogates the treacly nature of desire and the pain that it induces. Carson gives the impression “of someone from another world, either extraterrestrial or ancient,” Sam Anderson wrote in a 2013 New York Times Magazine profile. “Our modern earthly categories are too artificial and simplistic to contain anything like the real truth she is determined to communicate.”

Despite Carson’s inclination toward privacy, she has achieved a kind of celebrity rare among public intellectuals, as Anderson noted. During a performance of her play “Antigonick” for an overflow crowd at N. Y. U., he wrote, the audience reached a consensus: “People kept using the phrase ‘rock concert.’”

If you’ve never read any of Carson’s works, here are five books to start with.

A novel in verse and perhaps her most popular work, “Autobiography of Red” draws upon Carson’s obsession with Greek classics through a retelling of the fragmentary poem “Geryoneis,” by the poet Stesichorus. In the original myth, Geryon is a winged monster Heracles slaughters after stealing his cattle. Carson reimagines him in the present day as a gay teenager with a troubled family life. He falls into a state of deep infatuation with the Greek hero, who in this version is an older boy who eventually breaks his heart. “Carson writes in language any poet would kill for,” Ruth Padel wrote in her review for The New York Times, “sensuous and funny, poignant, musical and tender, brilliantly lighted.”

Save to your reading list:

This collection of three narrative poems contains “The Glass Essay,” a 36-page epic that interweaves the end of a romantic relationship with musings on Emily Brönte, whom Carson describes as a perpetual “whacher” — a deliberate misspelling — who constantly observes the English moors that inspired her novel “Wuthering Heights.” In Brönte, Carson finds kinship and a means of verbalizing her heartbreak. The author Anthony Doerr has referred to “The Glass Essay” as his favorite poem, writing that “it feels to me like a thousand floodlights switching on.”

Save to your reading list:

Her first work of literary criticism, “Eros” dissects and expands upon the Greek poet Sappho’s concept of “glukupikron,” a word that roughly translates to “sweetbitter” and encapsulates the simultaneous pain and pleasure of romantic love. Carson traces the idea of eros through the poetry of Sappho and other ancient Greek masters, before settling on her thesis of “eros as lack,” describing passionate love as a product of the thin-ridged edge between wanting something and having it.

Save to your reading list:

In the first chapter, Carson writes: “This imitation of a poisonous by a nonpoisonous species is called mimicry./My husband was no mimic.” She chronicles the dissolution of a marriage and her erotic fixation on the husband through 29 “tangos,” a poetic form of her invention that alternates long lines with shorter ones to evoke the rhythms of dance. Daphne Merkin wrote in her Times review, “I don’t think there has been a book since Robert Lowell’s ‘Life Studies’ that has advanced the art of poetry quite as radically as Anne Carson is in the process of doing.”

Save to your reading list:

Written after a five-year hiatus, “Nox” demonstrates Carson’s willingness to challenge what a volume of poetry should look like. Sold in a skinny, funerary box that opens to reveal pages that unfold like an accordion, “Nox” presents an elegy for her estranged brother in a scrapbook that contains photographs, illustrations and excerpts to illuminate her field of memory. Of its layout, Ben Ratliff wrote in The New York Times Book Review that “it carries a whiff of visual art multiple or gift shop souvenir or ‘Griffin & Sabine. But trust me: It’s an Anne Carson book. Maybe her best.”

Save to your reading list:

I remember reading Anne Carson's "Autobiography of Red" as a teenager and being stunned by how accurately she captured those adolescent feelings of heartbreak and growing pains. I was also impressed by the way she contextualized this book — and her others — through the lens of her background in classic Greek literature. "The Glass Essay" with its depictions of Emily Brönte's cruelty and artistry also stuck with me through my early adulthood. I would love to hear your favorite quotes from Anne Carson and all of your experiences reading her books, for the first time or the fortieth.

Russia’s Vague Account of a Mysterious Death Is Stoking Cover-Up Fears

The New York Times October 08, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

As rumors spread about a possible plague outbreak in Siberia, the Kremlin turned to a familiar playbook: offering little information about potential bad news.

By Neil MacFarquhar

As rumors swirled this week that a woman working in a Siberian lab may have died of the plague, news programs on Russian state television paid scant attention. The authorities in Moscow released little information.

Faced with this potential new threat, the Kremlin seems to be resorting to a familiar playbook: avoiding bad news.

The lack of information has caused unease around the world, particularly given the memory of China’s effort to withhold information about Covid-19.

In Russia, federal officials are generally reluctant, even fearful, about publishing anything that might cast the Kremlin in a negative light. The pace of news in Russia tends to be determined by the government, not by when events actually occur. The independent press has been driven into exile.

Perhaps the most notorious case was the hidden news that an explosion at the Chernobyl nuclear plant in April 1986 had contaminated a wide area with dangerous radiation. The Kremlin began to release information only after Sweden and other European countries, alarmed by high radiation readings, demanded an explanation.

In 1979, there was an accidental leak of anthrax spores from a secret biological weapon facility run by the Soviet military near what is now Yekaterinburg. Someone turned on a machine that dried the spores without realizing that a maintenance technician had removed a clogged exhaust filter.

More than 60 people died, as well as countless farm animals downwind of the facility. The Soviet authorities blamed the human toll on tainted meat, and the truth did not emerge until 1992, after the Soviet Union collapsed.

But the obfuscation did not stop, especially after Vladimir V. Putin became president in 2000.

In two of the most tragic episodes, the government either concealed the truth or promoted outright falsehoods. One was the sinking of the Kursk nuclear-powered submarine in the Barents Sea in 2000, with all 118 sailors aboard killed. In 2002, Chechen terrorists took over 900 people hostage during a performance of the “Nord-Ost” musical. Interior Ministry special forces knocked everybody out by pumping a chemical agent into the theater. But they failed to coordinate with the medical services, leading to the deaths of at least 116 hostages, as well as all 41 attackers.

Since Russian forces mounted a large-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, there have been examples of the government’s effort to camouflage the true scope of the war.

Earlier this year, when a bomb exploded in a Moscow restaurant where a top Russian general was celebrating, Russian state news initially reported it as a gas canister explosion. The Kremlin has resorted to extensive censorship to hide Russian losses in its war in Ukraine — which the government made illegal to call a war. Independent researchers have estimated that 450,000 Russian soldiers have died.

Although several state-run newspapers initially ran articles about the death in Siberia, the news disappeared from their websites.

Alexandra Arkhipova, a Russian anthropologist in exile, wrote on social media, “Instead of a straightforward description of what is happening in Irkutsk, news columns are filled with journalistic euphemisms — clearly by order from above.”

There is no mention of plague, she added, only headlines about the “Irkutsk infection,” referring to the region of Siberia where the woman, who was 28, died.

Local social media accounts are full of questions and concerns about the case, although the occasional comment reflects the official line that people should rely on government statements.

Alyona, reached via social media and identified by only one name to avoid retribution from the authorities, said she was an old school friend of the victim but had not been in touch for a long time. “Everyone is worried, especially since there have been no clear statements,” she said.

The mystery surrounding the death in Irkutsk deepened because the governor of a neighboring region had initially posted on social media that the woman had died of the plague, and then changed it later to say that she had “possibly” died of the plague.

Dmitri S. Peskov, the Kremlin spokesman, criticized the news media for reporting rumors rather than relying on official reports from the public health safety agency. Even though the agency’s head, a doctor, flew to Irkutsk to assess the situation, it avoids news conferences, communicating only by intermittent press releases.

Russia’s public health agency has said the pathogen that killed the woman was not the one she had been researching in the lab, for which she had been vaccinated.

On Thursday, the governor of Irkutsk, Igor Kobzev, who has been posting regularly on his social media channels, wrote that all preventive measures had been completed and after about 5,000 laboratory tests, nobody else the victim might have been in contact with at the institute or the hospital was infected. “Amid intense media scrutiny, the specialists ​thoroughly investigated the situation,” he wrote. “It was a test, but we passed it in worthy fashion.”

His post attracted comments from area residents asking for a clearer explanation of what exactly had happened and what had killed the woman.

Russian officials have said the lab worker in Siberia died from pneumonia, of an unknown cause, on Friday night. Although the World Health Organization sent an initial query, the Russian authorities did not provide an answer in the required 24 hours, but three days later, the organization said.

The W. H. O. said Russia had not yet provided the details needed to make a formal “risk assessment” about the disease’s possible spread. Senior officials in both the E. U. and the United States, including President Trump and Marco Rubio, the secretary of state, all encouraged Russia to provide more information.

From 2019 to 2025, 10 countries reported almost 4,000 plague cases and 423 deaths, according to W. H. O. statistics. The United States reports about seven cases annually — the most recent was a woman in her 50s who died in June in New Mexico. Plague can be successfully treated with antibiotics if caught early.

Wrestling with the Covid pandemic, which completely disrupted ordinary life, left a legacy of mistrust toward public health agencies and their ability to protect people.

At a news conference on Wednesday, Maria Van Kerkhove, director of epidemic and pandemic management at the W. H. O., said, “Covid is certainly in the back of everybody’s mind.”

“If this individual did not die from the plague, then how did she die?” Dr. Van Kerkhove asked, adding, “We expect further answers from Russia.”

Alina Lobzina, Ivan Nechepurenko, Paul Sonne and Milana Mazaeva contributed reporting.

Neil MacFarquhar has been a Times reporter since 1995, writing about a range of topics from war to politics to the arts, both internationally and in the United States.

France Is Veering Toward a Potential Debt Crisis, a Warning to the World

The New York Times October 08, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

French bond investors are demanding sharply higher interest rates, a cautionary development for other high-debt countries.

By Eshe Nelson

Reporting from London

France has been engulfed by turmoil, with students out on the streets to protest cuts at schools. Investors are rebelling against the government, too, by questioning the country’s ability to manage its huge debt pile.

France has emerged as the European epicenter of global turmoil in bond markets and serves as a warning to politicians around the world contending with higher borrowing costs. It’s a perilous financial backdrop to the protests. On Thursday, for the second time in a week, high school students and their supporters came out across France, calling for more teachers and the renovation of dilapidated school buildings.

Rising interest rates expose the vulnerability of countries with high debt burdens and stubborn deficits. When governments must spend more on debt payments, less money is left for other priorities like improving schools, building more housing or cutting taxes — and that can push frustrated voters into the streets or into the arms of populist political parties.

“These bond yield rises have very real implications,” said Mahmood Pradhan, a nonresident fellow at Bruegel, a think tank in Brussels, and former deputy director of the European department at the International Monetary Fund.

In a nightmare scenario, the dynamics become a self-fulfilling spiral: Politicians make more promises to appease aggrieved citizens, leading to more borrowing and, in turn, spooking investors, who demand even higher rates to keep buying government bonds.

France shows how quickly the situation can escalate when investor sentiment turns sour.

A widening gap between the 10-year yields on French and German government debt is a sign that investors are more nervous about lending to France.

Source: Investing. com.

Jason Karaian/The New York Times

This week, the yield on 10-year French bonds nearly touched 5 percent, the highest rate since 2002. More worrying, another measure of investors’ feelings toward French debt has attracted fresh attention: the so-called spread between 10-year yields on French and German government debt. The gap shows the premium traders are demanding to hold French debt over the alternative from Germany, which is considered the safest borrower in Europe.

This spread recently reached its widest disparity since 2012 after an astonishingly rapid increase this past month. Investors have also demanded higher returns to lend to France than to Italy and Greece, which were long considered Europe’s most problematic high-debt nations.

Across Europe, rising bond yields are testing the resilience of economies. The year started with low inflation and faster economic growth. But since the war in Iran began, energy prices have soared, pushing inflation back up and prompting the European Central Bank to raise interest rates twice this year. Traders expect another rate increase by the end of the year.

The rise in borrowing costs leaves governments exposed to new economic shocks like sudden increases in food and energy prices. It will give them less leeway to support businesses and households, in ways they have in recent years. “The limited ability of countries to deal with these shocks is a new world for us,” Mr. Pradhan said.

In France, interest payments are one of the biggest expenses in the government’s budget, and could eat up more than 90 billion euros ($100 billion) next year, more than planned spending on defense and education, according to the French finance ministry. Emmanuel Moulin, the governor of the French central bank, recently told The Financial Times that the country was at risk of being “strangled by interest rates” if it didn’t improve its public finances.

France’s incumbent political leaders — and some hopeful contenders — are scrambling to reassure skeptical investors. But so far, their overtures are having limited impact. The government said last week that it would aim to shrink its budget deficit next year, after failing to do so this year. But even then, debt levels will keep rising. France’s government debt is already nearly 120 percent of the size of the economy.

Investors have been tracking budget negotiations in Paris closely, but they expect that France’s fiscal problems could be intensified by presidential election next spring. So far all the leading candidates have made big spending promises and not presented convincing plans to reduce debt. Marine Le Pen, the far-right front-runner, vowed this week to cut the deficit but didn’t detail how, while Jean-Luc Mélenchon, the far-left candidate, has alarmed investors by proposing to cancel some of the country’s debt instead of repaying it.

France might get “some temporary relief in markets if they can get some measures passed in parliament,” Mr. Pradhan said. “But beyond that, France has a debt problem.” The country has large spending needs that have been politically difficult to restrain, in areas such as pensions, which are compounded by rising interest payments.

These are issues shared elsewhere. In some ways, the United States is at the core of the market tumult. In recent months the yields on U. S. Treasuries, the largest and most influential bond market in the world, have jumped and triggered a global sell-off.

The United States still enjoys plentiful demand for its debt, and one important factor driving up yields is Silicon Valley’s artificial intelligence boom. But economists warn that the country is continuing to push the frontier of what investors might accept from governments if they are seen as unwilling or unready to tackle rising debt levels. America’s gross national debt topped $40 trillion this summer, or more than 120 percent of the size of the economy, while annual deficits are set to keep expanding.

In Asia, Japan’s debt trajectory recently tested the nerve of the market. Japan’s debt has been more than twice the size of its economy for many years, but recent government promises to increase spending and cut taxes have punished Japan’s financial assets. The yen weakened so much that the U. S. Treasury supported an intervention to bolster the currency, and 10-year Japanese bond yields are trading at their highest levels in three decades.

The lesson applies broadly to high-debt countries. Many governments have drastically increased their borrowing in recent years to support their economies through a series of shocks, including the Covid-19 pandemic, the 2022 energy crisis after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine and another energy shock this year because of the war in Iran. At the same time, public spending on health care and pensions for aging populations is growing. In the short term there are also demands, especially in Europe, to spend more on defense.

Global public debt is near its highest levels since World War II and on track to grow beyond 100 percent of global gross domestic product, the International Monetary Fund said on Wednesday. “Advanced economies are the worst offenders,” said Kristalina Georgieva, the managing director of the Washington-based organization.

In Europe, the risk is that the tumult in French bonds could spread to other eurozone debt markets such as Italy’s and trigger another regional sovereign debt crisis, reminiscent of the one in 2012.

“The situation demands an urgent and comprehensive set of policy responses,” Ms. Georgieva said. Governments need to show credible plans to reduce their deficits even as many people have come to expect their political leaders to intervene in the face of economic shocks, she noted. This is normally done through some combination of reduced spending and higher taxes.

“Some very tough political choices stare us in the face,” she said.

Eshe Nelson is a Times reporter based in London, covering economics and business news.

The National Hurricane Center’s Boss Keeps an Eye on the Storms

The New York Times October 08, 2026

Hurricane Isaias

Advertisement

Supported by

The director, Michael Brennan, oversees 45 federal workers, including hurricane specialists and meteorologists.

By Johnny Diaz

Reporting from Miami

Tucked away inside a one-story concrete building dotted with satellite dishes in Miami is the headquarters of the National Hurricane Center.

During hurricane season, attention turns to the center and its director, Michael Brennan, as fresh forecasts are posted every six hours when a tropical storm or hurricane forms.

The center had been in Coral Gables, Fla., near Miami, but after Hurricane Andrew dealt Miami-Dade County a catastrophic blow in 1992, the office was heavily damaged and a stronger facility was needed.

In 1995, the center was built about 15 miles inland on the Florida International University campus.

Designed as a hurricane shelter, the facility withstood Hurricanes Katrina and Wilma in 2005 and staff members spent two nights there during Hurricane Irma in 2017.

“It’s a concrete bunker,” said Mr. Brennan, who became the director in 2023 and works in tandem with the Central Pacific Hurricane Center in Honolulu to cover the Pacific. “You can kind of get the whole staff in here, and everybody can be safe and we can continue to operate.”

Mr. Brennan, 49, a Virginia native, talked about hurricanes and what keeps him up at night.

The following is an edited and condensed version of that interview, which was conducted before Tropical Storm Isaias formed in the Gulf of Mexico on Wednesday.

What was your earliest interest in weather?

There was a big flood in western Virginia in November 1985. My grandmother lost her home in the flood. It was sort of the flood of record in the Roanoke Valley. I would have been 8 years old when that happened. So that was a pretty memorable moment from my early childhood of just seeing the impact that weather could have on a community and the amount of damage the flood can cause and the human impact of that.

The only exposure you had to meteorology was seeing local broadcast meteorologists. So that was something I was always interested in.

How big is your team?

In terms of hurricane center federal staff, there’s about 45, so the biggest part of that is our operations division and that includes the hurricane specialist unit. Right now, we have about 13 hurricane specialists on staff.

We’ve actually just hired some new staff in Hawaii. So we’ve been kind of combining forces here in Miami and Honolulu to cover that entire area all the way from the international date line into the Eastern Pacific and all the way to the Atlantic.

Do you have enough resources given federal funding cuts?

We have enough staff to cover, to meet all of our operational needs to do what we need to do. And as I did mention, we’ve actually been hiring some new staff here in the last six to nine months as we spin up this operation in Hawaii.

What are some differences between forecasting for the Atlantic and the Pacific?

The Atlantic basin, you can kind of get development all over the place. You can have long-track hurricanes that are storms that form right off the coast of Africa, like we would see at the peak of the hurricane season.

You can have storms form in the Gulf and the Caribbean off the East Coast. And this time of year, you can even have storms form up into the subtropics in the mid-latitudes because the water is very warm across much of the Atlantic basin.

On the Pacific side, most of the formation occurs at very low latitude. In the East Pacific, almost all the systems come from tropical waves that have moved all the way across the Atlantic and across Central America into the Pacific.

But the cold water in the Pacific comes a lot farther south than in the Atlantic, so the hurricane activity in the eastern Pacific, in particular, has a hard time getting much farther north than the Baja California peninsula of Mexico.

The other big thing that’s different is, in the Atlantic, we have a lot more data. We have aircraft reconnaissance we routinely fly into storms in the western half of the Atlantic. There’s a lot more buoy observations and ship observations and land-based stations and places like in the Caribbean or you know, the Lesser Antilles. You have radar.

You have a lot more data to work with in parts of the Atlantic, whereas, particularly in the eastern Pacific, is an area that’s pretty void of a lot of in-situ data.

There’s no land, there’s no islands there. There’s not a lot of radar. There’s very little ship traffic. There’s not a lot of buoys. We can occasionally fly hurricane hunter aircraft into hurricanes threatening the west coast of Mexico, and then also for storms threatening the Hawaiian Islands.

But largely, what we do in the Pacific is still based on your satellite imagery, satellite wind data, a lot of it remotely.

What is your worst-case scenario?

The worst-case scenario that you can think of is a storm that develops and strengthens very quickly near a populated area. I think we saw that in Otis, a couple of years ago in the eastern Pacific, the storm that hit Acapulco.

We went from a tropical depression to a Category 5 hurricane within a very short period of time and, you know, made a catastrophic landfall as a Category 5 storm, in a major metropolitan area.

What’s your outlook for the season?

The Atlantic side, I think it’s behaved a lot like you would expect a season to behave in a strong El Niño event. We’ve had a few short-lived, mostly weak storms in the Atlantic this year. We’ve got a lot of hurricane season left.

So I think my mind sits at the fact that, OK, it’s been a quiet season. We don’t want people to totally let their guard down about the rest of the season because we’ve had, you know, Hurricane Andrew is always the poster child event.

Johnny Diaz is a reporter for The Times covering breaking news from Miami.

Escalating Assaults on Ukrainian Cities Are Taking an Enormous Toll

The New York Times October 08, 2026

Russia-Ukraine War

Advertisement

Supported by

At least 30 people were killed in a Russian strike on a commuter bus in the country’s east, officials said, a day after an attack on an apartment building far behind the combat zone killed 22.

By Marc Santora

It was a devastating scene in a devastated city.

Under shredded netting meant to shield civilians from Russian drones, near residential buildings shattered by explosions, the charred metal skeleton of a commuter bus was all that was left on Thursday after another Russian strike in Kramatorsk in eastern Ukraine.

At least 30 people were killed, local officials said, the latest civilian casualties in Moscow’s unrelenting campaign to make Ukraine’s towns and cities unlivable.

As rescue workers in Kramatorsk were tending to the injured and gathering body parts from the street, President Volodymyr Zelensky was making his way to another Ukrainian city, Pryluky, where he implored the world to do more to counter Russian aggression.

He stood near the rubble of an apartment building destroyed by a Russian missile on Wednesday, killing 22 people, including five children. Entire families died in that strike.

Speaking in Pryluky, which was hit despite being about 200 miles from any combat zone, Mr. Zelensky said that Russia was seeking ways to expand its advantage in the skies and unleash more terror.

He warned that China was developing technology meant to compete with the Starlink satellite network and planned to share it with Russia. He called on the United States to allow Ukraine to use Starlink to target Russian missile and drone launch sites inside Russia.

The price of inaction, Mr. Zelensky said, was scenes like those in Pryluky, where he met with rescue workers and grieving families.

The Russian military has attacked civilian homes throughout the war. But the death toll is rising as Moscow fields an ever-growing supply of powerful precision weapons, stretching Ukraine’s air defenses with daily onslaughts.

The Kremlin has expanded its arsenal of newly developed jet-powered drones and increased the range of powerful guided bombs dropped from warplanes. Russia is also employing new communication tools that allow pilots to remotely guide munitions for precision strikes from hundreds of miles away.

Russia launched about 3,500 jet-powered drones against targets across Ukraine in September, compared with 350 in June, according to the Ukrainian Air Force. Ukraine is working furiously to develop interceptors that work against the jet-powered drones, which travel hundreds of miles per hour.

On Thursday morning, one of those jet drones smashed into a store in downtown Kyiv, the Ukrainian capital, killing three people and injuring 14 others, city officials said.

The store was hit a day after a large-scale bombardment on Wednesday killed at least 30 people across the country, including six in the capital.

Mr. Zelensky noted that the bombardment, which included the cruise missile strike on the apartment complex in Pryluky, coincided with President Vladimir V. Putin’s 74th birthday.

“This is the kind of ‘gift’ Putin gave himself for his birthday,” Mr. Zelensky said on Wednesday. “The killing of children, the killing of people.”

While drones and missiles pose the biggest threat across Ukraine, frontline cities like Kramatorsk, where the bus was struck, are being slowly destroyed by artillery and guided bombs that can pack hundreds of pounds of explosives.

In August, Russia dropped a record 8,700 guided bombs on military and civilian targets, according to the Ukrainian military. The only reliable defense against these bombs, which can hit targets more than 100 miles from where they are released, is to take out the warplanes that deliver them or destroy the warehouses where they are stored.

The epicenter of the fighting remains the eastern Donetsk region, where the majority of glide bomb strikes are recorded. Ukraine still controls around 20 percent of the territory, including Kramatorsk, Sloviansk and other cities that make up a belt of heavily fortified land.

Around 93,000 civilians remain in areas under Ukrainian control in Donetsk, including more than 4,200 children, according to local officials.

“The Russians are deliberately targeting civilians,” Vadym Filashkin, the head of the Donetsk regional military administration, said in a statement after the attack on the bus. “For them, a bus carrying passengers is an attractive target precisely because a single strike can kill as many people as possible.”

Nataliia Novosolova and Liubov Sholudko contributed reporting.

Marc Santora has been reporting from Ukraine since the beginning of the war with Russia. He was previously based in London as an international news editor focused on breaking news events and earlier the bureau chief for East and Central Europe, based in Warsaw. He has also reported extensively from Iraq and Africa.

In Trump’s Russian Oil Deal, Middle East Funds Are the Biggest Owners

The New York Times October 08, 2026

Russia-Ukraine War

Advertisement

Supported by

A majority of ownership in a proposed multibillion-dollar deal would go to a group of Middle Eastern investors, including some with business ties to U. S. negotiators.

By Anton Troianovski and Eric Lipton

Reporting from Washington

The Trump administration argues that its proposed multibillion-dollar Russian oil deal would advance American foreign policy interests and lower energy prices.

But most of the ownership in the deal would go to a group of Middle Eastern investors, including some with business ties to key U. S. officials involved in the negotiations, according to people familiar with the talks.

The deal, for a worldwide portfolio of oil fields, refineries and gas stations now owned by the sanctioned Russian energy giant Lukoil, has become intertwined with the U. S. talks with Russia over ending the war in Ukraine, The New York Times reported last week.

The United States government, through the U. S. International Development Finance Corporation, would get a stake of about 15 percent in the deal, without investing any cash up front, the people said.

The leader of the investor group, Todd Boehly, an American billionaire who has donated $2 million to pro-Trump causes in the last two years, would get a smaller minority stake.

But more than half of the equity will be cumulatively held by investors in the Middle East, according to three participants in the negotiations. The investors include entities tied to the royal family in Abu Dhabi and to two billionaire Syrian-born Qatari brothers, who are business partners with Jared Kushner, the president’s son-in-law, and Ivanka Trump, the president’s daughter.

The deal is structured in such a way that the United States — through Mr. Boehly and the government — would control a majority of the board of the resulting entity, some of the people close to the deal said. A senior administration official said the deal included a “substantial upfront payment and profits interest for the United States,” would enhance American “energy dominance” and outlast the current administration.

The Boehly group would acquire Lukoil stock with a face value of about $10 billion from non-Russian owners, although these purchases would be made at a significant discount, according to participants in the negotiations.

Once the purchase agreement is complete and approved by the Treasury Department, the assets would no longer be affected by U. S. sanctions on Lukoil, instantly driving up their value.

This deal is still in flux and could fall apart, but one of the previous bidders — the private equity fund Carlyle, based in Washington — is no longer actively pursuing the deal, after the U. S. government failed for months to sign off on Carlyle’s bid, according to parties involved in the deal talks.

The foreign-majority ownership raises new questions about who stands to most benefit from this complex transaction, which has involved negotiations with officials from the White House and the Kremlin, as well as a still-opaque list of investors from across the world.

President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia brought up the deal when he met at the Kremlin last month with Mr. Kushner and Steve Witkoff, a real estate developer, who both serve as Mr. Trump’s special envoys on the war in Ukraine. In Moscow, Mr. Putin is widely seen as having final say on the deal, even though Lukoil is a private company; in Washington, the Trump administration will need to approve it because of last year’s U. S. sanctions on Lukoil.

Whether or not the deal goes through, the behind-the-scenes negotiations over Lukoil show how Mr. Witkoff and Mr. Kushner have mixed their high-stakes diplomacy with talks that could provide a windfall to their business allies.

There is no indication that Mr. Kushner and Mr. Witkoff themselves stand to profit. The senior administration official said that the only interest guiding Mr. Kushner and Mr. Witkoff was “what is in the best interest of the American people.”

The deal’s proponents argue it would also be a windfall to U. S. taxpayers and a boon for U. S. interests because of the strategic assets in the deal, including key refineries in Eastern Europe. And the Trump administration has argued that showing Mr. Putin that the United States is prepared to do more business with Russia could help persuade him to compromise and end his war in Ukraine.

But for Mr. Putin, analysts say, the Lukoil sale has presented a chance to follow through on a strategy he has pursued ever since Mr. Trump returned to office: to use the promise of U. S.-Russia business deals to dissuade the White House from putting more pressure on Moscow over Ukraine.

Even better, from the Kremlin’s perspective, is that Mr. Kushner and Mr. Witkoff have business ties to two of the Middle Eastern investors involved in the deal, analysts say.

“The national security interests of the U. S. and U. S. allies, and private interests, are just so conflated,” Alexander Gabuev, director of the Carnegie Russia Eurasia Center, said. “That’s exactly the muddy waters that Putin and his K. G. B. negotiating school are thriving in.”

As Mr. Putin escalates his bombardment of Ukraine, Mr. Gabuev went on, “Lukoil just helps him to buy time.”

In the United Arab Emirates, one of the major investors is led by Sheikh Tahnoon bin Zayed Al Nahyan. He is a powerful member of the Abu Dhabi royal family whose business ventures have also invested in Mr. Kushner’s private equity fund and in World Liberty Financial, the cryptocurrency company co-founded in 2024 by Mr. Witkoff, as well as his and Mr. Trump’s sons. The White House has said that Mr. Witkoff has divested his position in the company.

In Qatar, the deal’s investors are the billionaire Syrian-born brothers Ramez and Moutaz Al-Khayyat, who are partners of Mr. Kushner and his wife, Ivanka Trump, in a proposed multibillion-dollar luxury Mediterranean coast resort in Albania.

The Khayyats and their Doha-based conglomerate have moved rapidly over the last year to expand business deals in the energy sector, including the oil industry, with investments now in Syria, Iraq, Libya and most recently in Venezuela.

The family has close ties to the royal family of Qatar dating back more than a decade, including with Sheikh Suhaim Bin AbdulAziz Al Thani, who serves on the boards of two of the Khayyats’ ventures.

Carlyle in January separately secured a “nonexclusive” purchase agreement, with a plan to put the payment at least temporarily into a locked up U. S. bank account, to avoid bringing profits to Russian investors who own Lukoil. But it then did not get the sign off it needed to complete the deal.

Some of the people close to the deal said the Carlyle deal was a nonstarter for the Russians, since they did not expect that the United States would ever release the money kept in a U. S. account.

These talks among possible buyers including Carlyle and Mr. Boehly started late last year after the Trump administration imposed sanctions on Lukoil, in an effort to force the end of the war in Ukraine. Lukoil’s international assets are spread across Europe, Africa, Mexico and the Middle East, and also include about 200 gas stations along the Mid-Atlantic coast of the United States.

The deal would need approval from the Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control, which has set as a precondition for lifting the sanctions that any transfer of the assets “not provide a windfall to Lukoil,” since the United States does not want to deliver profits back to Russia.

The move by the United States government to impose sanctions on a foreign company and then play a direct role in moving to buy these sanctioned assets is extremely unusual, according to two former federal officials involved in sanctions efforts.

“I cannot recall any remotely similar arrangement in the 20 years I’ve focused on sanctions,” said Jeremy Paner, a former Treasury Department sanctions lawyer who now handles corporate sanctions compliance efforts.

In a statement, an official with the U. S. International Development Finance Corporation said the proposed deal was good for the United States, as it “would advance the Trump administration’s commitment to strengthen U. S. economic security, advance U. S. foreign policy and lower energy prices for everyday Americans.”

The Trump administration, at least initially, would not put money into the deal, people familiar with the deal said, but the United States will still be in line to secure profits.

Once the sale of the Lukoil international assets is complete, the buyers plan to spend hundreds of millions of dollars to expand and retrofit different parts of these operations.

The negotiations are delicate, the people said, because Mr. Putin could still reject it if he sees it as unduly benefiting the United States. That is why, they said, the participation of Middle Eastern investors is important, since the Kremlin sees Qatar and the Emirates as friendly countries.

“Look at what’s happening to Lukoil,” Mr. Putin said at a conference last week, accusing the West of “the theft of our companies.”

The Treasury Department has set an Oct. 22 deadline for the negotiations over the sale. That deadline might be extended again, but on Wednesday two U. S. senators sent a letter to Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent insisting that they ensure no financial benefits go to Russian players if the Lukoil sale is approved.

“Every day that passes without maximum economic pressure allows Moscow to sustain this military escalation,” read the letter from Senator Roger Wicker, Republican of Mississippi, the chairman of the Senate Armed Services Committee, and Senator Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire, the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee.

Dmitri S. Peskov, Mr. Putin’s spokesman, declined to comment on the Lukoil sale process when asked about it in his daily conference call with reporters on Monday.

“I will only say that, indeed, the topic of interacting and cooperating in the energy sector is indeed being raised in conversations with American counterparts,” Mr. Peskov said.

Ana Swanson, Tyler Pager, Ivan Nechepurenko and Andrew E. Kramer contributed reporting.

Anton Troianovski writes about American foreign policy and national security for The Times from Washington. He was previously a foreign correspondent based in Moscow and Berlin.

Eric Lipton is a Times investigative reporter, who digs into a broad range of topics from Pentagon spending to toxic chemicals.

‘He’s Not Making Sense’: How Trump Has Alienated Voters for the G. O. P.

The New York Times October 08, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Signs are emerging that dispirited Republican voters may stay home in November, bringing a Democratic surge without many conversions.

By Sabrina Tavernise

Photographs by Jamie Kelter Davis

Reporting from Gobles, Stevensville, Paw Paw and Hudsonville, Mich.

If Democrats make big gains in the midterm elections in four weeks, it may not only be because their most loyal voters come out in force, or because their candidates have converted Republican voters to their cause.

Instead, the Democrats’ dream blue wave could come from Republicans who sour on President Trump and stay home. It already has a name: the red undertow.

Across the country, signs are emerging of an enthusiasm gap between Democrats and Republicans, even among those who consider themselves likely to vote. A stretch of rural southwest Michigan — long a Republican stronghold — illustrates the point, with more signs for blueberries and eggs than for political candidates. Volunteers are not showing up to door-knock. And many voters say they are tuning this election out.

“People are just more focused on everyday life,” said Lindsay Kronemeyer, 35, a conservative Christian mother of two who works in the construction industry. “I don’t hear the chatter on the Republican side of ‘Trump this, Trump that.’ He’s just not there in my head anymore.”

Jim Pasek, a retired pharmaceutical plant maintenance worker who lives in the tiny town of Gobles, Mich., was baffled by a president he has voted for twice.

“He’s not making sense,” Mr. Pasek, 80, said. “It confuses me, and then I just get disgusted and tune out.”

The idea of the red undertow was introduced last month by the political analyst Charlie Cook, who argued that the Democratic brand was still underwater, but that this election was not about a rising Democratic tide. It was about a drowning Trump brand.

In its wake, Mr. Cook wrote, an undertow will “pull many Republicans under.”

In nearly three dozen interviews in Western Michigan, a sense of fatigue was constant, and that feeling goes beyond that region.

“President Trump has been saying, ‘Vote as if I was on the ballot,’ and that’s exactly what I’m going to do — not vote,” said Brandon Tremaine, 24, a graduate student in Texas who voted for Mr. Trump in 2020. “You do not campaign on being the ticket of peace and start a war of choice that is directly hurting Americans here at home and gotten Americans killed overseas.”

Polls can be unreliable, and moods may be fleeting. Trump loyalists are also known for not taking the calls of polling outfits, and that may be overstating Democratic strengths. Disaffected Trump voters may yet rally to vote as the possibility of a Democratic victory nears, and many Americans still love Mr. Trump.

“I’ll go the length with Trump,” said Jeff Gilbert, 67, a friend of Mr. Pasek in Gobles.

The numbers aren’t drastically far apart. A New York Times/Siena University national poll from last month found that Democrats were more likely to say they were absolutely certain to vote than Republicans, 61 percent to 56 percent. While Democrats led Republicans nationally by seven percentage points among registered voters, that advantage rose to nine points among likely voters.

But in close races, a small gap could prove meaningful.

“People are tired,” Al Pscholka, a Republican and a former member of the Michigan House of Representatives, said of Mr. Trump. “The whole divider-in-chief thing, it’s gotten to the point where it’s just exhausting.”

The concern is showing in unlikely places. Representative Bill Huizenga, a Western Michigan Republican whose four House victories were all by comfortable margins, is in “the fight of his life” against a well-funded centrist Democrat from Kalamazoo named Sean McCann, said Rob Pocock, a retired Republican political consultant who has worked on campaigns in the region.

Nancy DeBoer, the local Republican state representative, also faces a serious fight against Joseph McClusky, a graduate of Hope College, a conservative Christian liberal arts college in Holland, Mich., who is openly gay.

“I would be shocked if Joseph wins, but I can’t believe he’s done as well as he has,” said Mr. Pocock, who teaches at Hope and had Mr. McClusky as a student. He said in Ottawa County, he was seeing Democratic yard signs in numbers he’d never seen before.

Western Michigan — home of Gerald Ford — may be seeing the ebb tide of the president’s MAGA movement, which had surged in this region, once known for a sober, Christian-inflected conservatism. In Ottawa County, ardent Trump supporters secured 8 of the 11 seats on the county commission after Covid. Pro-Trump forces won control of the state party, too.

Today, the MAGA wing is down to three seats in Ottawa County. They have also lost posts in Berrien and Kent counties.

“I think there’s a shift in the party back toward, we need a little bit of the establishment folks,” Ms. Kronemeyer said. “They exist for a reason.”

If anybody should be enthusiastic about the election, it is Ms. Kronemeyer. She ran for a statehouse seat in 2022. She door-knocked for Mr. Trump in 2016 and 2020. But she said that when a friend asked her recently about the races in her area, she had to admit she hadn’t been following them closely. She lives in deep-red Allegan County, where “traditionally in election years, yard signs would be peppered everywhere,” she said.

But the only signs she’d seen this year were for a judge, she said.

Ten years have passed since Mr. Trump took the country by storm, bringing a message of economic populism that appealed to millions of working-class Americans.

“He was a ball of energy,” Mr. Pasek said, sitting at breakfast in Gobles last week with his friend, Mr. Gilbert. “You could feel it. You could see it.”

Now, Mr. Pasek said, Mr. Trump seems to have lost his way. He started a war when he said he wouldn’t, sending the price of gas through the roof. And he seems to talk more about ballrooms and arches than he does about how he will bring prices back down.

“He’s losing touch with the American people,” Mr. Pasek said.

Mr. Gilbert said that he had stopped following the news closely, choosing to spend more time outside with his dog, Mabel. But he voted for Mr. Trump in 2024, and he said he stands by that choice. He said he believed Mr. Trump had a plan for Iran.

Mr. Pasek countered, “He says he has a plan, but then he doesn’t tell us what it is.”

Mr. Pasek cited gas prices: “He says it’s chump change. No, it’s not! It’s killing the people.”

He has noticed someone living in a car in a parking lot when he drives into town, he said. He worried about his granddaughter, 28, a college graduate from Michigan State University, who is working three jobs — one full-time and two part-time — but can’t find a house she can afford.

Those misgivings are being felt at the local party level. Doug Koopman, a member of the Kent County Republican Party’s executive committee, said that it had been a struggle to get the foot soldiers of the midterm elections — volunteer door-knockers and canvassers — to pick up brochures to distribute door to door, leaving bags of them sitting around the party headquarters.

“There’s very low energy on the Republican side,” he said.

In 2024, people lined up for nearly a mile in the rain in Grand Rapids to see Mr. Trump speak the night before the election. His campaign was dominant on social media, reaching younger people who’d never voted before, such as Sebastian Covey, who remembered Mr. Trump “popping” on his feeds. Mr. Covey had not voted before 2024; he did that year, for the president.

Now 24, he said his focus was elsewhere. He lives more than an hour away from his landscaping job in Hudsonville, a bustling suburb just west of Grand Rapids, because rents are cheaper, but the rising gas price has made his commute painful. He swapped his truck for a car, but a colleague he had been car-pooling with just found another job. He and his girlfriend have been looking for a rental closer to work, but so far they have not found anything they can afford.

He said he hadn’t thought about whether he would vote.

“I should care more, but it’s hard to keep up,” he said during a lunch break in a Wendy’s restaurant.

Even Republicans who are in politics say they are tired — worn out by the battles between pro-MAGA politicians and traditional Republicans. Bob Harrison, 76, a Republican county commissioner in Berrien County, where MAGA forces won control of the county G. O. P., said those forces took away the right to vote on party decisions from local elected officials like him.

Those officials “pretty much all walked away from the Berrien County Republican Party” to raise funds for their own political candidates, said Dr. Harrison, a retired community college president.

Dr. Harrison, who voted for Mr. Trump in 2024, said the hard-core Trump supporters remained unchanged, but “they’ve lost the support of the moderates like myself, people who think and choose and maybe split their votes.”

Warren Stewart, 69, who lives in Stevensville, Mich., and works restoring old homes, said he liked to think that Mr. Trump was working to restore the country, but he is starting to have doubts.

Clients often get nervous when the project is only halfway through, he said, but he assures them that he always has a plan for bringing the home back to its original beauty. He wonders if Mr. Trump does, too.

“Does he really know what he’s doing?” Mr. Stewart said.

He would never vote for a Democrat; he feels bludgeoned by liberals online, he said. But he’s not sure he’ll vote for Republicans, either.

“I just spent $60 on $30 worth of groceries and am about to go fill up for $5 a gallon,” he said, carrying two bags of groceries to his car. “It feels like they’re stress-testing us.”

I have been talking to Republican voters since 2016, and really for the first time, am hearing a big departure from Trump. It's remarkable to me, considering how electric he was in those early years -- speaking to working class people about trade and economics in a new way, and saying the Iraq war was a mistake -- something unusual for the Republican political class. But we are ten years in, with rising gas prices and a war that seems to be going badly, and, what I'm hearing now from so many Republican voters about Mr. Trump is what Mr. Pasek in my story said: "He's not making sense."

Ruth Igielnik contributed reporting and research.

Sabrina Tavernise is a writer-at-large for The Times, focused on political life in America and how Americans see the changes in Washington.
