Connections: Sports Edition

Connections: Soccer Edition

Connections Coach

They thought it might explain why their health had diverged. Instead, it stirred up feelings that weren’t so easily quantified.

Credit... Vivian Dehning; photographs by Annie Flanagan for The New York Times

Supported by

By Emily Baumgaertner Nunn

Photographs by Annie Flanagan

The notification lit up Michelle’s phone at 5:25 a. m. on the West Coast: a text from her older sister, Deb, who had an idea.

Deb had heard on a longevity podcast about a new technology that claimed to measure how quickly a person was aging. For $399, each sister could submit a blood sample and learn how her habits and experiences had affected the ways her genes behaved. The test, called TruAge, could supposedly tell them the functional ages of their brains, hearts, lungs and bodies overall.

“I think it would be super interesting to look at test results between siblings,” Deb, 56, had written. “You interested?”

“Yes, I would love to,” Michelle, 54, replied. “I fear the results, though.”

When it came to their genetics, the sisters seemed remarkably alike. (They asked to be identified using only their first names to discuss sensitive medical information.) They had the same deep-set, ice-blue eyes, the same prominent cheekbones, the same blond hair that swirled from a cowlick on the back-right corner of their heads. They both had astigmatism and night blindness; neither could roll her tongue or sing on pitch. And they had the same unusual variant of a gene called ABCC11, which meant their armpit sweat never had any odor.

Deb and Michelle, raised together in Detroit, knew they shared roughly half their DNA, but sometimes they had a hard time believing it. Deb, who now lived in Virginia, had always been hyper-disciplined, pragmatic and outgoing. A former Air Force nurse, she had traveled the world and raised three children, and seemed to exercise nonstop. Michelle was sensitive and bookish — so introverted that she didn’t even own a calendar. She had settled into the central valley of California after high school and never married. She lived a quiet, contented life with one companion: her Herder-Pit mix, Merlin.

There was another key difference: Deb had always been healthy, aside from mild joint pain and high cholesterol that medication kept under control. But Michelle had been obese in her teens and 20s and later struggled with autoimmune issues that no doctor had been able to fully explain. Every day was some constellation of extreme fatigue, nerve pain and tachycardia from low blood pressure. When Deb’s text arrived, Michelle was dealing with swollen lymph nodes, bumps all over her hands and a rash that stretched into her ear canals and nostrils.

Deb told her sister that maybe the test could help her better understand the causes and effects of her ailments. After years of feeling dismissed by doctors, maybe Michelle would feel validated if her biological age reflected her suffering.

Deep down, Michelle had a feeling that Debbie — she would always be Debbie to Michelle — just wanted to outperform Michelle. Still, Michelle wasn’t going to miss the first opportunity in years to do something with her sister. As adults, the two had grown distant, and then, after a bitter fight, stopped talking at all for almost two decades. They had reconnected only a few years ago, and even now, only through texts.

“Do you have a website so I can look at it?” Michelle asked.

The test’s marketing materials promise “the most complete picture of how your body is aging.” It analyzes almost one million chemical tags on DNA that make up a person’s epigenetics, the layer of biological instructions that controls how someone’s genes are expressed. By comparing a person’s unique pattern against large databases of other people’s results and health outcomes, its models try to assign an “age” that reflects the person’s predicted level of health.

Many aging test algorithms have proved effective for comparing large groups of people in scientific studies. But critics — and even some scientists who have developed the algorithms — say they are not meant to evaluate individuals, and that with so much statistical noise and potential for error, these tests are far too premature for commercial use. Most doctors believe a comprehensive blood panel is, for now, far more actionable.

And yet, biological aging tests like TruAge have in recent years exploded into an industry worth nearly $3 billion, a mark of a world that cannot resist the allures of personal wellness data. As with a personality test — or even a horoscope — proven accuracy is hardly a requirement. People crave new ways to define themselves.

When Deb’s test package arrived by mail, she arranged the contents neatly across her kitchen table. She pricked her middle finger with the lancet and squeezed dozens of drops of blood onto a paper card. Before she had even applied a bandage, she was using her other hand to text advice to Michelle, who had pricked her own finger but couldn’t seem to generate enough blood to fill the card.

“Wash hands in warm water,” Deb wrote her. “Do a few jumping jacks. Make fists. Really squeeze.”

“I bet this is a low blood pressure issue,” Michelle texted. “I’m trying.”

“Keep trying,” Deb replied.

Michelle pricked a second finger and eventually filled her card. Then both sisters packaged their samples and dropped them at their post offices, the envelopes addressed to the same lab in Kentucky.

Deb sent another text: “And now we wait.”

Deb was ahead of schedule, even for Deb. She stood at the kitchen counter of her glass-paned house, chopping vegetables for her homemade microbiome mix. She would combine them with plant-based protein powders and fiber mixes for her meal-replacement smoothie at lunch.

Deb and her husband, Steve, had become empty nesters in recent years, and Deb was often alone in a four-bedroom house so quiet she could hear the insects in the woods out back. Steve, a military contractor, typically worked 18-hour days, so Deb had taken on shifts as a nurse at a local aesthetic medicine practice, but she still had a lot of time to fill.

Years ago, to stay healthy, she had started walking 15,000 steps per day, strength-training at the gym and keeping a sugar-free diet. But as Deb became more interested in longevity, she added more habits, until she was using red light therapy daily, taking pills to increase antioxidant production and mitochondrial function, and experimenting with acupuncture and herbal patches.

She didn’t have a primary care doctor, and she didn’t think she needed one. All of her biohacks were already based on personalized insights. She had done a test to check for calcium buildup in her heart’s arteries, multiple scans to measure the strength of her bones, and a mail-order analysis called the 3X4 Blueprint that supposedly revealed which genes made her more susceptible to dementia, chronic inflammation and connective tissue decay.

Deb fed all her health information into ChatGPT, which then guided her to the best vagus nerve stimulators and chemical peels and fiber gummies — and also more assessments. It was ChatGPT that had convinced Deb to order the TruAge test in the first place.

“You’ve spent the past year optimizing almost every major longevity lever,” the chatbot told her after she asked it about the test’s value. TruAge, it said, “can help answer whether the protocol you’ve assembled is changing your biological trajectory.”

After she finished preparing her microbiome mix, Deb stopped by a refrigerator in her home office where she kept her vials of peptides. She injected one for tissue repair, another to reduce inflammation, another to help detox her skin and liver.

Then she reached for a small container of old photographs. Inside were snapshots of the life she and Michelle had once shared: a photo labeled “APRIL ’78” of the girls at ages 6 and 8, standing side by side in their grandparents’ house. Another marked “FEB. ’79,” of the two in matching white jackets, with identical bobs and wide, toothy grins that crinkled the corners of their eyes.

They were convincing portraits of a happy childhood, and Deb, a master compartmentalizer, preferred not to think about the chaos they elided: her mother’s erratic outbursts; their parents’ volatile fights; the constant extramarital affairs, which the girls often knew about. Sometimes the adults would disappear for long stretches of time, leaving the sisters to forge notes to their teachers and fend for themselves.

Increasingly, their paths had differed: Deb grew long and thin and gregarious, while Michelle withdrew behind more and more weight. Deb became a cheerleader, earned straight A’s and spent more time with her boyfriend’s family than her own. In the final photo of the sisters, taken on a Florida pier in “JULY ’84,” Deb’s arms were draped over a friend’s shoulders while Michelle stood off to the side, shorts bunched between her thighs, smiling alone.

“I’ve had a good life,” Deb said, tucking away the photos. “And Michelle really struggled.”

Deb couldn’t remember the details of their estrangement, but Michelle had long been a painful reminder that Deb, as the elder sister, needed to be the adult in the house, even when she was still a child. She was pretty sure the breaking point had taken place in their 30s, when Michelle got wrapped up in a horrible relationship with a guy Deb couldn’t stand. Deb had always been able to cut anyone out of her life without a second thought, so she did.

Then, after almost 20 years, Michelle reached out in a text message, apologizing for her role in the conflict. They began messaging again, but when Michelle called, Deb sent it to voice mail and texted her instead. Something about the thought of actually speaking to Michelle set off panic in Deb’s chest, even now.

Deb had always expected that her biological age would be younger than Michelle’s. But in the silence of her empty house, she began to consider other possibilities. What if Deb’s heavy partying in her 20s had super-aged her liver? What if her natural cholesterol levels, which were beyond her control, were causing vascular damage? What if her younger sister “had been able to trick her body in some way,” Deb wondered, and prove that all of Deb’s protocols were for nothing?

“I’m not going to crawl into bed and die,” she reassured herself. No, she would simply need to do more research.

In a sun-baked agricultural town across the country, less than two weeks before the TruAge results would arrive, Michelle arose before dawn with no agenda at all.

She curled up in an armchair in her sweatpants to watch the sunrise, then drew the blinds, blasting the air-conditioner and multiple industrial-grade fans to ward off her symptoms of heat intolerance.

Michelle watched a women’s basketball game and nuzzled her dog, Merlin, and decided not to worry about all the chores piling up during this latest bout of fatigue: the cobwebs in the ceiling corners, the listing side-yard fence, the suitcase she hadn’t found the energy to unpack. She had taken that trip a month ago.

Michelle wandered over to a shelf overflowing with tubs of salves and took her medicine. Then she donned her dark sunglasses, which helped her deal with extreme photophobia outdoors. “Come on, Bubba,” she said to Merlin, who leaped toward the door. Michelle wanted to go on one of their long drives — the road seemed to help her think.

Michelle had not dwelled much on the test since she’d taken it. A part of her thought the whole thing might be pseudoscience. Michelle had at least seven specialists in a regular rotation, including an allergist, a neurologist, a podiatrist and a dermatologist — almost two centuries’ worth of collective clinical experience that still left her “playing connect-the-dots,” she said. She was dubious that a few drops of blood were going to finally reveal the full picture.

But Michelle had a mental health counseling degree and read more than 200 books a year, many of them about psychology. She had been thinking lately about the ways toxic stress might leave lasting scars on human DNA. Now she couldn’t help but wonder if the kit’s algorithms might be programmed to measure something deeper.

As a child, Michelle had internalized the turmoil in their home — a factor she believed contributed to her rashes and sinus infections and overeating. She remembered the way their mother would throw items like screwdrivers and books at them; the tree Michelle climbed to hide herself on the roof of their detached garage; the maggots in the food when she and Deb were routinely left alone for weeks.

With every year, Michelle felt increasingly unstable, but somehow Debbie just became more capable, focused solely on the tasks at hand. When Michelle was 8 and came down with scarlet fever, Debbie put her on her bicycle’s handlebars and pedaled her to the corner store for medicine. When Michelle was 10 and broke her arm, Debbie taped two rulers together to hold it straight.

Michelle could tell that Debbie’s recollection of all those shared years was spotty — and that Debbie preferred it that way. It seemed as if Debbie mostly just remembered that she had managed the house, gone off to college and kept on thriving, in part because of her ability to simply choose what to forget.

But the trauma of their childhood had colored the first half of Michelle’s life. She ate addictively until she was 342 pounds and needed weight-loss surgery. She gravitated toward abusive relationships, staying in one for 14 years. And then, one night in 2007, Michelle was attacked by three men in a Walmart parking lot and sustained a traumatic brain injury, broken facial bones and a blown-out eardrum that left her partly deaf.

That was when Michelle decided to invest in “holistic healing,” she said. She earned her counseling degree, took a job with a disability advocacy group and started volunteering at a homeless shelter. She also eventually reached out to Debbie. Michelle finally found her stability — not in her physical being, but her emotional one.

Sometimes she suggested that Debbie consider therapy. “Seeing our younger selves is not reliving the childhood,” Michelle explained. But Debbie had no interest. “The trail is my therapy,” she would say. Now Michelle wondered: Could all that compartmentalization have done something to Debbie’s cells?

Driving along the California Delta, with Merlin’s paws perched on the center console beside her, Michelle felt at peace with most of her predictions for the test’s results. Her immune cell composition would not score well, and her brain had most likely undergone accelerated aging from the attack.

But Michelle couldn’t shake her worry that maybe it was Debbie who had not been able to outrun their childhood. There were 11 days until the reveal, and the test was starting to feel like a kind of ledger of their lives, both together and apart. She desperately hoped her own biological age would be older than Debbie’s — to protect her sister and maybe their newly mended relationship.

But if Michelle fared younger, then what? “Should I lie?” she asked herself as she pulled back into her driveway.

Perhaps this would be her way of finally taking care of the sister who had tried to take care of her. Maybe a “little white lie” — just for Debbie — would be worth it.

Deb had been refreshing her TruAge online portal every couple of days, but Michelle’s results landed first.

They ran to 73 pages of data, including stress markers, nutrient levels and toxin exposures. Plastered across the top were three key metrics: an overall score that encompassed a lifetime of chemical tags; another that measured the “pace” at which the body was supposedly aging; and, finally, a score that focused on the body’s organs, looking at markers associated with 11 different systems. Michelle leaned back in her recliner and began to scroll.

There was no sugarcoating the first score: Though Michelle was just 54, the test declared her overall “biological age” to be 62.

She threw back her head and laughed. “They’re saying I’m a senior citizen at this point,” she said. “If I was unstable mentally, this would not be a good thing!”

But the other two delivered what seemed like good news. Her aging “pace” score said that for every year that passed, she would age only 0.98 years — an indicator of a healthy lifestyle in recent months.

And her organ ages surprised her even more: All 11 organ systems together averaged to a relatively youthful 53.4. Her lungs were 53.6; her brain was 53.8, despite her traumatic brain injury. And even with all of Michelle’s autoimmune issues, her inflammation system was, inexplicably, 52.4. The report had even marked some of Michelle’s organ systems with mint green smiley-face icons to indicate slow aging.

“This is getting more interesting,” she said. But she had yet to hear from Deb.

“Your TruAge results are probably in your email,” she texted.

“Nope,” Deb replied. She had even checked her Spam folder.

Michelle had not anticipated this scenario, but she didn’t feel she could withhold her results. Soon, Deb was scouring through Michelle’s packets, taking in all the diagrams.

“I think considering all you’ve been through, the results are pretty darn great,” Deb texted. “It will be interesting what mine says.”

She waited another day — then another, and another. At the end of Week 4, she received an alert from the company that the laboratory needed to reprocess her sample because the results “did not meet one of the laboratory’s quality standards.”

“Now I’m anxious,” she texted Michelle.

On the last day of the sixth week, Deb had just returned from a morning walk when her inbox pinged: “Your full results are ready now.” She clicked into the portal and pressed “View My Results.”

Deb leaned closer to the screen and swallowed. The 56-year-old’s overall score was 58.3 — higher than she would like, but still younger than her sister’s, she reminded herself. And she was aging at a pace of 0.90 each year — good news.

But then she scrolled down to the organ results. She covered her mouth. “What the hell?”

Every result seemed astronomical — they averaged out to 63.5, more than a decade older than Michelle’s. Many were even scarier: Her lungs were 64.7. Her heart was 64.3. Her liver was 63.9. Her immune system was 66.7, compared with her immune-deficient sister’s 57.8.

Deb had longed to see those mint green smiley faces throughout her report. Instead, TruAge had marked Deb’s overall score and all 11 organ systems with magenta sad faces: “Aging Faster.”

Deb closed her laptop and got ready for work, but she spent the day in a private vortex of grief. Had she exercised too hard the day before she took the test, or not slept enough? Or maybe the results were accurate, and no amount of effort could override her unlucky DNA. Either way, she didn’t know what to do next.

That was the problem many health experts had with biological age test results: There was no consensus on how to act on them. A doctor would have told Deb not to worry much about her scores, to focus instead on age-old advice: Stay active, eat healthfully and enjoy her years. But the emotional undertow of the wellness era seemed to suggest that was no longer enough.

Michelle was concerned for her sister. She pinged Deb with encouraging text messages about all the reasons her results were probably skewed. Perhaps Deb should consider finding a primary care doctor, Michelle suggested, who could help put everything in perspective.

But Deb did not want to wait. She asked ChatGPT for advice instead, and it helped her choose a host of new biomarker tests she could order from a website that didn’t require a doctor’s visit and reported results using an A. I. assistant named Barry.

Deb texted Michelle a screenshot from the site, where she had spotted a host of new blood panels that the company planned to roll out. There was one focused on “genetic health insights”; another to detect brain changes related to Alzheimer’s disease; a third to measure PFAS, or “forever chemicals,” that might have accumulated in the body over time.

“Look what’s coming,” Deb wrote. “Fascinating.”

Michelle was happy for any excuse to correspond with Debbie. There still weren’t any phone calls — too emotionally triggering, Michelle guessed — and she assumed that when they ran out of wellness metrics to talk about, her sister’s texts would dry up. But for now, Michelle and Debbie wrote back and forth about lab orders they would place together and chatted about all the ways their genes must be expressing themselves: the same antibody deficiencies, the same pattern of graying hair. Together, they marveled at how much two sisters could share.

I thought I’d be reporting a straightforward story: a comparison between a sister who was healthy and one who was not. Instead, the quest to measure their bodies exposed a much more complex dynamic between two people who were deeply connected and disconnected at the same time. These sisters share so much history, yet they haven’t seen each other or even spoken by phone in decades. They text often, but when I visited Deb and Michelle on opposite ends of the country, each asked me what her sister was like. I learned that, before I showed up, they didn’t have anyone else to ask.

Emily Baumgaertner Nunn is a national health reporter for The Times, focusing on public health issues that primarily affect vulnerable communities.

In Maine Senate Race, Spiking Heating Oil Costs Put Susan Collins on Defensive

The New York Times October 08, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Half of homes in Maine rely on heating oil. Rising costs driven up by President Trump’s war with Iran have become central to the state’s Senate race.

By Tim Balk

Reporting from Bath, Maine

As the Senate race in Maine heats up, the state is getting cold.

And for many Maine voters, chilly weather could present a particular challenge this year: New England’s northernmost state is singularly reliant on heating oil, and the price of the product is surging because of President Trump’s war with Iran, which has clogged a vital oil shipping corridor.

The issue has started to move to the center of the race between Senator Susan Collins, a vulnerable fifth-term Republican, and her Democratic challenger, Troy Jackson, who has blamed Ms. Collins for the rising fuel oil costs. Their contest could be critical to determining which party controls the Senate.

For Ms. Collins, who initially supported the war but has opposed it for months, the rising fuel costs pose a significant headwind as she works to fend off Mr. Jackson, voters and strategists in both parties say.

“It’s a huge issue up here,” Lance Dutson, a Republican strategist in Maine, said Tuesday night as temperatures in parts of the state dipped into the 40s. Ms. Collins can point to her work to bring federal heating assistance funds to the state, he added, but that might go only so far in assuaging an “emotional electorate” facing deep financial strain because of the price increases.

In Maine, the cost to fill a standard heating-oil tank as of Wednesday was $1,650, up roughly 80 percent from a year earlier, according to the National Energy Assistance Directors Association, which represents state governments in securing federal money for heating bills.

Although sticker-shocked consumers across the country are feeling the economic impact of the Iran war — when they fill up their car’s gas tank, grab a six-pack of beer at a liquor store or buy some tomatoes at the supermarket — the spiking costs of heating oil are felt uniquely in the frosty northeast.

Just 3 percent of U. S. households use heating oil to warm their homes. But 50 percent of homes do in Maine, according to the state. (The price of natural gas, used to warm most American homes, has remained relatively flat.)

Speaking in the lodge-like hall of the Maine Maritime Museum in coastal Bath one night this week, Mr. Jackson told voters gathered for a town hall-style event that he did “not know how people are going to heat their homes” this winter.

He scoffed at the efforts of Ms. Collins to lobby the Trump administration for the emergency release of oil from strategic reserves, arguing that she was too close to Mr. Trump and had “turned her back” on working-class Mainers.

“No one’s going to just sit there and freeze to death — they’ll do things to try and heat their home,” Mr. Jackson said. Referring to the pride Ms. Collins has expressed in her efforts to secure federal funds for fire stations, Mr. Jackson added, “It’s a good thing that Susan Collins got all those fire stations, because we’re going to have a lot of fires.”

Some in the crowd laughed. One woman in the back muttered that the line was not funny.

Ms. Collins has tried to get ahead of the issue.

Last month, she joined Senator Angus King of Maine, an independent who caucuses with Democrats, in writing a letter to Mr. Trump urging the administration to secure the emergency release of heating oil. And she has pushed the federal government to increase its funding for heating assistance, joining a bipartisan letter from senators and backing a call by Gov. Janet Mills of Maine, a Democrat, for more federal support.

“I have repeatedly urged the Administration to use every tool available to increase supply and bring down energy costs,” Ms. Collins said in a statement last week.

But in recent years, federal heating assistance programs have not kept up with rising prices. Earlier this year, Mr. Trump tried to eliminate a federal program to help poor Americans cover their heating and cooling bills, arguing that the United States needed to prioritize military needs.

Debbe Kelley, 70, an engineer in Windham, Maine, said she thought fuel oil costs, layered on top of broader inflation, had become the most pressing issue in the Senate race.

“The issue that’s going to affect most Mainers is how they’re going to afford to get by this winter,” Ms. Kelley, wearing a long coat, a woven teal alpaca scarf and a dark hat, said as she braced herself against the fall wind outside the town hall in Windham, the sort of politically divided town that could be critical to determining the Senate race.

Ms. Kelley, a Democrat, said that she planned to vote for Mr. Jackson, and that she knew political independents who had voted Republican in the past but were being drawn toward Democrats by the economic conditions. She said it had cost her $1,982 to fill the tank of her house with fuel oil.

“A lot of people are struggling,” Ms. Kelley said. “It’s going to be a very tough year for Maine.”

At Nearly $300,000, Some Recent Duke Graduates Out-Earned All Their Peers

The New York Times October 08, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Your Money

Federal data show Duke math majors earning a bigger median income four years after graduation than any other majors from any school. It’s a small cohort.

By Ron Lieber

If you earn $297,029 four years out of college, something probably went right during your four years as an undergraduate.

But neither the math majors at Duke — the school and program that are responsible for that median figure — nor the faculty are doing a chest-beating victory dance.

Duke math majors sit atop a relatively new set of federal earnings figures that became available thanks to legislative and regulatory changes in recent years. To provide both transparency and accountability, the federal College Scorecard website, among other places, now shows what people with different majors earn after graduating from particular institutions.

The current data set has just 17 people from Duke’s math program, since the data measures only graduates from a two-year period starting in 2017 who received federal financial aid. “That definitely made my eyebrows go up,” said Katie McKeown, a Duke math major from the class of 2019 who went on to get a Ph. D. in math and now works for a nonprofit.

A 2025 law designed to provide accountability for schools that produce low earners has also shined a light on schools that lead to affluence. My colleague Arfa Momin and I created a tool where you can search it all — and build a custom list of schools and majors that interest you.

Select a school and major to compare.

Note: Earnings represent the median income reported on I. R. S. tax records for students who graduated from a particular program in 2017–18 or 2018–19. A program is listed if there were more than 15 graduates who had received federal aid. Programs in Puerto Rico, Guam and the Northern Mariana Islands are excluded. Major classifications come from the National Center for Education Statistics.

Right behind Duke, in the second and third slots, is Carnegie Mellon University. Its computer science graduates earned $268,121, and its electrical, electronics and communications engineering specialists clocked in at $250,168. Both groups have over 100 people in the data set.

Carnegie Mellon appears three times in the top 30, more than any other school. The university is poised to expand the number of students who can aim that high, thanks to a $3 billion donation last month that will help pay for a new campus in Miami.

The HEA Group, a higher-education research organization and consultancy, sorted and published the new data this year.

College is one of the biggest investments you’ll ever make. We built a tool to compare the earnings of all available majors in a federal data set at nearly every school.

In interviews, Duke math whizzes tried to express what the field meant to them and how interested students ought to evaluate the school.

Irina Cristali is a native of Romania who graduated in 2019 and now works as a machine learning research scientist at an artificial intelligence start-up. In trying to figure out who the high earners were, she tried to recall classmates who might be, say, vice presidents of engineering now and could have cashed in for $300,000 or more.

Her stronger memories of Duke were things that college shoppers should seize on beyond earnings. There were opportunities to get one’s name on published research as an undergraduate. Faculty members helped her get an internship offer and counseled her when she felt uneasy about her career direction.

“It was the American mind-set that you don’t have to have your life figured out at 18 or 22,” she said.

Indeed, Dr. McKeown barely had math figured out. She grew up in a single-wide trailer in rural Arkansas and spent two years at Duke in more remedial math classes. She got a 27 percent mark on her first quiz, but free tutoring and an instructor who believed in her helped her stick with the subject.

Duke math majors often study something else, too. “I don’t know a single math major who was only doing math,” said Faisal Alsaadi, who graduated in 2019 and has worked at start-ups in Saudi Arabia. He double-majored in math and economics.

“I like it when I’m able to train young people to think mathematically and then they take it into every part of the world,” said Ezra Miller, a Duke professor. He pointed to three current undergraduates — all double majors — who just won an international math competition by building models to maximize the performance of a soccer team.

Professor Miller does not shy away from the fact that if you want to get a job, it’s good to major in math. “But it does also attract people who are interested in beauty and truth,” he said.

According to math majors from the era in question, professors maintained a kind of studied neutrality about their students’ futures. And they remain wary of narrow methods of measurement.

“I am hesitant to celebrate earnings as the sole marker of educational success,” said Greg Herschlag, a Duke math professor, via email, while emphasizing his enthusiasm for the field and any teenager who pursues it. “I would rather universities and departments be judged not simply by how well their graduates do for themselves, but by how much value they create for others: how much they contribute to society, who benefits from that labor and whether that work is improving people’s lives.”

Duke math majors earn a lot of money. So do former students of computer science at highly rejective colleges. Data on earnings outcomes are helpful, but they are probably not the only thing you should be examining if you're shopping for college. So what is the data you wish existed about undergraduate programs (or the schools that offer those majors) but don't just yet? I'd like schools — with all of their PhD brainpower — to come up with a way to measure return on friendship. Just how good is an institution at creating the ties that bind?

Ron Lieber has been the Your Money columnist since 2008. His beat is beating the system.

Inside the Russian Warehouses Bombarded by Ukraine

The New York Times October 08, 2026

Russia-Ukraine War

Advertisement

Supported by

Middle-of-the-night evacuations and fears about death have become the norm for workers at Russian e-commerce companies targeted by Ukraine.

By Paul SonneAnastasia Kuts and Milana Mazaeva

Reporting from Berlin

It was two days before the start of school, and David Zelensky, 16, was earning some final summer cash at an e-commerce warehouse in the Russian city of Belgorod.

The oldest of nine children, David had landed the job a few weeks earlier at the online retailer Ozon, an upgrade from his former gig delivering food. He settled in for an evening shift on Aug. 30 that would put him closer to his dream of buying a motorcycle.

Then came the Ukrainian missiles.

First, the city air raid sirens wailed. Next, an explosion from what seemed to be the interception of a rocket rang out.

As workers ran across the warehouse floor toward a shelter, a missile slammed into the building. The lights went dark. Walls and metal shelves crashed down on a group of high school and college students as a fireball engulfed part of the facility.

David, who communicated with fellow workers by writing on a phone because he was deaf and unable to speak, was killed. A 21-year-old college student also died, and a 16-year-old boy was critically injured.

“It was hard to process the fact that, just moments ago, I had seen people alive and well, and then suddenly they were gone,” said another student who was injured at the warehouse.

The student was one of more than a dozen e-commerce workers interviewed by The New York Times from warehouses across Russia. They described how incoming drones, hourslong middle-of-the-night evacuations and fears of injury or death had become the new norm at work.

Some of the workers spoke on the condition of anonymity out of fear of being fired. In other cases, The Times is withholding their identity for security reasons.

The events in Belgorod illustrate the danger that civilian employees at Russia’s two e-commerce giants, Ozon and Wildberries, are facing as Ukraine has transformed the companies into a new front in the war.

For years, Moscow’s invasion has forced Ukrainians to make life-or-death decisions every day. Now, more Russians are having to do the same, as Kyiv’s missiles and drones shatter the illusion of normalcy carefully conjured by President Vladimir V. Putin.

“Personally, to be honest, I can’t believe it,” said a 19-year-old employee at a Wildberries warehouse outside Moscow.

The employee encountered his first drone strike at the facility last month. “It’s an absolute nightmare,” he said.

Ukraine has argued that the warehouses are legitimate targets because the retailers sell components that can be used to fix Russian military drones and protective equipment for Russian soldiers.

Russian officials and the head of Wildberries, Tatyana Kim, have dismissed the rationale, calling the strikes “terrorist attacks” against civilians. Wildberries and Ozon did not respond to requests for comment.

The toll of the Ukrainian attacks on Russian warehouses is vastly exceeded by the civilian suffering that Russia is causing in Ukraine.

Two months of frequent strikes on Wildberries and Ozon facilities killed 12 people and injured 135 through Sept. 11, according to the Conflict Intelligence Team, an open-source research group tracking wartime civilian casualties.

By comparison, Russia killed more Ukrainians in a single attack on a shopping mall in the Ukrainian city of Kryvyi Rih on Aug. 21. In that strike, 16 people died and another 136 were injured, according to the research group. Moscow has also attacked large numbers of Ukrainian warehouses.

Broadly, the Conflict Intelligence Team figures show that 66 percent of reported civilian deaths in the war this year have taken place in Ukraine, compared with 19 percent in Russian-occupied parts of Ukraine and 15 percent in Russia itself.

Still, for many employees at the Russian warehouses, the regular threat of attack has come as a shock.

At a Wildberries warehouse near Domodedovo Airport in the Moscow region, workers ran out of the facility one morning at 3 a. m. as drones descended on the area. They took cover under the bridge of a nearby highway, waiting four hours until after the sun came up to return, one worker recalled.

Outside Moscow, at a Wildberries warehouse in Novoselki, workers repeatedly flee into the woods during evacuations. They wonder whether they will freeze this coming winter when they have to drop everything and leave on cold days.

A worker at that warehouse recalled taking a cigarette break on a recent day and watching as a Ukrainian drone exploded in the parking lot 50 yards away, without any siren or alarm going off.

“When one actually lands right next to you — when you can even hear the metal ball bearings raining down from the sky — that’s when the real fear kicks in,” the worker said, noting that some employees now flee calmly, while newer hires run in panic.

A few of the warehouse workers who spoke to The Times decided to quit, citing safety concerns. But the vast majority have stayed on the job, noting that the work pays better and is more flexible than other options.

Wildberries workers say they can show up and leave whenever they want, including in the middle of the night, and work for as many hours as they choose. Workers also receive most of their pay immediately. Some say they can earn as much as $2,900 a month, well over double the average monthly pay in Russia, though earnings vary based on the volume of work.

As a result, many have adapted to the fraught new reality.

One worker at a Wildberries warehouse in Yekaterinburg recalled how even after a drone slammed into the parking lot and burned about 50 cars belonging to employees, workers kept showing up. They simply parked their cars next to the burned-out vehicles.

Another worker who was employed at a Wildberries warehouse in the Tula region described how, after his workplace was blown up, he started traveling two and a half hours a day to work at a different Wildberries warehouse, in the Moscow region. He said he faced hostility there from people worried that the influx of labor would reduce wages and work.

In recent weeks, the Russian authorities have pressed companies to erect defenses, with nets and scaffolding going up around installations to blunt the impact of drone attacks.

In Yekaterinburg, the Wildberries warehouse put water barrels on the roof to suppress fires, erected nets and fencing, and installed an exhaust system to clear smoke rapidly, the worker there said.

On the evening of the attack at the Ozon warehouse in Belgorod, where David worked, supervisors gathered the staff for a five-minute safety briefing.

David had a shift from 5 p. m. to 10 p. m. at the placement station, where workers load incoming packages into bins for sorting, according to another worker who saw him that day.

What exactly transpired in David’s final minutes is unclear.

While he most likely could not have heard the siren go off or the initial blast from the intercepted missile, he could have received other alerts. Hand-held inventory scanners used by workers would flash warnings during attacks, sometimes with a delay, one worker said. David may also have been warned by others or may have seen co-workers running.

Regardless, there was very little time.

In drone attacks, people often have time to take cover. But missiles arrive quickly, and one worker said that no one had expected the Ukrainians to use missiles on the comparatively small Ozon warehouse.

Ozon has since barred minors from working at its warehouses in some regions, according to Russian news outlets. The company also offered compensation to the Belgorod workers, with higher sums for those with more serious injuries, employees said.

Not long after the strike, David’s family gathered for a funeral.

His father, also born deaf and nonspeaking, and his mother, born with a hearing impairment, were there, his aunt, Anna Polushkina, told The Times. So were four of his eight siblings, all of whom are also either deaf or hearing-impaired, she said. While the family shared the same surname as President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine, there was no indication that they were related, Ms. Polushkina said.

At the funeral, the attendees hugged and cried. His friends placed a small motorcycle atop a display of roses and carnations at the grave. There were wafer cakes, a nod to his love of sweets.

David’s school, a special educational institution for children with disabilities, put out a statement calling his death an irreparable loss. The regional sports ministry said that he had shown great promise as a player on a basketball team for the hearing impaired.

“He dreamed about a motorcycle,” Ms. Polushkina said. “He really loved to ride.”

“As for an attack,” she said, “we never imagined anything like this.”

Alina Lobzina contributed reporting.

Paul Sonne is the Moscow bureau chief, leading coverage of Russia, the Caucasus and Central Asia. He is based in Berlin.

Milana Mazaeva is a reporter and researcher, helping to cover Russian society.

The Atlantic’s Near-Record Hurricane Drought Is About to End

Wired October 07, 2026

The 2026 Atlantic hurricane season has been mercifully dull, but that’s set to change this week. Tropical Storm Isaias is forecast to become the season’s first hurricane before making landfall somewhere between Mississippi and Florida by the weekend.

El Niño has turned the Atlantic basin into a graveyard by changing winds high in the atmosphere so that they rip apart storms. That’s helped depress tropical cyclone activity to near-record-low levels and resulted in zero hurricanes. That could change imminently, though.

Isaias is churning in the Gulf of Mexico with winds of 65 mph, according to the latest update from the US National Hurricane Center. That’s just a shade below hurricane strength. The storm is forecast to pass over a patch of abnormally warm water, providing fuel for it to blossom into a hurricane. It could peak as a Category 2 storm with winds of 110 mph as it lumbers to the northeast. The storm is expected to weaken due to those aforementioned gnarly winds shortly before it makes landfall somewhere along the Gulf Coast.

The NHC has issued hurricane watches for all the coastline in Mississippi and Alabama as well as parts of the Florida Panhandle. (Tropical storm watches extend into Louisiana as well.)

Folks in that region can expect rainfall totals of up to 7 inches, though some spots in the Panhandle could see as much as 10 inches and storm surge as high as 7 feet. Tornadoes aren’t out of the question either. In other words, it’s a storm to take seriously.

Isaias could make also (or at least tie) history as the latest first Atlantic hurricane to form on record. The current record was set in 1905, when the season’s first hurricane formed on October 8. There’s still one more update scheduled for Isaias on Wednesday, so it’s possible it could just miss out on tying that mark.

Record or not, Isaias is indicative of the hurricane season that wasn’t. This year’s Atlantic hurricane season was forecast to be below average. But it’s been even quieter than expected owing to an El Niño that’s been dubbed “super,” “Godzilla,” and “supersized.” The superlatives—which meteorologists will be quick to tell you are not official designations—are indicative of the strength of this year’s event. El Niño is measured by ocean temperatures in a part of the tropical Pacific, and this year’s iteration has seen record highs throughout the summer and first part of fall.

The intensity has had a heavy hand in rearranging the atmosphere around the world, including over the Atlantic. Saharan dust has also played a role in quieting things by making the air in one of the major areas where hurricanes develop too damn dry.

For a sense of how that has impacted the Atlantic hurricane season, we can look at some averages. From 1991 to 2020, the basin saw an average of 14 named storms, seven hurricanes, and three major hurricanes—that is, storms of Category 3 or greater—annually, according to NHC data. This year has seen eight tropical storms and one soon-to-be hurricane.

Another metric to measure the season is accumulated cyclone energy (ACE for short), which takes into account not just the number and intensity of storms but how long they stick around. The ACE to date for 2026 is 10.8 units. The average for this time of year? Nearly 102, according to data maintained by Colorado State University. Most of that energy typically accumulates from mid-August through late September.

None of this is to say there might not be another surprise storm in the coming weeks. But with El Niño continuing to intensify and the peak of the season well past, the odds of this season seeing a sudden spurt of activity are minimal at best.

Elon Musk’s America PAC Is Quietly Funding November’s Most Consequential Elections

Wired October 07, 2026

Elon Musk’s America PAC is focusing its war chest on the most consequential Senate races this midterm cycle—and doing so by financing attack ads on Democrats, as voters nationwide sour on the Trump administration’s agenda.

The trend of political parties and outside groups focusing on trashing their opponents is not a new phenomenon. But America PAC's approach has been unusual: for every dollar it has spent supporting GOP Senate candidates, it has spent almost three dollars attacking Democrats.

To monitor America PAC's spending ​on digital ads and mailers this cycle, our ace team at WIRED has created a live tracker that updates daily and highlights where Musk's political contributions are heading as we enter the waning years of Trump’s second term.

The political stakes are especially high for Republicans this midterms cycle because of the possibility of Democrats taking the majority in the US Senate, should the party flip four battleground races and retain three of the Senate seats it currently holds.

For Musk, the implications of a Democratic-controlled Senate would also be far-reaching, as he personally could become the target of congressional investigations, while his companies might be affected by bills related to tech and AI regulation.

For the critical Texas Senate race, America PAC has poured more than $9.4 million into ads opposing Democratic candidate James Talarico and roughly $1.8 million into ads backing Republican candidate and ​state ​attorney ​general Ken Paxton​.

The lopsided spending here is perhaps the least surprising of all of the close Senate contests. ​Paxton comes with so much personal baggage—from facing impeachment charges that were eventually dropped to having his wife (who has since endorsed him with an ad that doesn’t mention him by name) file for divorce on “biblical grounds”—that trying to boost him with ads highlighting his background is tough.

Republicans in Texas also cannot realistically do positive ads of President Donald Trump and Paxton together, since both men have terrible approval ratings.

The largest single expenditures by America PAC have been two $1.3 million digital media buys opposing Talarico. America PAC has not put any money into television ads, which is being handled by other groups, like MAGA Inc., the Trump-affiliated super PAC.

Meanwhile, the Senate Republican Conference–affiliated Texas PAC has so far booked the lion's share of television ads. Punchbowl News reported last month that Texas PAC has booked around $120 million and was looking to buy $100 million in ad slots before November 3.

In Ohio’s Senate race, America PAC has spent $3.3 million against Democrat Sherrod Brown compared to $1.6 million supporting Republican candidate Jon Husted.

Husted has been struggling to distance himself from supporting data centers at a time when voters in the state have become fed up with rising costs associated with the projects. Husted has been tagged as "the face of data centers" because of a planned Nvidia data center project in Ohio that will be leased by OpenAI, and for his past support for data centers when he served in the state government.

The effort by Brown to cast Husted as the champion of data centers has in fact been so effective that a memo by the Senate Republicans' campaign arm in August said it was tying an anchor around the neck of Husted's public polling.

At a rally this week in Ohio, despite the cratering public support for data centers, Trump could not help himself and declared to the crowd: “We want them.” Husted’s campaign quickly replied that it should be a “local decision.”

In Iowa, America PAC has spent $1.5 million hitting Democratic candidate Josh Turek, while only spending roughly $100,000 supporting the Republican candidate Ashley Hinson—the biggest disparity, according to the WIRED tracker.

To put that another way: To date, Musk's political operation has spent a staggering 14 times more attacking Turek than supporting Hinson.

This could be because Hinson has taken great pains to distance herself from Trump's agenda. She recently called on Trump to ban diesel exports and end the Iran war (after previously voting six times against the House resolution to end the conflict), after Turek called for both of those measures.

To illustrate the upside-down nature of this race, Hinson recently launched attack ads against Turek, accusing him without evidence of having “received tens of millions in support from men in the Epstein files,” a remarkable situation given that Trump has sought to tamp down any mention of the files because of the negative blowback on him personally.

Once again, pro-Republican ads are likely not helpful when the candidate is trying to run a race apart from Trump and is barely ahead in the polls in what should be a safe Republican seat. In the most recent New York Times/Siena poll, Hinson was just one single, solitary point ahead of Turek.

The Science Behind the Nobel-Winning Technology That Controls Neurons With Light

Wired October 07, 2026

The Karolinska Institute awarded the 2026 Nobel Prize in Medicine to researchers Karl Deisseroth of Stanford University, Peter Hegemann of Humboldt University in Berlin, and Georg Nagel of the University of Würzburg. Their discoveries led to the development of optogenetics, a technique where scientists can turn individual nerve cells on or off using beams of light.

According to Per Svenningsson, chair of the Nobel Committee for Medicine, “Optogenetics provides opportunities for mapping the brain in a way that we could once only dream of.” No other technique allows for such precise study of a living brain, helping researchers better understand the functions of our nervous systems as well as various neurological diseases and disorders.

But this prize is not just a celebration of neuroscience. It also serves as a triumphant example of what can happen when different disciplines of biology converge, as the findings that served as the basis for the development of optogenetics emerged from research in microbiology.

At the end of the last century, Peter Hegemann began a series of studies to understand how the single-celled alga Chlamydomonas is able to detect and react to light. Previous research documented that Chlamydomonas has an “eye spot,” a small orange dot on its surface that contains a light-sensing molecule called retinal.

Hegemann used tiny electrodes to measure the electrical signals generated by the alga and to expand our understanding of this structure’s rapid response. The scientist discovered that the organism was capable of producing an electrical impulse about 0.5 milliseconds after receiving light. This response time is 20 times faster than that of the human eye, whose light detection process takes at least 10 milliseconds.

Hegemann suggested that light detection in the alga must be the result of a much simpler process than that identified in the human eye. In the early 1990s, he proposed that the eye spots contained a protein that both detected the light and responded to it, likely opening as a channel to let ions through. At the time, this hypothesis sparked controversy. Many ion channels had been documented up to that point, but none could respond to light on their own.

To test his theory, the scientist attempted to isolate the light-sensitive proteins from the eye spot. However, when removed from their natural environment, these proteins became unstable. Later, a group of Japanese researchers sequenced the complete DNA of Chlamydomonas, which allowed Hegemann’s team to identify two genes that would create proteins with the expected characteristics of a possible light-sensing channel.

Georg Nagel took the next step of verifying the function of the genes. He introduced copies of each of the identified genes separately into different groups of frog eggs. The eggs began to produce the corresponding proteins, which eventually localized to the cell membranes. Nagel then turned on the lights.

Both proteins functioned as ion channels that opened when exposed to light. He named the genes channelrhodopsin-1 and channelrhodopsin-2. Further experiments showed the protein produced by this second gene—called ChR2 for short—opened especially quickly, the flow of ions occurring in just 0.2 milliseconds. It explained the extraordinary speed of the light reaction originally observed in Chlamydomonas.

When the researchers introduced the gene into mammalian cells—which do not normally respond to light—the cells generated an electrical signal when illuminated. This is what got the neuroscientists particularly excited.

Ion channels are important across many types of cells, but they do some especially heavy lifting in our nervous systems. The electrical impulses that neurons use to communicate with one another, as well as other tissues in our body, are mediated by the flow of ions in and out of the cell. If you can control the ion channels, you can control the neuron.

This is where Karl Deisseroth comes in. Deisseroth was searching for a method that would allow him to toggle the activity of specific nerve cells in a living brain. In his view, this tool could expand our understanding of brain functions and open new avenues for treating conditions such as depression and schizophrenia.

Following the discovery of ChR2, he asked Nagel for the DNA sequence so he could introduce it into rat nerve cells. The neurons, growing in dishes, produced ChR2 and, when illuminated with blue light, reacted immediately—sending an electrical impulse that propagated to other neurons. This result, obtained in 2005, was decisive in establishing ChR2 as a tool for neuroscience.

In the following years, Deisseroth, Hegemann, and Nagel collaborated to identify other proteins capable of activating or deactivating neurons using different wavelengths of light. With this toolkit, researchers can now design experiments where one group of neurons is turned on by one wavelength of light and another set of neurons is controlled by a different wavelength.

The term optogenetics was coined in 2006 and has since been implemented in a variety of studies. “Using optogenetics, researchers have been able to reveal neural circuits governing specific memories, feelings, and behaviors relevant for neurological and psychiatric disorders. In clinical medicine, researchers are using the method in attempts to restore sight in people with visual impairment,” the Nobel Assembly at the Karolinska Institute stated in a press release.

Meet the Vendors Selling ‘Cornell Seven’ Merch

Wired October 07, 2026

Last weekend, the clothing brand Cherrykitten published an Instagram post promoting T-shirts, crop tops, and sports bras with the slogan “I Am Jane Doe” emblazoned on the front. “ALL OF US ARE UNTIL NONE OF US ARE,” the company wrote in the caption, adding that it would donate 5 percent of the net sales proceeds to the National Organization for Women.

A reference to the “Cornell Seven” case, in which an anonymous woman accused seven Cornell University fraternity members of sexual assault, among other counts, #IAmJaneDoe started going viral last week. Many sexual assault survivors used the hashtag in solidarity with the alleged victim after trolls attempted to dox her on social media. (All seven of those accused have denied wrongdoing, and none have been charged with a crime.)

The message, while powerful, may have been ill-suited for appropriation by Cherrykitten, a brand perhaps best known for selling tank tops and crop tops with slogans like “Pls do not give me a cigarette no matter what I say” and “AI cannot generate tits like these.” The company received immediate backlash on social media for selling the shirts, with many accusing it of tastelessly capitalizing off of a grisly sexual assault case. “Using the cornell seven sexual assault as a merch idea and then donating ONLY 5% to a womens charity.. oh cherrykitten.. you’re fucked,” one tweet with 2.2 million views read.

The brand removed the post, issuing an apology for “turning a real and deeply serious situation into a product,” according to a screengrab of a now-deleted Instagram post. (Cherrykitten did not respond to WIRED’s requests for comment.) But Cherrykitten is far from the only brand attempting to market apparel around the Cornell Seven case, which has garnered outrage around the world.

On Amazon, there are more than 6,000 results for “I Am Jane Doe” T-shirts; on platforms like Etsy and Redbubble, there are hundreds of sellers promoting such merch, including T-shirts, sweatshirts, hats, bracelets, mugs, and bumper stickers. The listings, which include keywords like “feminist,” “true crime,” “protest,” and (weirdly, on Redbubble) “lizzieborden,” often feature AI-generated photos of women with shiny hair and broad grins modeling the merch.

One such seller, who requested her name be withheld to protect her privacy given the sensitive nature of the case, is the owner of a three-year-old shop on Etsy which sells T-shirts with progressive slogans. Her “I Am Jane Doe” sweatshirts in shades like ash, dark chocolate, and purple cost between $19.53 and $27.93; she’s sold 21 since October 1.

An assault survivor herself, the seller tells WIRED via email she came across the Cornell Seven story on social media, and was “deeply moved” by the #IAmJaneDoe movement. “I wanted this shirt to be a small but visible way of saying: we see you, we believe you, and we stand with you,” she says.

“[When] I came across the Jane Doe story on social media, I saw yet another woman who had been failed by people and systems, and I felt really strongly about that. That we need to stand up for her. That she deserves justice ... For me, ‘I Am Jane Doe’ was not about turning anyone's pain into a trend,” she says. “It was my way of saying that I see her, I believe her, and I stand with her.”

It’s not uncommon for Etsy vendors to sell items inspired by current events. It happened after the murder of George Floyd in 2020 and during the 2022 Johnny Depp/Amber Heard defamation case, where much of the merch was pro-Depp and featured quotes from Depp on the stand. As WIRED has previously reported, the rise of mass-produced print-on-demand goods, as well as Etsy’s relatively lax policies toward AI-generated listings, allow vendors to rapidly create, design, promote, and sell such items in accordance with the news cycle.

Yet there are often ethical questions associated with commodifying social movements for a quick buck, and it can be difficult for consumers to vet the motives of those selling such products.

“If [people are] raising money to support survivors, that’s OK,” Simintha Esson, chief development officer for RAINN, the country’s largest anti-sexual-assault organization, tells WIRED when asked about the recent onslaught of Jane Doe merch. “We know the need is there—calls to RAINN’s National Sexual Assault Hotline are up 73 percent in the last week. But if it’s just exploiting Jane Doe’s name and case for profit, people are better off giving to an organization that is trying to make things better.”

Even those who purport to be financially supporting survivors are worthy of skepticism. The website I Am Jane Doe Merch, for instance, includes such bestselling items as an “I Am Jane Doe” baby tee, an “Educate Your Sons” crop top stenciled with a butterfly, and a “Dead Men Don’t Rape” T-shirt featuring the serial killer Aileen Wuornos. (According to website data, more than 700 Aileen Wuornos T-shirts have sold.)

The website, which was created on October 2, according to the domain reverse-search tool WhoIs, includes a description stating that an unspecified percentage of the proceeds will go directly to Jane Doe herself, “to help her legal expenses and related costs.” “Any contribution, no matter the amount, can help lessen that burden and support Jane in accessing support, advocacy, and/or justice and accountability,” the description reads.

When reached for comment, however, Thomas P. Giuffra, the attorney for Jane Doe, tells WIRED that there are no authorized fundraising sites for Jane Doe. While she has requested that all donations go to RAINN, other efforts such as I Am Jane Doe Merch are “not affiliated with us, and we urge the public to use caution before contributing to one,” he says in a statement. (Though WhoIs data has kept the identity of the owner of I Am Jane Doe Merch anonymous, WIRED has reached out to an email address associated with the website for comment.)

Some influencers selling “I Am Jane Doe” merchandise are donating all or most of the proceeds to organizations benefiting sexual survivors. Justin Kralemann, a content creator and activist who goes by the handle the Woke Ginger, says he was inspired to sell shirts after women flooded to his comments section to share their own experiences with sexual assault and trauma.

“Their stories broke my heart,” he says. “I’m a cisgender man and can’t directly speak to women’s lived experiences, but I wanted to do something beyond sharing news updates to help those fighting sexual violence against women.”

With EQNQ Studio, a company that makes “progressive apparel that celebrates equality, community, and the courage to speak up,” according to its website, Kralemann is selling “I Am Jane Doe” T-shirts in teal (the color associated with Sexual Assault Awareness Month) and dark heather for $24.95 a pop. He says approximately 67 percent of the proceeds will support the national organization End Rape on Campus, and approximately 33 percent will go to EQNQ Studio, the small business producing, hand-making, and shipping the shirts. Per EQNQ, they have sold 255 shirts thus far.

A few days after we started corresponding, the Etsy vendor selling sweatshirts provided an update: she had decided to stop selling the “I Am Jane Doe” sweatshirt and to donate the remainder of the profits to RAINN. She didn’t think that she or those who purchased the sweatshirt had bad intentions—“we all know how difficult it is to change things as individuals, [and] at the very least, we can show our support with a shirt,” she says. But she said that she has come to understand the potential ethical issues raised by “turning a story like this into something that is sold, even when the intention behind it is solidarity.”

“Even though we don't know who Jane Doe is, and we don't need to know, this is still her story,” she says. “I have decided that stepping back from this particular design is the right thing for me to do.”

These Researchers Made AI Drive a Toyota Corolla to Get In-N-Out

Wired October 07, 2026

Aditya Ramabadran, Simon Mahns, and Tobias Gessler, three AI engineers at a startup called Axiom, recently fancied In-N-Out Burger for lunch.

They weren’t about to drive themselves, though. Sitting in a 2024 Toyota Corolla near the Bay Area restaurant’s drive-thru lane, they opened a laptop and asked OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra to take the wheel. They linked a chat interface to a server, which was connected to several windscreen-mounted cameras and the car’s power steering system. A safety driver kept one foot above the brake, just in case.

The AI model, which is normally tasked with generating text, code, and the odd image, slowly but surely navigated the vehicle up to the take-out window so they could collect their food.

“Maybe AGI is here after all,” one of the engineers remarked, referring to artificial general intelligence, the much-ballyhooed idea of machines that can match human intelligence.

Self-driving cars are nothing new, of course, but they’re normally operated by algorithms specifically trained and engineered for the task. In this case, the operation came from a model designed to output text, and it happened on the fly, with no prior coaching by the trio. The fast-food stunt, as well as a number of other experiments, suggest that language-based AI models are starting to gain a rudimentary but useful understanding of the physical world.

Though nothing overtly alarming happened during the trio’s lunchtime jaunt, they admit that putting a general-purpose model in charge of a fast-moving, two-ton hunk of steel is a high-stakes undertaking. As physical understanding improves, we could see AI models reach into the real world in impressive—and perhaps dangerous—new ways.

Today’s smartest models are incredibly good at answering complex questions and even performing some virtual tasks autonomously, but their skills tend to be limited to the world of computers and the internet. Take these models into the real world and they quickly become befuddled. Despite claims that AGI has arrived, AI companies evidently see physical reasoning as a yet-to-be-conquered frontier for AI.

Some researchers have left big companies to found startups focused on solving physical reasoning. Andrew Dai, the CEO of one such outfit, called Elorian AI, previously worked as a researcher at Google DeepMind. He says better visual reasoning will open up a lot of new applications for AI, like systems that understand whether diners are enjoying their meal in a restaurant or robots capable of functioning in a home. Dai says robotics is a crucial test case for physical reasoning skills. “It’s pretty essential for robotics,” he says. “You can’t really imagine home robotics without this.”

Elorian and Scale AI, a company that provides training data to big AI labs, recently developed a new benchmark, Humanity’s Sixth Sense, which measures models’ ability to understand physical scenes.

“Most visual AI research is about perception,” says Xingang Guo, a research scientist at Scale AI who was involved with developing the benchmark. “We wanted to ask what it would actually take for a model to understand a scene intuitively, the way a person does without thinking about it.”

For Ramabadran, Mahns, and Gessler, the goal with their In-N-Out project, done outside of their work at Axiom, was to measure how well models can operate in the messy real world.

They got the idea to test models’ driving skills while hanging out one weekend. They noticed that models like Astra were capable of building complex 3D simulations, and wondered if it might translate to an ability to navigate the real world.

“We all live in the Bay Area, and we’re exposed to Teslas and Waymos, so maybe that played a role,” Ramabadran tells me.

The engineers tried testing SpaceXAI’s Grok before experimenting with the latest models from OpenAI and Anthropic. At first, the models refused to take control of the vehicles—they spat back things like, “I can help interpret road images, but I can’t issue motion commands to a physical car.” But with a little careful prompting, they could be coaxed into going further. The three were stunned when models began driving.

The engineers say big AI companies seem to be focusing on improving the spatial reasoning capabilities of their latest models, but they doubt this means they’re actually training them to drive cars. The models’ vehicular talents likely materialized as part of training focused on 3D reasoning, they say. “This could be like an emergent capability of just scaling up the multimodality of the model,” Mahns tells me, referencing inputs like images, video, and 3D models that are now used to train models.

Still, a new vehicular benchmark from the trio, called DrivingBench, suggests that these models still have a long way to go before they could pass a driving test. The benchmark measures a model’s ability to drive around a simple course, set up in a parking lot. Only Astra is able to complete the course—and very slowly at that. Claude Fable 5.1 made it 45 percent of the way around, and Grok made it just 11 percent of the way.

Ramabadran says the latest models seem capable of adjusting to errors; they apparently adapted to the car's controls and improved their driving in real time. “The models really did seem to be adjusting or in-context learning based on their mistakes and learning how to better navigate the controls,” he says. GPT, take the wheel.

This is an edition of Will Knight’s AI Lab newsletter. Read previous newsletters here.

The New ChatGPT Is More Show Than Tell

Wired October 07, 2026

When you ask a chatbot a question, you’ll often get a wall of text back, maybe with an image or two pulled from the web. That may no longer be the case soon, as OpenAI overhauls how ChatGPT answers prompts.

On Wednesday, OpenAI unveiled an “Intelligent UI” update for ChatGPT that generates visual, custom elements—when helpful—for answering a user's questions. The company's new experience is powered by its recent GPT-6 model, which rolls out to paid users today and to free users tomorrow.

Courtesy of OpenAI

I got a quick test of the user interface before launch, and these visual elements felt like a welcome change. When I asked for a diagram of a slug, ChatGPT generated an anatomy-focused visual with buttons I could press for each different part, from the upper tentacles to the muscular foot. I also generated a San Francisco apartment affordability calculator with movable sliders to adjust income and other expenses, showing what percentage of my take-home pay different units would cost.

My favorite part of this quick hands-on with ChatGPT’s Intelligent UI was an airplane seat explorer. I’m not a fan of sitting in the exit rows, so I asked ChatGPT to generate a custom tool to compare the cabin layouts between four different Alaska and Delta planes. In its output, I could tap any seat on the map for more details, and ChatGPT highlighted the exit rows in green.

While useful in some results, every ChatGPT answer won’t suddenly include a chart or graphic. “We have a design team that spent a lot of time figuring out when adding a diagram, chart, or buttons adds value versus when it's starting to feel cluttered,” says Aarush Selvan, a product manager at OpenAI. If a user isn’t interested in visuals, they can tell ChatGPT to generate fewer of those outputs.

These visual results are similar to what Google announced earlier this year for Search when it expanded the bespoke results users may see. Google’s version is called “generative UI.” One example: If you want to better understand deep space, Search can output an adjustable graphic that breaks down how black holes work, using multiple sliders.

Chatbot experiences have increasingly become multimodal, meaning that text, images, and voice blend into one user experience. OpenAI's launch of an updated ChatGPT that's easier on the eyes and more interactive for over a billion users signals that the multimodal era is here. However, a larger shift toward generative user interfaces may spark an identity crisis for designers, as AI dictates more of what software looks like for individual users.

With AI tools now able to quickly generate custom software, the future of chatbots is further personalized and attuned to what I want to see, and what I want to see is slug diagrams. Good riddance to walls of text.
